"The failing Islamic Republic of Iran is not paying large segments of their military, while at the same time killing protesters, even when they are not protesting, at levels not seen before," he wrote on Truth Social.
"It is a humanitarian crisis of epic proportions, and must be stopped, NOW," he added.
It was not immediately clear what new information had spurred the early morning post, but there has been a steady increase in executions since the outbreak of the war on 28 February.
Third of vessels blacklisted by Iran attacked around Hormuz
One-third of the vessels Iran threatened to confiscate for breaching Strait of Hormuz transit rules have already been attacked during the US-Israeli war on Iran, an AFP data analysis found.
Since the war erupted in late February, Tehran has sought to impose its own shipping corridor in a bid to control traffic through the strategic chokepoint, which had been open before the war and governed by international maritime law.
But not all vessels have been passing through this Iranian-approved route in the northern part of the waterway.
On Sunday, the Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA), created by Iran in May to oversee the strait, published a list of 45 vessels on its X account that face future "restrictions" during their next passage, including "fines, seizures or confiscations".
The maritime authority said the measures were in response to previous "violations" of Iranian rules.
Of the 45 vessels on the list, at least 14 have already been damaged in incidents in or around the strait that were confirmed by the International Maritime Organisation.
All of these incidents were classified as attacks by Britain's maritime security agency UKMTO, which does not specify who was responsible.
Almost all took place off Oman's coast, along a route backed by the United States and banned by Iran.
Israel moves to evict UN training centre for Palestinians
Israeli police raided a vocational training centre run by the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) in an occupied east Jerusalem suburb on Tuesday, in a move a far-right fundamentalist minister said aimed to "remove" the body from the site.
The attack follows repeated warnings by UNRWA that Israeli authorities were threatening its Qalandia training centre, located between the east Jerusalem neighbourhood of Kafr Aqab and Qalandia refugee camp.
The centre was established in 1952 and offers vocational training to around 340 Palestinians from the occupied West Bank every year, according to UNRWA.
"Making history! This morning we are starting work to remove UNRWA from Kafr Aqab," national security minister Itamar Ben Gvir posted on his Telegram.
The Jerusalem Governorate, the Palestinian local authority for the region encompassing Qalandia camp, said Israeli forces had raised the Israeli flag in the courtyard of the training centre.
Mohammad Saeed Aslan, from the Popular Committee for Services in Qalandia camp, pointed out Israel seeks "to take control of UNRWA's institutions in general".
The raid on the Qalandia training centre comes a day after representatives from more than 25 diplomatic missions and international organisations visited the site.
Anas al-Sharif and Israel's war on Gaza's journalists
One year after Anas Al-Sharif and four colleagues were killed in Gaza, Suha Shroof reflects on his legacy and the silencing of Palestinian journalists.
The US Navy aircraft carrier the USS Abraham Lincoln will dock in Thailand next week, a Thai official said on Tuesday, following a prolonged deployment for the Iran war and reports of mental health concerns and deteriorating conditions aboard.
The Lincoln, which left the Middle East on Saturday, has not made a port call in more than 200 days, setting a modern-day record for consecutive days at sea, according to Democratic lawmakers. Typically naval deployments are for between six and nine months, but during times of conflict, that can be extended.
The ship, which has roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines aboard, will be in Thailand for "rest and recreation after their long sea journey," the official said, asking not to be named.
The Lincoln left its home port of San Diego in November and was later redirected to the Middle East to support US military operations in the war with Iran.
Two military-focused outlets, Navy Times and Stars and Stripes, this month reported suicide attempts and declining morale on the ship.
Israel threats to expel Gazans over kite-flying 'outrageous'
The United Nations on Tuesday slammed Israel's threat to expel people, notably children, from areas where kites, drones and balloons are launched from in Gaza, lamenting "unacceptable rhetoric" coming from Israeli leaders.
"On the threat of expulsion due to children's kite flying, I hope we can all agree that this is outrageous," UN rights office spokeswoman Ravina Shamdasani told reporters in Geneva.
Israel warned Hamas on Sunday that it would increase its attacks in Gaza if launches of kites, drones and balloons towards Israel continued, after Israeli media reported that four kites were found in communities near the Gaza border on Saturday and one was shot down by the army on Sunday, bringing the total number recovered in recent days to around 10.
The UN spokeswoman highlighted that Israel's recent statement was only the latest in a string of threats.
"We continue to see unacceptable rhetoric coming from the highest level of the Israeli authorities, showing utter contempt for international human rights and humanitarian law, and advocating and inciting violence amounting to atrocity crimes," she said.
The UN spokeswoman stressed that Israel's threat was only the latest in many. [Getty]
US sanctions on Iran are unilateral and Qatar is supportive of mediation efforts to resolve the issue between the two countries, a Qatari foreign ministry spokesperson said on Tuesday.
US to send diplomats back to Middle East embassies
The US State Department is preparing to return diplomats to embassies in the Middle East that were evacuated before and during the war with Iran, the New York Times reported on Tuesday, citing an internal State Department document.
The return of Foreign Service officers and the scaling back of emergency measures at US missions in the region could begin as early as this week, the report said.
Embassies slated to restore higher staffing levels include those in Israel, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, Oman, Iraq and Kuwait, according to the report.
An oil tanker has been struck by an unidentified projectile and disabled about 9 nautical miles northeast of Oman’s Ash Shishah, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations says.
The strike damaged the vessel’s engine room, while its crew are reported safe, UKMTO says in an advisory note, adding the environmental impact isn't immediately known.
From Colombia to Venezuela, Palestine is a litmus test
Since Assad's fall, Israel has operated with few constraints over Syrian airspace. Turkey's growing military presence threatens to change that, writes Paul Iddon.
Asian shares were mostly lower Tuesday after US stocks drifted to a mixed finish ahead of potentially market-moving events later in the week.
Regional benchmarks traded in a narrow range and US futures were nearly unchanged.
Oil prices were little changed after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced fresh sanctions against Iran and warned that countries persisting in doing business with the Islamic Republic would face retaliation.
Tokyo's Nikkei 225 gained 0.4% to 65,811.19 and the Kospi in South Korea fell 0.4% to 6,675.88.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng lost 0.3% to 25,453.19, while the Shanghai Composite index edged 0.1% lower, to 3,878.38.
In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.6% to 9,158.70.
Taiwan's Taiex edged less than 0.1% lower, while the Sensex in India lost 0.3%.
Oil prices saw little change as US treasury secretary announced fresh sanctions. [Getty]
Turkey welcomes US decision to remove Syria from terror list
Turkey on Tuesday welcomed the United States' decision to remove Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, hoping that it would boost efforts to integrate the war-torn country with the world.
"We believe this decision will lend momentum to efforts to strengthen Syria's ties with the international community and to establish lasting security and stability in the country," the foreign ministry said in a statement.
Syria 'shakes off dark stain' with US terror list removal
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa hailed early on Tuesday the United States' removal of his country from the state sponsors of terror list, a major sanctions relief step.
"Today, Syria shakes off a dark stain and tears away a painful chapter of its past to embark on a path of development, reconstruction and rebuilding," Sharaa said in a speech.
Washington's decision on Monday rescinded a decades-old designation that came with severe economic restrictions, marking another step in warming ties between the countries following the 2024 ouster of longtime Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad.
The Treasury Department announced corresponding sanctions relief.
Sharaa expressed his "many thanks to the President of the United States of America, Donald Trump, and to all the friendly and supportive nations that stood by us".
China will 'safeguard own interests' as US sanctions Iran
China said on Tuesday it would safeguard its interests after Washington laid out plans for the "economic asphyxiation" of Beijing's economic partner Iran, issuing penalties on some entities including in China and expanding secondary sanctions threats.
"China has already stated many times that it firmly opposes illegal unilateral sanctions... China will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own rights and interests," foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian told a regular news briefing.
Israel is using Qusra to show Palestinians price of staying
Just two commodity vessels transited the key energy chokepoint of the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, for the lowest daily tally since early May, with both entering the Gulf, shipping data showed.
The figure was also well below the 10-day average of 14, with just one very large gas carrier and one very large crude carrier entering the strait from the Gulf of Oman, according to shiptracker Kpler early on Tuesday.
German GDP growth revised upwards, defying Iran war turmoil
German growth rose faster than previously thought in the second quarter thanks to strong exports, official data showed Tuesday, as Europe's biggest economy defied the turmoil unleashed by the Iran war.
Gross domestic product grew 0.3 percent from April to June compared with the first three months of the year, according to revised data from the statistics office Destatis. A first estimate in July had put growth at 0.2 percent.
Iran promised to retaliate against expanded U.S. sanctions that the Americans said would cut Iran's economic lifeline, with Tehran expressing confidence that major trading partners would resist Washington's pressure campaign.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled the measures on Monday but stopped short of the most punishing sanctions, saying countries that continued trading with Iran risked being forced out of the dollar-based financial system.
After the sanctions were unveiled, Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said, "We are fully prepared for the US sanctions."
He told state television, "Naturally, the enemies intend to launch an economic terrorist attack on us, but we also have our own tools and know how to play the game. Our defense is no longer so defensive; the enemies should wait for an attack."
Neither China nor Russia had "accepted" the US measures, he added, predicting that other countries would resist them.
Pakistan and Iran made 'significant progress' in talks
Pakistan and Iran made "significant progress" in talks that focused on the US-Israeli war on Iran and a path to peace, Pakistan's interior minister said on Tuesday, at the end of a visit to Tehran.
Talks between the two sides focused on measures to prevent further escalation, reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and an expedited termination of the conflict, a statement from the Pakistani military said about the meeting between the country's army chief, Asim Munir, and the Iranian leadership.
The two sides also exchanged views on regional peace and the way to arrive at a negotiated settlement to the dispute, the statement said.
"The Iranian President candidly shared his government's perspective and we had a very constructive exchange on the issues involved," Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who accompanied Munir to Tehran, said in a post on X.

articles.title: Ukraine allies pledge more air defense support despite Russian threats
articles.body:
Ukraine’s allies pledged on Aug. 24 to increase military support and make air defense an urgent priority, saying Russian threats would not deter them as leaders met in Kiev and by video link on the country’s Independence Day.
The Coalition of the Willing meeting was chaired by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Burnham was in Kiev on his first overseas trip since taking office, alongside several European leaders.
In a joint statement, the coalition condemned Russia’s escalating attacks on Ukrainian cities, infrastructure and civilians. Its members pledged to strengthen Ukraine’s air defenses, expand cooperation with its defense industry, share technology and increase sanctions on Russia’s military-industrial sector.
“Despite Russia’s outrageous threats to my country, we will continue our support for Ukraine’s defense,” Burnham said.
He told the meeting that negotiations should begin from the current line of contact and that Ukraine should not be expected to surrender territory Russia had failed to capture on the battlefield.
Macron warned that Moscow was likely to increase provocations against European and NATO countries to deter them from assisting Ukraine.
The European Union separately approved 6.1 billion euros ($7.1 billion) for air and missile defense systems, interceptors, ammunition and radars, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
The funding is part of a 90 billion-euro loan for Ukraine, including 60 billion euros for military needs.
Zelensky said deliveries of Patriot interceptor missiles had fallen sharply despite an increase in Russian ballistic attacks. Ukraine received 675 interceptors in 2023 and 364 in 2025, while 264 were projected for 2026, he said.
Kiev is seeking at least another 300 interceptors for the coming winter.
Britain also authorized defense firm MBDA to release classified information on British components used in the SCALP cruise missile, the French version of Britain’s Storm Shadow. The decision will allow France and Ukraine to proceed with plans to establish local assembly lines in Ukraine.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov accused London of obstructing peace efforts and said Russia would seek to identify and destroy facilities producing the missiles.
Burnham and Zelensky also signed an artificial intelligence partnership giving Britain access to Ukraine’s Avengers battlefield database. The platform uses millions of images gathered by cameras and infrared sensors to train military AI systems.
In return, British universities, researchers and technology companies will provide expertise to support the development of new systems.
The coalition also said it would continue preparations for a multinational force to support Ukraine once a credible ceasefire was in place.

articles.title: Iranian Rial Hits Record Low as the U.S. Unveils New Sanctions
articles.body:
Iran’s currency plummeted in value Monday, hitting a record-low open-market rate of 2.02 million rials to the dollar, amid the White House’s launch of “Operation Economic Outcast,” which aims to force concessions from Iran through isolation and a financial stranglehold.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Sunday that an “economic D-Day” was coming, and he shared a first sense of what that might look like at a press conference the following day.
"D-Day marked a historic campaign with our allies,” Bessent said Monday. “Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe."
The U.S. announced sanctions on more than 60 targets while expanding sanctionable sectors to digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping—which Bessent described as some of the country’s “most vital lifelines.”
The government may also impose secondary sanctions on Iran’s trade partners, Bessent said, adding that those sanctions could roll out in a matter of weeks.
The threat is meant to deter countries from bolstering the country’s waning economy and “collapse every last option for Iran,” Bessent said, describing it as "economic asphyxiation."
Read More: The U.S.-Iran War: By the Numbers
Though Bessent didn’t identify which Iranian partners might be targeted by a new round of sanctions, he did name one financial institution: Bank Melli, the Iranian government-owned bank with branches in about a dozen countries. Bessent said that “every branch” of the bank must be “shuttered and dark” or it will lose access to the U.S. dollar. The Treasury has previously claimed that the bank provides services to entities that support Iran’s nuclear and ballistic programs.
Since the start of its war with Iran on Feb. 28, the Trump Administration has applied both military and economic pressure to achieve its goal of dismantling the nation’s nuclear program.
Bessent’s remarks elaborate on President Donald Trump’s announcement on Aug. 19 that the U.S. would launch “the most crushing economic operation ever mounted” against Iran.
Iran initially dismissed the threat. Its foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, on Sunday called the U.S. “desperate.” And Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told state television on Aug. 22 that Iran would turn against any neighboring Gulf states that yield to the U.S. in what he called an “economic war.”
“Any country that takes part in imposing economic restrictions on us will be regarded as an enemy,” he said.
Given Iran’s sustained control over passage through the Strait of Hormuz, any retaliation could push Brent crude oil above Monday’s closing price of about $92 per barrel or the wartime high of about $120 per barrel.
In a war that has been largely defined by its threat to the global economy, experts wonder whether sanctions against Tehran’s trade allies will further isolate it—and if that will succeed in forcing Iran to capitulate to the demands of the United States.
Could U.S. sanctions force Iran to end the war?
The Trump Administration has argued that in tightening sanctions against Iran, the country will face unprecedented isolation and economic pain.
But Trita Parsi, the executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, tells TIME that the move doesn’t guarantee compliance.
“We really need to keep in mind here that Iran has been under U.S. sanctions for the last 40 years, and we've had several moments in which we have done some sort of a major escalation,” he says. “And each time, it has failed to translate into a policy change from Iran.”
Parsi notes that neither Bessent nor Trump has outlined specific demands for Iran—focusing more on maximum isolation rather than defining clear, achievable diplomatic terms.
Because of this, he argues that Iran is even less likely to succumb to increased pressure.
“What we know of the pattern in the past is that the Iranians will not capitulate—they will escalate,” Parsi says. “This is the same miscalculation Trump made when he thought that the threat of war would cause them to surrender, and instead they prepared themselves for war, and they fought back. And six months later, we're here.”
Further complicating matters is the fact that Iran is meeting with its neighbor, Oman, about regulating passage through the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of the world’s oil formerly passed. Oman’s foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, is visiting Tehran on Tuesday to continue high-level talks on “bilateral and regional issues.”
Controlling the waterway—a pain point for the global economy—has been Iran’s greatest strength in the war. Any agreement could affect Iran’s leverage over the waterway, although Oman has not publicly endorsed Tehran’s broader demands.
Trump last week threatened that the U.S. would target Oman next if it cooperated with Iran on this matter, telling Fox News: “We’ll bomb the s— out of them.” Experts have said, however, that this is an idle threat and that bombing Oman would be a mistake.
Continuing to enforce its blockade on the Strait does, however, come at a cost to Iran. A June analysis from the Foundation for Defense of Democracies estimated that Iran may be incurring economic damages of about $435 million per day while enforcing it.
How is the plummeting value of the rial affecting Iranians?
Ryan Costello, the policy director at the National Iranian American Council, tells TIME that implementing additional sanctions may not achieve the desired result—but will likely hurt Iranians.
“Regrettably, it has had very harsh impacts on ordinary Iranians—pushing millions out of the middle class, which is often seen as an engine for successful democratic change over time,” Costello says. “This currency depreciation has a real cost for ordinary Iranians, making their life ever more unaffordable.”
According to the International Monetary Fund, Iran’s average annual inflation rate is projected to reach 68.9% in 2026. The depreciation of the rial—which was already the world’s least valuable currency before it dipped this week—will strain Iranian citizens who are already struggling to buy groceries and pay for monthly living expenses.
There is a “real risk” of greater global market destabilization the longer the Strait of Hormuz is closed, Costello says.
“Iran's leadership is signaling that it will respond to intensified economic pressure by further restricting energy flows, and it appears to have the capacity to act on their threat,” Costello says.
In addition to its command of the Strait, he explains: "Iran and other aligned forces are demonstrating an ability to strike energy targets with missiles and drones, both in the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. So Iran and/or its allies could target commercial ships, as well as pipelines, ports, refineries, and other critical energy infrastructure."
And there’s a second major risk if the U.S. places sanctions on certain global powers who buy Iranian oil—particularly economic powerhouse China.
“China could take steps to punish the U.S. economy in turn,” Costello explains.
He says that both risks could be “very damaging,” with economic ramifications that span the globe.
Why Trump is escalating economic pressure on Iran
The U.S.-Iran war is nearing its six-month mark, and peace negotiations have effectively stalled.
The memorandum of understanding established in June—which gave the nations 60 days to work out terms for Iran’s nuclear program and renew uninterrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz—expired Aug. 17. It unraveled in July as the U.S. struck hundreds of targets in Iran, and Tehran retaliated against its allies in the region, including Kuwait and Bahrain. But as the U.S. continued to draw down its munitions stockpiles, Iran held steady with its blockade of the Strait.
Now, Trump has changed his tactics.
“This is where the real problem is: He's going back to economic warfare because military warfare didn't work,” Parsi says.
If additional sanctions fail to force Iran to yield to some of Trump’s demands, Parsi says the President may be running out of options.
“The only exit out of this is actually through diplomacy,” he says. “Otherwise, the U.S. is just going to go back and forth between economic and military action.”
One route to relief may come by way of Pakistan, which helped mediate the June ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran. It dispatched a high-level delegation, led by Field Marshal Asim Munir, to Tehran this week to encourage its leadership to work toward a more lasting peace agreement.
But Parsi contends that the stream of threats from the U.S. may make Iran even less likely to reconcile, saying: “This does not end up becoming the end of the conflict. It just ends up becoming another cycle in the escalation spiral.”

articles.title: Two killed, refinery on fire in Russia’s Krasnodar after drone attack
articles.body:
Two killed, refinery on fire in Russia’s Krasnodar after drone attack
Ukraine hits Russia’s Afipsky oil refinery and gas plant in latest attacks targeting energy infrastructure.
A fire broke out at the Afipsky oil refinery in Russia’s Krasnodar region following a drone attack, local authorities have said, while two employees at the Russian-controlled Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant were injured in another Ukrainian drone attack.
At least two people were killed, and two others were injured, due to falling drone debris at the Afipsky railway station, Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said on Tuesday.

The nuclear plant’s management said that the strike occurred near the plant’s hydraulic structures and wounded two maintenance and construction workers. Russian-installed management did not provide details on any damage caused by the attack.
Ukraine has been targeting Russia’s oil refineries and other infrastructure, attempting to undermine Moscow’s war efforts and reduce financial revenue.
Ukraine’s General Staff said its forces struck facilities at Afipsky.
It added that its forces also hit a gas processing plant in Russia’s Astrakhan region overnight.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its forces had struck a cargo vessel carrying goods for the Ukrainian army in the port of Pivdennyi near Odesa, as well as port infrastructure facilities used for unloading military cargo.
The ministry said Russian air defences shot down 148 Ukrainian drones overnight.
Ukraine has ramped up attacks on Russian energy infrastructure in recent months, escalating a fuel crisis in the country.
Ukrainian air strikes in Russia’s Rostov oblast damaged a MiG-29 fighter jet on Monday, Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed Tuesday, in an attack at Millerovo airbase.
Kyiv also claimed strikes on a radio-electronic station targeting a Starlink communication jamming station in Myrnyi in occupied Crimea, a Peresvet-M electronic warfare system in Luhansk oblast, and a Russian military warehouse in Primorsk, Zaporizhia oblast, according to reports from Ukraine’s Kyiv Independent publication.
Amid the continuing attacks, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on Monday that would allow the state to take temporary control of critical infrastructure found to be inadequately protected from attack.
The attacks come after a meeting in Kyiv where Ukraine’s allies pledged to continue supporting the country during the ongoing war.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the assembled leaders in an evening address that he wanted to “raise production” of drones and missiles to wage “more attacks” on Russia, matching its strikes on Ukraine.
The meeting was attended by 30 leaders of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, including British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who called for negotiations with Russia, and French President Emmanuel Macron, who participated remotely and predicted that “NATO countries will be targeted and the provocations will multiply”.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb was also in attendance, urging Ukraine’s allies to help expand its ability to strike deeply inside Russia.
The Kremlin said on Tuesday that Burnham and Stubb belonged to the “party of war”.

articles.title: Open letter on Iranian prisoners draws criticism over its framing of war
articles.body:
Open letter on Iranian prisoners draws criticism over its framing of war
TEHRAN- An open letter signed by a group of Western academics, writers, activists and former and current political prisoners has drawn criticism from other scholars and anti-war activists, who argue that its focus on Iran’s domestic developments risks obscuring the central issue of the conflict: the foreign military assault on the country.
The letter, addressed to what it calls Iran’s “prisoners of conscience,” condemns executions, arbitrary arrests, torture, alleged sham trials and the targeting of ethnic minorities. It describes Iranian political prisoners as being caught “between two blades of a scissors” — one representing the Islamic Republic and the other the United States and Israel.
The signatories call on the Iranian authorities to end executions and release political prisoners, while also calling on Washington and Israel to end what they describe as their “barbaric wars and brutal sanctions.”
The list of signatories includes figures such as Angela Davis, Mumia Abu-Jamal, Judith Butler, Rashid Khalidi, Robin D. G. Kelley, Ruth Wilson Gilmore and Walden Bello, among others.
 
 Yet the letter has prompted a broader debate over whether placing Iran’s political prisoners at the center of the discussion, while the country is under military attack, creates a misleading equivalence between domestic developments and an external war.
Critics question the letter’s political framing
One critic, writing under the name Carlos on X, described the letter as politically problematic despite believing that its signatories included people with long records of opposition to imperialism and political repression.
Noting the participation of figures including Davis, Abu-Jamal, Khalidi, Kelley, Gilmore and Butler, Carlos wrote that these were not people who could simply be dismissed; several had spent their lives in anti-imperialist and Black liberation movements.
But he argued that the letter nevertheless adopted 'a misleading framework.'
Its central metaphor, he wrote, was the image of the Islamic Republic on one side and US-Israeli imperialism on the other, with the Iranian people caught between them. According to Carlos, the framing “inserts a symmetry” between the two sides while failing to adequately distinguish between a state facing an external military attack and the domestic political system governing it.
Carlos also questioned the timing and potential political consequences of the letter. He argued that, regardless of what individual signatories intended, the text could function as part of a broader political narrative used to justify pressure on Iran.
He specifically criticized the letter for invoking allegations including sham trials, systematic torture and the targeting of minorities without providing detailed sourcing in the text. He argued that similar language has historically been used in campaigns preceding regime-change efforts.
His criticism was echoed, in a different form, by Ajamu Baraka, an international human-rights activist and political organizer. Baraka did not reject criticism of Iran itself. Instead, he distinguished between criticizing a government and taking a political position in the context of war.
“No one is above criticism,” Baraka wrote. “Comrades who signed that letter need to understand the difference between criticism & political positioning.”
He argued that the signatories had chosen a political position that, in his view, gave legitimacy to U.S. military violence against Iran.
The reaction from legal scholar Nina Farnia was also critical. Farnia shared material relating to the letter while defending her own position on the conflict. Her broader intervention questioned the decision by progressive voices in the United States and elsewhere to focus publicly on condemning Iran at a moment when, in her view, greater attention should be directed toward opposing the war and sanctions imposed by their own governments.
Historian and scholar Adnan A. Husain similarly questioned the political timing of the letter. In a post responding to the debate, he maintained that publishing an open letter focused on condemning Iran, while the United States and Israel were engaged in military and economic pressure against the country, risked shifting political attention away from opposition to the war.
Husain wrote that the Western left was moving toward public condemnation of Iran “just when” the United States was turning increasingly to economic pressure and political subversion. He argued that activists should instead organize against the war and sanctions imposed by their own government.
David Miller, Political sociologist, producer, and former professor at the University of Bristol said, all signed the disgraceful letter to the Guardian denouncing the Islamic Republic of Iran, the world’s leading anti-imperialist state.
Worse, they compare the Republic with the Zionist/US imperialist aggressor. What we (and they) should be doing is defending the Republic. The Islamic Republic of Iran is not only defending itself, the Palestinians, Lebanon, and the resistance movement. It’s also defending all of humanity and indeed civilization against the depredations of Jewish supremacist imperialism. This is an existential matter for the whole world.
Susan Abulhawa, Palestinian author and activist, has issued a sharp critique of mainstream framing that portrays the US-Israeli confrontation with Iran as a balanced conflict between two equal sides.
In a statement shared on her platform, Abulhawa argues that such framing ignores a "profound asymmetry of power." She describes Iran as a nation crippled by decades of sanctions, now fighting an "existential anti-imperial struggle," while facing a nuclear-armed U.S.-Israeli empire with unlimited military resources, surveillance, and near-total dominance over global political, legal, and information systems.
Abulhawa takes issue with minimizing language in a recent letter, which referred to "current, indiscriminate waves of US-Israeli military assaults." She says that this understates the scale of destruction, citing unprovoked attacks on a school that killed 180 children and teachers, the assassination of Iran's spiritual leader and much of its leadership, and strikes on civilian infrastructure including water systems, farmland, and power grids. She also highlights the downing of Iran Air Flight 655 by the U.S., which killed 290 civilians, and decades of assassinations of Iranian scientists and commanders—all of which went unanswered.
The activist also criticizes the letter for failing to contextualize Iranian arrests of detainees, arguing that while some imprisonments may be wrongful, others involve individuals who confessed to espionage for Mossad or terrorism, including a group that brutally murdered a young Quran reciter. She insists that any fair assessment must engage with Iran's legitimate security concerns.
Abulhawa concludes that the conflict is not a symmetrical confrontation but an anti-imperial struggle against overwhelming imperial force distinction, she says, is crucial for honest analysis.
Questions over the signatories’ motives and the letter’s focus
Without direct statements from each signatory, it would be difficult to establish that they all interpreted the letter in precisely the same way.
The criticism therefore raises a legitimate journalistic question rather than providing a definitive answer: what exactly did each signatory intend to endorse?
That question is particularly relevant because the letter was published during a period of military confrontation. The document gives substantial attention to Iran’s domestic political developments, while the external conflict appears largely as one half of a broader framework of “dual oppression.”
For critics, this framing risks placing the government of a country under attack and the states conducting military operations against it within a single conceptual structure, without sufficiently addressing the different forms of power and responsibility involved.
But the timing and framing matter. A government’s policy inside the country and another state’s decision to wage war against that country are separate questions. They can both be condemned, but they carry different legal, political, and moral implications. Treating them as interchangeable risks obscuring the question of responsibility for the conflict itself.
The debate over the letter therefore goes beyond Iran’s domestic politics. It raises a broader question for international intellectual and human-rights circles: how should activists respond when a country facing external military attack is also accused of serious internal repression?
What remains less clear is whether all those whose names appear beneath the letter share the same interpretation of that argument.
That uncertainty is itself significant. The prominence of the signatories may lend the letter considerable political weight, but a list of names cannot, by itself, establish a uniform political position. Determining what each individual intended to endorse would require direct confirmation from the signatories themselves.
Its critics, however, contend that the document’s framing places the aggressor and the state under attack within an overly symmetrical narrative and risks diverting attention from the central question of the war: who initiated the military action, what legal basis was claimed for it, and who bears responsibility for its consequences?

articles.title: AI startups are reshaping the US defense industrial base
articles.body:
- Defense startups like Hadrian and Castelion are using AI-driven manufacturing to compress production timelines once dominated by legacy prime contractors.
- Missile stockpiles fell sharply during the Iran War, driving urgency behind AI-enabled efforts to accelerate rare earth processing and munitions output.
Procurement bottlenecks, rigid legacy contracts and a rare earth supply chain dominated by China have combined to slow the production of missiles and interceptors just as the Iran War has drained U.S. stockpiles to their lowest levels in years. Dr. Guy Kioni, critical minerals initiative fellow at the Cambridge Middle East and North Africa Forum and CEO of the geostrategy consultancy Missang, argues that artificial intelligence, applied from mineral separation through missile assembly, is the tool now compressing decades of slow, incremental progress into a matter of years, and opening the defense sector to a new generation of startups competing with the primes.
Historically, when gas prices go down, consumption goes up. Emissions go up too; people drive more, and the avenues of commerce accelerate. Consumers and entrepreneurs, alike, plan more and do more. Cheaper goods allow people to be more productive. That same relationship holds true for Artificial Intelligence in American industry, which allows more productive firms to grow, hire, expand and scale. In fact, US firms that have invested in integrating AI into their workflows have since expanded their entry-level headcount by 12%, defying expectations that AI would reduce jobs.
No industry shows this better than the Defense sector, where AI is being paired with government contracts that seek accelerated production. The American defense industry has historically been very slow. There are procurement bottlenecks, with long-running chains of bureaucracy that delay and dull innovation. Legacy manufacturers have become inflexible with long-term repetitive contracts and complex supply chains, often structured to appease Congressional constituents. The process has produced a variety of domestic and international chokepoints.
Another chokepoint sits entirely upstream of the factory floor. China refines close to 90% of the world’s rare earths and roughly 94% of the sintered permanent magnets used in missile guidance and radar systems, and it has shown it will restrict export licenses to US defense suppliers with little warning. AI does not change that concentration of power; it shortens how long it takes to build an alternative to it.
AI is doing similar work upstream, separating the critical chokepoint beneath the factory floor. Isolating individual rare earths from complex ore matrices is a chemical engineering challenge requiring dozens of solvent extraction stages, a craft China has refined across four decades. AI is improving the extent to which Western companies can change the calculus.
Aclara Resources and Argonne National Laboratory are now building an AI digital twin to simulate those stages instead of running them by trial and error, accelerate ramp-up timelines and reduce uncertainty at a planned Louisiana separation plant. A comparable AI-controlled rare-earth separation facility in Saskatchewan is now entering commissioning. Neither has replaced Chinese capacity yet. But it’s the same compression driving the factory floor. This is decades of learning curve compressed into years.
The same compression is happening downstream, where the minerals become missiles, and none of it is speculative. AI’s boost to production, jobs, the economy, and defensive readiness is already occurring. Business development within legacy companies like Raytheon and Boeing has been riddled with delays and procurement stagnation; however, at the startup level, entrepreneurship and accelerated manufacturing using AI have begun to reshape how the defense industry functions.
Many new companies stand out. Three-year-old company Castelion, for example, manufactures hypersonic missiles using AI-automated rapid iteration and vertical integration to build out industrial systems constructed for agility and scale. They joined a separate Pentagon agreement to scale production of the Blackbeard hypersonic missile. Manufacturing company Hadrian is another startup that has impressed the defense sector by creating its own AI model, named Opus, for integration into its ‘factory of the future‘ for defense production.
Hadrian provides automation tools that can be integrated across factories, for example, reducing lead times for production for Anduril Industries by over 50%. Hadrian, founded in 2020, prioritizes flexibility in the manufacturing process, using Opus to automate production on reduced timescales with sudden changes in procurement needs. The company has hit an $8 billion market cap as it rapidly expands production and its workforce, focusing on building parts for naval defense capabilities.
Zone 5 is another company working to rapidly produce low-cost cruise missiles and interceptors. Caracol AM, similarly, applies Large Format Additive Manufacturing (LFAM) and Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) to the defense sector. Both methods are robotic technologies for casting and forging complex and dual-use military components. The company can print parts directly from CAD models using AI, heavily reducing overall lead times.
Under the parallel LCCM program, new agreements and contracts with startups like these will help the Pentagon reach its goal of procuring more than 10,000 low-cost cruise missiles over three years, beginning in 2027. These are just a few examples among many of how AI is used to create real material increases in output.
The ambition is driven by urgency. The Iran War reduced stockpiles of Patriot missiles from 2,200 before the war to fewer than 827. THAAD missiles dropped from 452 to 278. Over 1,000 Tomahawk missiles have been expended since the war began, nearly half of the US’s global inventory. The number is striking considering the US only produced 207 Tomahawk missiles for FY2026. New requests for more will likely not arrive until 2030, after 34 months of production lead time, though a $22.9 billion contract awarded this month aims to ramp annual production past 1,000.
This is why companies that accelerate production are crucial for national security, and it is why AI will show its biggest successes within the defense sector first. Artificial Intelligence has become a tool for increasing productivity by finding efficient new workflows for manufacturing processes, offering substitutive solutions, and accelerating innovation by analyzing and tracking material production. Defense industries have been among the first to showcase these benefits of AI, and increasingly AI has empowered defense startups to receive government contracts in ways never before possible. In the past, they would have been quickly overlooked as incapable or too small, but now AI has advanced the competitive playing field, expanding the number of defense companies and government contracts.
AI is not simply automating the sector. It is one reason startups are now winning contracts once reserved for prime contractors, alongside a deliberate Pentagon shift toward faster, non-traditional procurement. Many economic benefits will stem from the Pentagon’s new strategy. The Defense Department has prioritized contracts that transform industry even amongst legacy companies like Lockheed Martin, which received $53.86 billion for tripling the capacity of PAC-3 MSE interceptors by 2030. They also broke ground on a new facility in Alabama in May of this year, preparing to nearly double production lines for THAAD interceptors. Using AI within the factory will allow Lockheed to produce more at a fraction of the cost while also employing more people to handle the increases in output.
They will undoubtably face heavy competition from startups. That competition, driven in part by the use of AI, should however, result in a more robust, efficient, and productive defense sector, benefiting both national security and the broader American economy.

articles.title: London agreed to provide Ukraine with the blueprints for SCALP missiles for production by Ukraine - media
articles.body:
London agreed to provide Ukraine with the blueprints for SCALP missiles for production by Ukraine - media
Kyiv • UNN
Britain has allowed the blueprints for Scalp components to be handed over to Ukraine for missile production. Italy has withdrawn from military exercises within the coalition.
The UK government has agreed to hand over drawings of British components for the Scalp missile, the French version of the British Storm Shadow cruise missile, which will allow Ukraine to produce this long-range weapon domestically, the BBC reports, writes UNN.
Details
The BBC and Reuters report that on Monday the UK announced it would give Ukraine access to classified technology to begin its own production of Storm Shadow long-range cruise missiles, capable of striking deep inside Russia, and that France had already agreed to license this technology for the European missile.
The UK government, as the BBC points out, is allowing British defence company MBDA to declassify information about its components for the Scalp missile, as Ukraine and France seek to establish assembly lines in Ukraine.
Scalp missiles and their UK-produced version, Storm Shadow, have already been supplied to Ukraine by both the UK and France and used to strike Russian military targets, the publication notes.
In response, the Kremlin, Reuters notes, said that the use of secret British technology would "add fuel to the fire" of deteriorating relations, after warning London last week of "consequences" for supplying drones to Ukraine.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, during his first official visit to Ukraine in office, promised to continue putting pressure on Russia despite Moscow's "outrageous threats." He said the Coalition of the Willing "is doing everything possible," while calling on the US Congress to "step up" economic pressure on Russia.
In a joint declaration following the Coalition of the Willing meeting, the allies, as Euronews notes, condemned the "systematic and intensifying strikes on Ukrainian cities, critical infrastructure and civilians" and promised to strengthen Ukraine's air-defence system, calling this a "matter of the utmost urgency."
The leaders also pledged to share relevant technologies, including through the Coalition for Missile Defence, as Ukraine prepares for another winter of Russian strikes on its cities and energy infrastructure.
Large-scale joint military exercises will take place between October and November, aimed at testing the operational capabilities of the countries that have joined the format and preparing for possible intervention after the hostilities end, French President Emmanuel Macron said while speaking at a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing.
"We have made a decision," Macron explained, stressing that the exercises are intended to demonstrate the Coalition's operational readiness and its ability to act after the cessation of hostilities. The goal, the French president added, is also to strengthen the credibility of the security guarantees offered to Kyiv.
Italy took a position different from that of the others on this point. Rome will not participate in the military exercises announced by Macron. In the evening after the meeting, as Euronews writes, government sources confirmed this, saying that the choice reflects the line repeatedly articulated by Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. Italy supports Ukraine and is part of the Coalition, but does not intend to send its service members to Ukrainian territory.
Italy's decision comes as the government prepares a new package of aid for Ukraine. According to sources in the executive branch, Italy is focusing primarily on hospitals, schools and energy infrastructure, as well as new defensive equipment, including generators and air-defence equipment.
For Macron, as noted, the exercises are becoming an element of a deterrence strategy and future security guarantees. "It is very important to continue demonstrating our determination and our readiness," the French president said.
Italy’s choice, however, the publication writes, introduces an important distinction within the Coalition: Prime Minister Meloni, who joined the summit remotely, confirmed Italy’s support for its partners and the negotiating path. But on the issue of the direct involvement of the Italian armed forces, the position remains unchanged: no participation in ground operations.

articles.title: Air Force ‘Closely Following’ Navy’s New Long-Range Air-to-Air ‘Malice’ Missile
articles.body:
A new Navy missile could fill a long-range air-to-air need for the U.S. Air Force’s fourth-, fifth-, and sixth-generation fighters.
The Navy’s portfolio acquisition executive for munitions posted information on the AIM-424 Long Range Air-to-Air Missile online on Aug. 22, the same day it unveiled the project at the service’s annual Tailhook Symposium in Reno, Nev.
The Raytheon missile is geared for Marine and Naval aviators’ fighter platforms, from the Boeing F/A-18 Super Hornet to the Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II, with a range “in excess of 250 nautical miles.”
“Also known as Malice, the LRAAM directly supports the Department’s contribution to integrated deterrence by increasing range, lethality, and combat effectiveness for Marine and Naval Aviation forces that are defending our fleets, our interests, and our homeland,” according to a Navy statement emailed to media. “Further details regarding specific capabilities and deployment timelines remain classified to protect operational security.”
Malice’s advertised range is well more than that of the Lockheed Martin AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile, said to be beyond 120 miles, and the Raytheon AIM-120D Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, around 100 nautical miles. The Air Force is taking the lead in developing JATM for itself and the Navy.
“With increased range, lethality, and combat effectiveness for naval forces, the AIM-424 delivers a generational leap in long range air-to-air combat capability that can out range any threat,” Phil Jasper, president of Raytheon, said in an email statement.
Malice Data
- Contractor: Raytheon
- Propulsion: Solid-propellant rocket motor
- Length: 13.5 feet
- Diameter: 13.5 inches
- Wingspan: 26.2 inches
- Weight: 1,500 pounds
- Range: In excess of 250 nm
- Warhead: Blast fragmentation
Source: Navy
But while Malice represents a major increase in range over current missile programs, it falls short more ambitious efforts early in development like the Air Force Long Range Weapon, which seeks distances of more than 1,000 nautical miles. The Air Force first revealed plans for the AFLRW in June.
“The Air Force is closely following the progress of the Navy on the AIM-424 Long Range Air-to-Air Missile Program,” an Air Force spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine on Aug. 24. The spokesperson declined to answer additional questions.
The two services often partner on missiles for their aircraft, such as JATM, AMRAAM, and the AIM-9X Sidewinder.
“The Navy and Air Force have different operational requirements, but in areas such as fighter-launched offensive weapons, each can benefit from the other’s technological advances, testing, and development,” said retired Air Force Col. John “JV” Venable, senior resident fellow at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies. “Malice appears to be another example of how parallel efforts can accelerate capability and produce benefits across the Joint Force.”
The Navy has also developed the AIM-174B Gunslinger, which has a range of 150-200 nautical miles, but that missile won’t fit in the internal weapon bays of the F-35 and F-22, limiting its usefulness to the Air Force.
The new Malice missile, on the other hand, is meant to go a wide range of aircraft, including sixth-gen fighters like the Navy’s not-yet-named F/A-XX and the Air Force’s parallel project, the Boeing F-47.
“The long-range missile fight is much like a jousting contest: the fighter with the longer lance has a major advantage,” said Venable, a former F-16 pilot and commander. “Chinese beyond-visual-range missiles are assessed to outrange many current U.S. weapons, potentially giving Chinese fighters the opportunity to shoot first by dozens of miles.”
The Malice missile would “extend U.S. engagement range, improve first-shot opportunities, and help restore our tactical advantage against peer adversaries,” he said.
Beyond the tactical level, Venable noted, having a missile like Malice in the fighter community’s quiver would give commanders greater flexibility in operational planning and offset numerical disparity with a potential peer fight.
“The People’s Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF) already holds a significant advantage in the numbers of fighters it can generate over Taiwan compared with the U.S. and allied forces,” he said. “We need every technological advantage available to offset that numerical disparity.
Roots
Aviation Week reported that Malice has a two-stage design—reminiscent of a decade-old program known as the Long Range Engagement Weapon, developed in the mid-2010s under then-Secretary of Defense Ash Carter.
Flight Global reported at the time the LREW effort was also a two-stage design that would eventually transition to multiple services. The Air Force was known to be working on the weapon while also developing the JATM – both efforts sought to replace the decades-old AMRAAM, which debuted in the mid-1980s.
The JATM is seen as a direct replacement for fighters to carry instead of the AMRAAM. But the LREW’s two-stage design promised a far greater range.

articles.title: Will Iran withdraw from nuclear non-proliferation treaty?
articles.body:
Will Iran withdraw from nuclear non-proliferation treaty?
August 25, 2026
Lawmakers in Iran have once again raised the possibility of leaving the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) as tensions over Tehran's nuclear program and its standoff with the United States continue.
Iranian MP Ghasem Ravanbakhsh said a proposal to withdraw from the landmark treaty had been submitted and was being considered.
Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of the National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, said a withdrawal would be the "best response" to increased US economic pressure.
The idea is not new. Iranian officials and lawmakers have repeatedly raised it during periods of tension with Western governments. However, it remains unclear whether Tehran is actually preparing to leave the treaty or whether the threat itself is the objective.
What would leaving the nuclear treaty mean?
In 1970, Iran ratified the agreement, which is the main international treaty on nuclear non-proliferation.
The NPT has 191 member states and is based on preventing the spread of nuclear weapons, promoting peaceful nuclear cooperation and pursuing nuclear disarmament.
Any member can withdraw if it believes that extraordinary events related to the treaty have put its supreme national interests at risk.
It must give three months' notice to the other members and the UN Security Council and explain its reasons. Leaving the treaty is therefore legally possible.
Behrooz Bayat, a nuclear expert and former consultant to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), told DW that the process would take time.
"A withdrawal would almost certainly be seen internationally as a signal that Iran intends either to keep open the option of developing nuclear weapons or to move toward doing so," Bayat said.
He said such a perception could sharply increase political and economic pressure and potentially raise the risk of further military action.
For that reason, Bayat believes Tehran's repeated threats are more useful as diplomatic leverage than as a policy it actually intends to pursue.
Why withdrawal may not benefit Tehran
Shahin Modarres, an international security analyst and researcher at LUISS University in Rome, told DW that the renewed debate should be seen in the context of stalled negotiations over uranium enrichment and Iran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium.
Iran has about 440 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium that is enriched up to 60% purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90%, according to the IAEA.
Inspectors from the UN's nuclear watchdog were unable to verify the location of much of the material after the June 2025 US and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities.
Iran has already sharply reduced international oversight. In July 2025, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian signed legislation to suspend access for IAEA inspectors into the country until the "security" of its nuclear facilities is guaranteed.
That created what Modarres describes as a potentially more useful position for Tehran than formally withdrawing from the treaty.
"Withdrawal would remove that ambiguity without offering any clear advantage, turning a dispute over compliance into an explicit declaration of intent," the analyst said.
"By remaining formally within the NPT while limiting inspections, Iran can maintain uncertainty about its capabilities and intentions without openly leaving the global non-proliferation system," he added. "Withdrawing would remove much of that uncertainty."
A countdown could increase military risk
Withdrawal could also have security implications for Tehran. Under Article X of the treaty, states must give three months' notice before withdrawing. That period would give Israel, the United States and other governments time to reassess Iran's intentions.
Some analysts argue that governments already concerned about Iran's stockpile of 60%-enriched uranium could interpret a withdrawal as a sign that Tehran was moving closer to a nuclear weapons capability.
Bayat said that makes actual withdrawal considerably less attractive than threatening to do so. He added that leaving the treaty could also "complicate Iran's civilian nuclear cooperation."
Membership in the treaty "provides the broader legal and political framework through which non-nuclear states gain access to peaceful nuclear technology," he said. "Russia remains involved in Iran's civilian nuclear sector, particularly at the Bushehr nuclear power plant."
"Formally withdrawing from the treaty could make future cooperation much more difficult politically and legally, even though existing agreements would need to be assessed separately," added Bayat.
Opposition inside Iran
There is no clear consensus in Iran. Rahman Ghahremanpour, a Tehran-based analyst who has written extensively about Iran's nuclear program, told DW that withdrawing from the treaty has been discussed repeatedly but has never become government policy.
"The issue of leaving the NPT is not new and has been raised many times before," he said. "But right now, there are significant legal and political obstacles, and there is still no full consensus within Iran."
Ghahremanpour said the international community would closely examine any attempt to invoke Article X. He points to the ongoing legal debate over North Korea's withdrawal as an example.
North Korea announced its withdrawal from the NPT in 2003. Although Pyongyang is generally treated internationally as no longer being a party to the treaty, some UN documents note that its formal status remains uncertain.
The treaty itself, however, does not require UN Security Council approval for withdrawal. It requires only that states notify the council.
For Ghahremanpour, the political message is more important than the legal process.
He believes talk of leaving the NPT is mainly aimed at pressuring Washington, and particularly European governments, to make concessions.
Edited by: Keith Walker

articles.title: UK, France approve Storm Shadow/SCALP missile production in Ukraine, Zelensky says
articles.body:
Ukraine has received approval from the U.K. and France to produce long-range Storm Shadow/SCALP missiles, President Volodymyr Zelensky said during a press conference with Estonian President Alar Karis in Kyiv on Aug. 25.
Zelensky said French President Emmanuel Macron had confirmed that restrictions on the SCALP missiles and related licenses would be lifted.
"We will act. I believe this is a strong positive and a strong decision," Zelensky added in a post on Telegram.
The announcement came as Zelensky and Karis met in Kyiv. The Estonian president arrived in Ukraine to mark Independence Day on Aug. 24 and discuss military support, air defense, and broader cooperation.
The decision helps Ukraine move closer to producing the missiles at home. The U.K. has agreed to let European defense company MBDA share classified technical information on British-made parts of SCALP missiles with Ukraine, the U.K. government said on Aug. 24.
The Kremlin criticized the move. Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov called it "fuel on the fire," and said Russia was already gathering information on possible missile production sites in Ukraine.
The SCALP is a long-range cruise missile built jointly by France and the U.K., which calls it the Storm Shadow. It has a range of up to 250 kilometers (155 miles) and is designed for precision strikes on fixed targets, including at night and in bad weather.
Zelensky also said Ukraine expects to receive a timeline within seven to 10 days for further work on Freyja, a joint anti-ballistic missile system project by European and Ukrainian defense companies.
Norway has also confirmed $9 billion in financial support outside the EU framework for Ukraine in 2027, Zelensky said, adding that Oslo wants to help finance the Freyja project.
Ukraine also received confirmation that it will receive several Crotale air defense systems and their VT-1 missiles, as well as AIM missiles and additional missiles for Patriot systems, Zelensky said. The president did not specify which country will provide this assistance.
Karis said Estonia was doing everything it could to help Ukraine receive more air defense systems.
"We cannot produce them ourselves yet, but we are using every diplomatic opportunity so that Russian missiles no longer hit civilians and infrastructure," Karis said.

articles.title: General Atomics Plans ‘Wildfire’ Drone for Pentagon’s Low-Cost MMA Program
articles.body:
General Atomics Aeronautical Systems predicts the new drone it plans to pitch for the military’s “Massed Modular Aircraft” program will exceed many of the military’s requirements for a successor to the MQ-9 Reaper.
Wildfire, as General Atomics has dubbed it, “meets every wish on the [MMA] list and exceeds most of them,” company spokesman C. Mark Brinkley said in a statement, though he declined to specify the drone’s expected capabilities or cost. Aviation Week first reported the company’s plans for Wildfire.
MMA is intended to be a low-cost, attritable drone that could fly in groups if needed and take on some missions now performed by the MQ-9 Reaper, which was also made by General Atomics. The Defense Innovation Unit released a solicitation July 7 asking companies to submit ideas for the new drone concept, which is meant “to execute missions that the MQ-9A performs today.”
The Air Force is partnering with DIU on the MMA effort, which it said “will directly inform the requirements for the MQ-9’s successor.”
DIU’s solicitation called for drones to be able to carry a payload of at least 2,800 pounds—roughly the weight of one Long-Range Anti-Ship Missile, or LRASM—and have an unrefueled combat radius of at least 2,300 nautical miles, while carrying a payload, as well as being able to fly a one-way ferrying flight of at least 8,000 nautical miles.
The Pentagon wants MMA drones to be able to launch weapons, collect intelligence, conduct electronic warfare, or relay communications while staying airborne for long periods. DIU said that is intended to exhaust an enemy and force them to burn through pricey anti-aircraft missiles and other resources.
While General Atomics did not detail what Wildfire—a medium-altitude long endurance drone—will be able to do, Brinkley’s statement hinted at some of the goals the company set out to achieve.
“How do we come out of the box, day one, with a 10,000 nautical mile ferry range?” Brinkley said. “Can we carry four LRASMs? Can we swarm 100 aircraft under semi-autonomous control? Can we fuse all of that data into a highly effective common operating picture? Can we do that at scalable, affordable mass?”
The Air Force has lost dozens of MQ-9 drones since operations against Iran launched in late February. The Washington Post reported earlier in August that about 45 Reapers have been lost, in some cases shot down, during Operation Epic Fury.
In its original solicitation, DIU said that with adversaries increasingly using low-cost antiaircraft capabilities to create layered defenses, the military won’t be able to rely on “exquisite” aircraft with price tags north of $30 million. For that reason, DIU and the Air Force said, the military needs drone capabilities that can weather some losses while still being able to accomplish their missions.
The Air Force and DIU want these new drones to be modular so they can be quickly updated with payloads like full-motion video sensors, so an MMA could carry out some of the MQ-9’s current missions. An Air Force official told reporters earlier in August that the service wants to start awarding contracts by the end of this year.
DIU also wants contractors to be able to flight test a full-scale prototype 21 months after receiving the award and to be able to deliver 20 mission-ready aircraft by fiscal 2031.
Brinkley said General Atomics “can deliver Wildfires years earlier than the current schedule.”
However, Brinkley said, the military has an “immediate, critical ISR gap” that Wildfire would not be able to fill in the short term. General Atomics has options that could serve as an interim bridge, he said, and the company is now discussing those with Pentagon decision-makers.
General Atomics did not reveal any imagery or concept art for Wildfire.

articles.title: ‘Not an isolated incident’: Russian drones stalk Ukraine’s civilians in ‘human safaris’
articles.body:
‘Not an isolated incident’: Russian drones stalk Ukraine’s civilians in ‘human safaris’
The video of a Ukrainian cyclist being targeted and killed by a short-range drone posted – and later deleted – by the Russian military Friday left viewers outraged and shaken. But it’s not the first time that Russian drone operators have been accused of terrorising Ukrainian civilians by deliberately targeting them in “human safaris” denounced as a war crime by an independent UN commission.
First, he freezes, caught off guard. Then the young Ukrainian cyclist begins to backpedal awkwardly, his eyes never leaving the Russian drone that hovers ahead of him. It moves closer, and he swings his leg over the bike and tries to run. He doesn’t make it.
Even though the footage, posted Friday on the official Telegram account of the 3rd Army Corps of the Russian armed forces, cuts off before the moment of impact, the video’s description leaves no doubt of the outcome. The Russian soldiers congratulate themselves on having taken out an “enemy combatant” in the Ukrainian district of Kramatorsk, not far from the front line in the northern Donetsk region.
Two years of ‘human safaris’
But the cyclist was visibly unarmed, wearing civilian clothes and looked like any other young man riding his bike down a country road. Independent Russian media outlet Astra quickly accused the Russian military of trying to pass off an unarmed cyclist as a Ukrainian combatant.
The video spread swiftly across social media as influential accounts, including prominent Kremlin critic and former world chess champion Garry Kasparov, reposted the footage to denounce the Russian military’s apparent cruelty.
Less than 48 hours and hundreds of outraged comments later, the 3rd Army Corps took the video down.
It’s far from the first time that Russian drones laden with explosives and controlled from a distance have targeted civilians in Ukraine’s frontline regions. The Ukrainians have even found a term for these deadly drone hunts – “human safaris”.
“On the one hand, I'm very happy that there is more attention on this,” said Olga Tokariuk, a specialist in Ukraine at the British think-tank Chatham House. “On the other hand, this is not something new. This has been happening for two years. And the impunity that Russia faces for these attacks just means it can continue.”
Watch moreKherson under fire: The reality behind the Russian drone strikes
The “human safari” carried out by Russian drone operators seems to have begun in July 2024 in Kherson, a city on the banks of Dnipro River in the country’s south.
“Kherson in 2024 was the point at which isolated incidents developed into a sustained campaign,” said Will Kingston-Cox, a specialist in Russia and the Ukraine war at the International Team for the Study of Security in Verona. “Initially, small quadcopters followed individuals and vehicles and dropped explosives. Since then, we have seen FPV (first-person view) impact drones expanding the practice in scale, frequency and geography. Documented targets include pedestrians, cyclists, private cars, buses, ambulances and rescue workers.”
In Kherson, Russian forces installed on the opposite bank of the Dnipro can easily use short-range drones to target the population who had either remained in or returned to the city following its recapture by the Ukrainian army at the end of 2022.
‘Those seconds are so precious’
Numerous eye-witness accounts, including several reported by FRANCE 24’s Observers team, describe a climate of constant fear of being targeted and killed by a Russian drone.
Read moreHow Russian drones are terrorising civilians in Ukraine
Tokariuk, who wrote a report on the “human safaris” in 2025, said that people she’d interviewed in Kherson had spoken of being under a state of almost permanent tension.
“Something really striking that they told me was they would only go out there if the weather was bad – because drones cannot really operate in rain or snow or fog,” she said. “And they would also tell me they would drive really fast in their cars, because that maximises your chances of survival if you're hunted by a drone … People wouldn’t use their seatbelts when they're driving, because those seconds are so precious when they see a drone hovering above their car about to hit them, and they need to get out of the car really quickly.”
For its part, the UN’s Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine condemned these “human safaris” as a war crime, for deliberately targeting a civilian population, and a potential crime against humanity, for its possible use as a tool to carry out forcible population transfers.
“They are targeting precisely not only civilians in their day-to-day life, but also hospitals and shops and very basic things that sustain day-to-day life for people,” said Ivan Klyszcz, a specialist in Russia at the Centre of Defence and Security in Tallinn, Estonia. “So there's definitely a pressure on the civilian population, and inevitably this leads to people to relocate. I cannot say that this is part of a larger plan for population transfer – but it is working out that way.”

The UN commission reported that roughly 150 civilians had been killed and hundreds more wounded in Kherson region by short-range drones since the end of 2024.
Veronika Hinman, a specialist in the Ukraine war at the University of Portsmouth who has studied the use of drones in the conflict, said that while she wasn’t convinced the practice could be described as official army tactics, it certainly seemed tolerated by the military brass.
“I've been trying to think whether this could be just an isolated incident, whether we could consider these drone operators as 'bad apples' or rogue soldiers acting independently – or whether, if you look at the company itself that, they are remnants of an informal militia integrated into Russian forces later on,” she said. “But no, it doesn't seem anything like that. It's not an isolated incident.”
Cutting promos
Although Kherson remains ground zero for this grim practice, the fact that Friday’s cyclist was targeted by a drone in the distant Kramatorsk district shows that these “human safaris” have spread beyond the battered city.
Tokariuk said similar attacks had also been reported in Ukraine’s border region of Sumy, as well as in Kharkhiv, which sits across the border from Russia’s Belgorod region.
She maintained it was impossible that the drone operators didn’t know the people they were targeting were civilians.
“They know exactly what they’re doing,” she said. “The operators of these drones, they can see the real-time footage of who the drone is chasing.”
The practice is also likely a macabre way to train Russian troops to pilot the remote-controlled drones, Hinman said.
“Civilians are not protected. They are easy targets because of what they are wearing, as opposed to soldiers on the battlefield,” she said.
It may be that these “human safaris” can also allow Russian officers to made sure that the drone operators under their command won’t be overcome by remorse during combat operations. After all, soldiers who are apparently prepared to target old people leaving their homes and children playing in the street – cases documented by the UN commission – would likely be ready to carry out any other order.
Read moreZelensky calls on allies to cover €27 billion gap for Ukraine’s air defence needs
Hinman said that these videos also served encourage Russian viewers to donate money for the production and purchase of more drones to deploy at the front.
“One of the reasons why they post these on social media, why they make these social media posts, can be to show off what these drones are being used for to the people who fundraise for them,” she said.
By seemingly trying to pass off an unarmed civilian for a hardened Ukrainian soldier, Kingston-Cox said, Friday’s video appeared to have backfired – possibly, he said, explaining why it was later taken down.
“That discrepancy made the video both a propaganda liability and potentially important evidence,” he said. “Operational security concerns cannot be excluded, but reputational and legal containment appears more plausible – particularly because the footage appeared on a channel associated with the army rather than an anonymous pro-war 'miliblogger' (Russian military blogger) account.”
But Tokariuk said she didn’t think the controversy the video had caused would have any real impact on the Russian army’s use of these tactics.
“These drones are cheap to operate – they are flying the distances that they need to,” she said. “In those border regions they use drones because it works. It really keeps civilians in terror. It makes people flee.“
She said the seeming impunity that Russia had enjoyed for more than two years now over its “human safaris” made her worry that other states or actors could start to carry out their own version of the low-cost war crime.
“It is very easy to replicate elsewhere,” she said. “And civilians are completely defenceless against it.”
This article has been adapted from the original in French.

articles.title: Ukraine to Produce French-British Storm Shadow Cruise Missiles Domestically
articles.body:
- Category

Ukraine to Produce French-British Storm Shadow Cruise Missiles Domestically
Ukraine will begin producing Storm Shadow long-range cruise missiles domestically after the United Kingdom approved the transfer of relevant technology. British and French defense companies will also participate in the effort, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said during a visit to Kyiv, according to RBC-Ukraine on August 24.
Burnham said Britain had been the first country to provide Ukraine with long-range weapons in 2023 and that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had since asked London to share Storm Shadow technology to enable Ukraine to develop the capability independently.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Storm Shadow, jointly developed by Britain and France, is an air-launched cruise missile designed for precision strikes against high-value targets at long distances. France operates the missile under the name SCALP-EG.
Burnham said the decision was intended to further strengthen Ukraine’s ability to conduct long-range strikes as Russia continues missile attacks against Ukrainian cities and civilian infrastructure.
According to the British prime minister, Russian leader Vladimir Putin is seeking to prevail through what he described as a campaign of terror involving ballistic missile attacks against Ukrainian civilians.
Burnham said Russia must be prevented from launching missiles by imposing sanctions that disrupt its supply chains and by supporting Ukraine’s long-range strike campaign.
Several hours earlier, Britain had authorized missile manufacturer MBDA to share classified technical information on British-made components incorporated into SCALP missiles.
The authorization allows the Franco-British defense company to provide Ukraine with technical documentation covering UK-origin components used in the missile, paving the way for the establishment of local assembly and production capabilities.
