articles.title: Kremlin rejects idea of "buffer zone" in Donbas, saying region "belongs to Russia"
articles.body:
Kremlin rejects idea of "buffer zone" in Donbas, saying region "belongs to Russia"
Dmitry Peskov, press secretary for Russian ruler Vladimir Putin, has said the Kremlin rejects the proposal to create a "buffer zone" in Donbas as part of a joint Ukraine-US-EU plan, claiming that Ukrainian Donbas, which Russian forces are attempting to seize, "is a Russian region".
Source: Kremlin-aligned news agency Interfax
Quote from Peskov: "In this context, I would nevertheless say that Donbas is the territory of the Russian Federation, a constituent entity of the Russian Federation... And it is hardly possible for any third party to administer the regions of the Russian Federation."
Details: Meanwhile, the Kremlin spokesman claimed that Russia continues to wage the war because it sees no peaceful way to end it. "Russia remains open to peaceful solutions, but in the absence of such solutions, we continue the special military operation [the term Russians use for Russia's war against Ukraine – ed.]," he said.
Peskov once again made the unsubstantiated claim that the Kremlin "not only expects but is also convinced that victory will be achieved", although he added that "this will depend on the current situation".
Background:
- The Times reported that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had said Ukraine, together with the United States and Europe, had developed a number of proposals to end the war in Ukraine. The plan would include a ceasefire, the mutual withdrawal of Russian and Ukrainian troops from the front line and the creation of a buffer zone. "There are several more ideas from the American side, as far as we know. They want to find the right moment to share them. We are waiting for them," Zelenskyy said.
- On 22 August, Putin described Ukraine's proposals for a peaceful settlement as "exotic" and unacceptable to Russia.
- On 24 August, Zelenskyy said in an address to Ukrainians marking the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's independence that "the Russians must be brought to the negotiating table". "There finally must be sanctions that will make them howl. Ukraine must be given everything that will force them to end the war. And this is possible," the head of state said.
- Earlier, Serhii Kyslytsia, First Deputy Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, said Putin does not want talks now and will be even less willing to negotiate once the cold weather arrives because he believes Ukrainians will not be able to survive the coming winter.
- On 14 August, Russia's Defence Ministry posted a photo of attack drones accompanied by a threat to "freeze" Ukraine this winter. The Strategic Communications Directorate of Ukraine's Armed Forces responded by promising to "keep warm by the fire of Russian oil refineries".

articles.title: US asked Ukraine to refrain from striking Moscow during CIA chief's visit, source says
articles.body:
US asked Ukraine to refrain from striking Moscow during CIA chief's visit, source says
Editor's note: The story has been updated with the latest details.
The U.S. asked Ukraine not to strike Moscow and St. Petersburg while CIA Director John Ratcliffe is visiting Russia, a person familiar with the situation told the Kyiv Independent on Aug. 25.
"They don't believe in the strength of (Russian President Vladimir) Putin's air defenses," they said, adding that Kyiv agreed to pause strikes against the cities between Aug. 24 and 26.
A U.S. official confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that Ratcliffe is scheduled to meet senior Russian officials, but it remains unclear what is on the agenda. The Kremlin has not officially commented on the visit.
This marks Ratcliffe's first known official trip to Russia. The CIA director has nevertheless maintained contact with his Russian counterpart, SVR chief Sergei Naryshkin, who has previously signaled readiness to meet the U.S. spy chief.
The Ukrainian side was told that a U.S. delegation would travel to Russia, but was not initially informed that Ratcliffe would be a part of it, a source told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukrainian officials are expected to receive a debrief after the trip, though it is unclear whether the CIA director will travel to Kyiv in person, they said.
Earlier on Aug. 25, the Flightradar24 tracking service reported that a U.S. Air Force C-17 military transport plane departed Riga in the morning and landed at Moscow's Vnukovo Airport at around 10 a.m. local time.
The plane was previously stationed at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland — the base also used by Air Force One and other planes carrying top U.S. officials.
Shortly after the plane landed, Moscow media shared footage of a convoy of cars with U.S. diplomatic license plates driving through the city.
The U.S. and Russia have seen intensified bilateral contacts since U.S. President Donald Trump took office last January and pledged to negotiate a peace settlement in Ukraine.
Despite repeated visits by Trump's peace envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, to Moscow, the negotiations have effectively stalled as both Russia and Ukraine remain far apart on territorial issues.
Both Witkoff and Kushner were expected to make their first visits to Ukraine this week, but the trip was postponed.
A source denied earlier reports that the envoys delayed the trip due to intensified Russian attacks, noting that Trump wanted to keep the diplomats close due to the unresolved standoff with Iran.
Ukraine's top negotiator, Rustem Umerov, spoke by phone with Witkoff on Aug. 23, and the latter promised to eventually travel to Ukraine, they added.
Despite the deadlock in peace talks, Washington and Moscow continue to keep their diplomatic channels open, which on Aug. 11 helped to broker the release of former U.S. Marine Robert Gilman, who had been imprisoned in Russia for four years.
The CIA has previously played a role in prisoner exchanges between Russia and the U.S.

articles.title: New US sanctions put pressure on Iran as petrol queues form
articles.body:
Washington has turned to pulling economic levers six months into a war on Iran that has ground to a stalemate militarily, with peace talks stalled and most traffic through the crucial Strait of Hormuz blocked.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday laid out plans for the "economic asphyxiation" of Iran, saying the "objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime".
Announcing the new sanctions, Bessent said countries that did not support the US economic campaign would "share in the isolation" of Iran, adding Trump was making phone calls to world leaders asking that they halt interactions with Tehran.
The Treasury Department said expanded secondary sanctions would target Iran's digital assets and its technology, gold, aviation and shipping sectors.
It also issued new sanctions against 60 individuals, companies and vessels that allegedly aid Iran in oil revenue generation, weapons procurement and cyber operations.
Iran, however, was dismissive of the threat and predicted "another defeat" for Washington.
"We've been waiting for these plans for a long time, and the government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," said Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh.
Katz vows to keep Israeli troops in Syria during visit
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz made a rare visit to troops in southern Syria on Tuesday, reiterating a pledge to keep forces in the area as long as there were "threats" to his country's security.
The visit comes a week after Israel bombed the disused Abu Duhur base in northwestern Syria, claiming it wanted to prevent Turkish troops deploying to the facility. Ankara has denied any visit to the site.
In southern Syria, Israeli forces have been stationed in a "security zone" since the fall of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
They occupy what was previously a buffer zone patrolled by the United Nations that had separated Israeli and Syrian forces in the Israeli-occupied Golan since 1974.
"There is daily activity here to thwart threats, to eliminate remnants of the old regime, to prevent dangerous consolidation of the new regime," Katz said according to a video statement from his office.
"The message is clear to the president of Syria as well: when you wake up in the morning in your palace in Damascus, look up at Mount Hermon and see the [Israeli forces]-- you know we are here to protect our communities and our border," he added.
"As long as there are threats, the [Israeli forces] will remain here to guarantee our security -- this is what we have done and this is what we intend to continue doing in the future," Katz said.
Israel has carried out hundreds of strikes in Syria since the fall of Assad and made repeated incursions into Syrian territory.
Trump says executions of Iran protesters must stop
US President Donald Trump expressed outrage on Tuesday at the mounting number of executions in Iran of people allegedly involved in mass protests earlier this year before the Middle East war began.
"The failing Islamic Republic of Iran is not paying large segments of their military, while at the same time killing protesters, even when they are not protesting, at levels not seen before," he wrote on Truth Social.
"It is a humanitarian crisis of epic proportions, and must be stopped, NOW," he added.
It was not immediately clear what new information had spurred the early morning post, but there has been a steady increase in executions since the outbreak of the war on February 28.
The joint US-Israeli strikes which kicked off the war came weeks after the violent quelling of mass protests in Iran.
Rallies initially began in late December over outrage at the high cost of living, but rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on January 8 and 9.
Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, but attributed the violence to "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the United States and Israel.
Rights groups based abroad recorded a far higher toll and said the security forces had fired on demonstrators.
Airlines have largely resumed services through parts of the Gulf, but some destinations remain disrupted.
Dubai continues to be one of the most affected destinations, with several European and Asian carriers extending suspensions into October or later.
Multiple Lufthansa Group airlines maintain suspensions to destinations including Dubai and Beirut through late October.
British Airways, Air Canada, Singapore Airlines and Wizz Air have also extended suspensions on a range of Middle East routes. Air France is meanwhile moving towards resumption of its Middle East destinations.
Airlines moving toward resumption
Air France: Beirut flights are suspended until September 1, flights to Riyadh and Dubai suspended until August 25.
Oil down as traders weigh US sanctions threat against Iran
Oil prices slipped for a second day on Tuesday as traders judged the latest US warning of sanctions against Iran to have reduced the risk of renewed military strikes, after six months of war in the Gulf.
The measures appeared softer than analysts had expected, and were accompanied by news of further shuttle diplomacy as a key Pakistani mediator met with the Iranian president on Monday.
The news helped calm oil markets, with prices falling around three percent and the international benchmark Brent back below $90 a barrel.
The main US exchanges rose in early trading, matching earlier gains in Europe, though London slipped back into the red in the afternoon.
Talks to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have remained stalled for weeks, which had pushed oil prices up for most of August -- fuelling inflation fears and unnerving bond investors.
The US said expanded "secondary" sanctions would target Iran's digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping sectors -- but gave no timeline and named no specific countries beyond Iran.
Long queues have formed at petrol stations across Tehran as motorists rush to refuel amid growing concerns over fuel supplies and the impact of Washington’s latest sanctions on Iran.
The developments come as the US intensifies economic pressure on Tehran, while Iranian officials insist the country is prepared to withstand the measures.
Follow our live coverage for the latest updates from Iran, the US and the wider region.

articles.title: Philippines seeking to expand military drone capabilities in modernization push, defense chief says
articles.body:
The Philippines plans to expand its unmanned capabilities, including through the development and acquisition of drones as part of efforts to modernize its military, its defense chief said on Tuesday.
US defense ally the Philippines also plans to acquire additional guided-missile corvettes and other major defense assets to beef up its external defense capabilities, Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro told a budget hearing in the lower house of Congress.
The Philippines has shifted its security focus from internal threats to external security as tensions rise with Beijing in the South China Sea, where confrontations between them over disputed features inside Manila's exclusive economic zone have grown in frequency in recent years.
The armed forces currently operate a fleet of unmanned aerial vehicles that provide intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, Teodoro said.
"As we mature on the cycle, then we can acquire more," Teodoro said in pitching to lawmakers a 6.3% increase in the defense ministry’s budget for 2027, from the 305.5 billion pesos ($4.95 billion) spending plan approved for this year.
Drone expansion is part of a proposed 50 billion pesos ($810.4 million) allocation for the Philippines' modernization program next year, 25% higher than that of the current budget.
Philippines seeking integration for drones
The priority was also developing the systems, connectivity, and operational know-how needed to use drones effectively, Teodoro added.
"More than the personnel, it is the integration into the operation, what do you do with them and how do you use them," he said. Developing secure communications and network capabilities was crucial, he added.
Teodoro declined to identify specific systems under consideration, saying the details were classified and highly sensitive.
"They are very, very sensitive to compromise, particularly with AI," he said, adding that the Philippines was in close contact with several countries with expertise in drone technology.
Yuliia Fediv, Ukraine’s ambassador to the Philippines, told Reuters in June that Kyiv has been in discussions with Manila over drone technology cooperation.
In June, the United States said it has given the Philippine military four solar-powered sea drones to boost its maritime surveillance.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Drones Reach Russia’s ICBM and Military Satellite Launch Hub for First Time
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s Drones Reach Russia’s ICBM and Military Satellite Launch Hub for First Time
Ukrainian drones reached Russia’s northern Arkhangelsk region, home to the strategic Plesetsk military cosmodrome used to launch military satellites and intercontinental ballistic missiles, according to OSINT analysis published by Russian independent media outlet Astra on August 23.
The incident appears to mark the first documented case of Ukrainian drones reaching the Arkhangelsk region, extending Kyiv’s deep-strike reach into Russia’s far north.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian monitoring resource Locator Rossii reported that at least two drones reached the Plesetsk area.
ASTRA analyzed photographs taken by local residents and said smoke could be seen rising in the vicinity of the military spaceport. The images were reportedly taken from Mirny, a closed city established during the Soviet era specifically to support operations at Plesetsk.
The exact target and consequences of the reported drone operation remain unclear.
Astra also geolocated footage published by Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ showing a drone flying above Kargopol in the Arkhangelsk region. The aircraft was traveling in the direction of Plesetsk, located roughly 170 kilometers, or 105 miles, away.
Local residents separately recorded two drones flying through the region and posted footage of the aircraft online.
Temporary flight restrictions were introduced at an airfield near the Plesetsk Cosmodrome because of the potential drone threat, under Russia’s emergency airspace closure procedure known as the Carpet Plan.
Plesetsk is Russia’s principal northern military spaceport and plays a significant role in both its military space program and strategic missile testing.
Russia has repeatedly launched Soyuz-2 and Angara rockets carrying military spacecraft from the facility. The cosmodrome is also being used to deploy Rassvet communications satellites, part of Moscow’s effort to build a domestic satellite internet network comparable to SpaceX’s Starlink.
Russia plans to have 292 Rassvet communications satellites in orbit by the end of 2027, making the program increasingly important for Moscow’s communications infrastructure.
Plesetsk also serves a separate strategic military role as a launch site for Russian intercontinental ballistic missiles.
No confirmed information has yet emerged regarding damage at the cosmodrome or whether Plesetsk was the drones’ intended target.
Russia continues to deploy its “Rassvet” satellite constellation, which is intended to serve as an analogue to Starlink.
However, the project requires regular launches of carrier rockets. The first two groups of Rassvet satellites were launched into orbit using Soyuz-2.1b rockets manufactured by the Progress Rocket Space Centre in Samara.
Production of carrier rockets is one of the key constraints on the deployment of the constellation. The satellites can also be launched from the Plesetsk and Vostochny spaceports in Russia, as well as the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.

articles.title: Russia extends improvised ship defenses to Baltic Fleet
articles.body:
- Multiple Russian Baltic Fleet vessels were observed during exercises fitted with improvised netting and irregular camouflage patterns.
- Russian naval forces have lost multiple warships to Ukrainian drone and unmanned surface vessel attacks in the Black Sea since 2022.
Russia’s Baltic Fleet has fitted several of its warships with improvised netting and irregular camouflage patterns as makeshift protection against drone strikes, according to footage circulating from a recent fleet exercise.
The images show at least three vessels equipped with different combinations of netting, deformation-pattern paint and other visual countermeasures on their bridges, radar housings and weapons systems.
The netting and camouflage now visible on multiple Baltic Fleet vessels are not part of a standardized Russian navy protection program. Similar improvised measures, including cage-like screens, netting and disruptive paint intended to interfere with visual and optical drone targeting, have appeared on Black Sea Fleet and Caspian Flotilla vessels over the past two years, often applied unevenly across different ships within the same fleet.
The measures follow the first confirmed Ukrainian drone strike on a Baltic Fleet installation. Ukrainian drones struck the corvette Boikiy, a Project 20380 vessel, while it sat in a dry dock at the Kronstadt naval base near St. Petersburg on the morning of June 3.
Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, announced the strike and published video of the attack, saying two Baltic Fleet ships were hit; he did not name the second vessel. Pro-Russian military blogger Boris Rozhin confirmed a drone struck the Boikiy’s superstructure, and video circulating on social media showed a fire at Kronstadt following the attack.
Russia’s Defense Ministry did not comment on the reported strikes, and the extent of the damage to the Boikiy has not been confirmed. The Boikiy had spent 2025 escorting tankers from Russia’s so-called shadow fleet through European waters, according to Brovdi.
Russia’s naval forces have lost multiple warships to Ukrainian drone and unmanned surface vessel attacks since 2022, primarily in the Black Sea. The Black Sea Fleet withdrew much of its surface combat force from Crimea’s western ports following repeated strikes by Ukrainian Neptune missiles, Magura-class unmanned surface vessels and aerial drones. The June 3 strike on the Boikiy was the first confirmed Ukrainian drone attack specifically on a Baltic Fleet installation, according to NV.ua, though
The Insider reported the Boikiy was the third Baltic Fleet vessel damaged by any means since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with two missiles including ballistic one; 124 of 150 drones neutralized
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with two missiles including ballistic one; 124 of 150 drones neutralized
Kyiv • UNN
Russia launched two missiles and 150 drones at Ukraine. Air defense destroyed or suppressed 124 unmanned aerial vehicles; hits were recorded at 17 locations.
Russia launched a ballistic missile, another missile and 150 drones at Ukraine overnight; 124 of them were shot down or suppressed, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Tuesday, according to UNN.
Details
According to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, during the night of August 25 (since 18:00 on August 24), the enemy attacked with an Iskander-M ballistic missile from Rostov Oblast, a Kh-31P guided aviation missile from Bryansk Oblast, as well as 150 Shahed-type attack UAVs (including jet-powered ones), Gerbera UAVs and Parody-type decoy drones from the following directions: Orel, Primorsko-Akhtarsk – Russia, the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk, and Hvardiiske – the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 09:00, air defense shot down/suppressed 124 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera UAVs and drones of other types in the north, south and east of the country. Impacts by enemy air attack weapons were recorded at 17 locations, as well as the falling of downed objects (debris) at 7 locations
The attack is ongoing; several enemy UAVs are in the airspace.

articles.title: South Korea pledges to help Trump revive talks with North Korea’s Kim
articles.body:
Advertisement
South Korea pledges to help Trump revive talks with North Korea’s Kim
Trump’s recent olive branch to Kim and criticism of Seoul have raised concerns of a strain on long-standing Asian alliances
2-MIN READ2-MIN
4
South Korea and the US agreed to maintain close coordination on efforts to revive dialogue with North Korea, days after Pyongyang rebuffed President Donald Trump’s overtures and launched a barrage of short-range ballistic missiles.
South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun told US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a phone call late on Monday that Seoul would work to ensure that Trump’s recent messages lead to renewed US-North Korea discussions and peace on the Korean peninsula, Seoul’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Tuesday.
The US State Department issued only a brief statement on the phone call, which comes at a period of tension between the allies. Trump recently announced a scaling back of joint military exercises and praised nuclear-armed North Korea, while saying that Seoul had not helped his efforts to try to denuclearise Iran.
The State Department said Rubio and Cho discussed “a range of issues in the US-ROK Alliance”, referring to South Korea by the initials of its official name, the Republic of Korea.
“The secretary noted the need for the two countries to remain in close coordination on matters that are integral to the alliance,” it added.

articles.title: Could Mecca defence pact be first step to new Middle East order?
articles.body:
Advertisement
Opinion
Could Mecca defence pact be first step to new Middle East order?
As security deal shakes up calculations for the US, China and Russia, a regional order shaped by regional states is no longer unthinkable
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Senior Colonel Zhou Bo (ret) is a senior fellow at the Centre for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University and a China Forum expert. 
The Mecca security pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan stipulates that an armed attack against one shall count as an attack against all three. Yet the real message is directed at the United States: if being an American ally offers no immunity against attack, there is little point in waiting for Washington to honour its security guarantees.
That there has been no official White House statement casts some doubt on whether Donald Trump is really “very happy to see that Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have recently, and finally, signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement”, as the US president wrote on social media. “It shows that the Middle East is coming together and how countries will finally be able to defend themselves in a more meaningful way.”
Superficially, the needs of the three nations are complementary: wealthy Saudi Arabia lacks military capacity, Turkey harbours ambitions across Eurasia and nuclear-armed Pakistan seeks financial support. Their strengths fit neatly together, cemented by a shared Sunni faith.
But it is too early to argue that the Middle East is coming together. The concept of “middle power” may be in vogue after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called for middle power solidarity amid great power rivalry in his landmark Davos address. Yet neither Pakistan nor Turkey, plainly middle powers, are strictly Middle Eastern countries, despite ambitions to extend their influence.
And the major powers will not walk away. America’s role in the Middle East might shrink in the long term but a new regional security architecture is unlikely to be short of its presence. The European Union, for instance, has talked about strategic autonomy for over a decade. The Ukraine conflict, however, exposed the hollowness of that ambition, as European security still fell back on American leadership and Nato’s military umbrella.
Besides, eroding US influence in the region runs counter to Israel’s interests. Even if Washington were inclined to step back, Tel Aviv would go to great lengths to drag it back into the fray and cling tightly to its American backing – notwithstanding the fact that Israel’s killings in Gaza have shifted public opinion across sizeable segments of the US population, including young Jewish communities.

articles.title: Russian military confirms classified satellite launch from Plesetsk
articles.body:
- Russia launched a classified military satellite from Plesetsk on August 24, a day after Ukrainian drones reached the surrounding region.
- Russian officials confirmed the satellite reached orbit but did not disclose its identity or mission.
Russia launched a classified military satellite from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome on August 24, the country’s Ministry of Defense said, a day after Ukrainian drones reached the surrounding Arkhangelsk region in an apparent attempt to disrupt the launch. A Soyuz-2-1b rocket lifted off from Site 43, Pad 3, at 05:40 Moscow time.
Russian officials said the payload, listed only under the generic designation “Kosmos,” reached orbit as planned and that ground stations established telemetry contact with the satellite. The Ministry of Defense did not identify the spacecraft’s mission or specifications.
Ukrainian and Russian monitoring channels reported drones over Arkhangelsk region on August 23, with local officials describing the targets as “strategic facilities.” The Russian monitoring channel Locator Russia said at least two drones reached the vicinity of Plesetsk, and residents in the area filmed footage of drones overhead, according to the Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi. Governor Alexander Tsybulsky of Arkhangelsk region ordered residents to take shelter and said mobile internet service would be suspended, without disclosing the outcome of the attack. Russian authorities said 40 drones were shot down over the region in total.
It was the first reported case of Ukrainian drones reaching Arkhangelsk region, according to Militarnyi. Roscosmos director general Dmitry Bakanov said in April that Ukrainian forces had previously attempted a drone attack on Plesetsk during preparations for a March 25 satellite launch, an attack he said Russian space and air defense units repelled.
Plesetsk is Russia’s primary launch site for military satellites and has also been used to test the Sarmat intercontinental ballistic missile, according to Militarnyi. The site has hosted multiple Soyuz-2 and Angara rocket launches in 2026 carrying military satellites and batches of Rassvet-series communications satellites, built by the Russian company Bureau 1440.
Similar warnings reappeared in mid-August for a period between August 19 and August 30, overlapping with separate restriction notices tied to a presumed Angara-1.2 launch. On August 15, authorities in the Komi Republic announced closures of the Vashka and Zheleznodorozhny rocket-debris impact zones, sites previously used for GLONASS satellite launches on Soyuz rockets, without specifying an exact launch window beyond “the second half of August.” A similar warning followed on August 21 from officials in the Tyumen region regarding a debris impact zone in the Uvatsky district.

articles.title: CIA chief in Moscow for unannounced talks, US media reports
articles.body:
CIA chief in Moscow for unannounced talks, US media reports
- Published
The head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has travelled to Moscow for unannounced talks, the BBC's US news partner CBS has reported.
John Ratcliffe reportedly arrived in the Russian capital earlier on Tuesday. Neither Washington or Moscow have confirmed the nature of the visit or who he was due to meet.
In-person talks between high-level American and Russian officials are rare.
BBC News has contacted the CIA, the White House and Pentagon for comment.
Flight tracking data confirmed a large US military aircraft travelled to Russia from the US via Latvia on Tuesday.
Footage posted on social media showed the C-17 transport plane approaching Moscow's Vnukovo international airport.
It departed Riga airport at 05:50 GMT and appears to have landed at around 07:04 GMT, according to data from FlightRadar24.
Footage on social media also purported to show a diplomatic motorcade travelling through Moscow.
The trip is thought to be Ratcliffe's first trip to Russia as CIA director, although he has maintained contact with his intelligence counterparts in Moscow.
He played a role in negotiations for the release of Russian-American citizen Ksenia Karelina's, who was jailed in Russia for over a year after being accused of providing support to Ukraine.
The CIA was also involved in a 2024 prisoner swap deal with Russia that saw the release of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich, as well as former US marine Paul Whelan and Russian-American journalist Alsu Kurmasheva.
The US has had strained relations with Russia since it launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since then, Russia has been isolated on the world stage and faced international economic sanctions.
Ratcliffe appears to be one of the highest-ranking US officials to visit the country during President Donald Trump's second term.
Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin at a summit in Alaska last year but the meeting did not lead to a breakthrough. Subsequent US-led peace talks between Russia and Ukraine appear to have stalled.

Ukraine has received missiles for Patriot systems but needs more, Zelenskyy says
Ukraine has received missiles for Patriot air defence systems and AIM missiles following recent meetings in the NB8 and Coalition of the Willing formats.

Details: "To be honest, some Patriot missiles have also arrived. I cannot say how many, but some. We need more," Zelenskyy said during a press conference with Estonian President Alar Karis in Kyiv on 25 August. He did not specify which type of missiles Ukraine received.
According to the Ukrainian Defence Ministry, Patriot systems can use three types of missiles: PAC-2, PAC-3 CRI and PAC-3 MSE. PAC-2 missiles are primarily designed to engage aircraft and cruise missiles, while PAC-3 CRI and PAC-3 MSE can intercept ballistic assets.
As the Defence Ministry noted, AIM missiles have been in service with the Ukrainian Armed Forces for several years and are launched both from F-16 fighter jets and from ground-based NASAMS air defence systems. Ukraine uses AIM-9 Sidewinder, AIM-120 AMRAAM and AIM-7 Sparrow missiles to engage aerial assets.
Zelenskyy added that Ukraine had received confirmation that several Crotale air defence systems and missiles for them will be delivered.
Crotale NG is a French short-range surface-to-air missile system designed to engage aerial assets at low and very low altitudes. France has previously supplied Ukraine with two such systems.

articles.title: Chernihiv Oblast hit by 45 Russian attacks as 5 killed, dozens injured across Ukraine in past day
articles.body:
Chernihiv Oblast hit by 45 Russian attacks as 5 killed, dozens injured across Ukraine in past day
Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least five people and injured 99 others over the past day, local authorities said, with Chernihiv Oblast among the hardest hit after Russia launched a wave of strikes following Ukraine’s Independence Day.
Russia launched an Iskander-M ballistic missile, a Kh-31P guided missile, and 150 drones at Ukraine, the Air Force said. As of 9 a.m., air defenses had downed or suppressed 124 drones, while strikes were recorded at 17 locations. The attack was still ongoing at the time of the report.
In Chernihiv Oblast, 38 people were injured as Russian forces carried out 45 attacks across the region, Governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
In the city of Chernihiv, 25 people were injured in a strike on a high-rise residential building. The blast also shattered windows in nearby residential and administrative buildings and damaged more than 20 cars.
Later in the evening, a Russian attack drone struck a building in the center of the city of Mena that houses telecommunications operators, injuring 12 people, including four teenagers. Three people were hospitalized in moderate condition.
"Another absolutely cynical Russian strike — the city center, many people, purely civilian objects all around," Chaus said.
Russian forces also launched waves of Gerbera and Geran-type drones at Koriukivka overnight, striking several local businesses and damaging warehouses, outbuildings, and trucks. A 15-year-old girl was injured.
Russian drones also struck a woodworking enterprise, the Yalivshchyna regional landscape park, and open areas in Chernihiv, while critical infrastructure across the region was also hit, Chaus said.
Elsewhere across Ukraine, Russian attacks continued to cause civilian casualties.
In Kherson Oblast, two people were killed and 23 others, including one child, were injured in Russian attacks over the past day, Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, two people were killed, while one woman was injured in attacks on Zaporizhzhia and the surrounding district, Governor Ivan Fedorov said.
In Kharkiv Oblast, one person was killed and 13 others, including a 13-year-old girl, were injured in Russian attacks, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks injured 15 people, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
Three people were injured in Russian attacks across Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, local authorities said.
In Sumy Oblast, five civilians, including a 14-year-old girl, were injured in Russian attacks, local authorities said.
In Kyiv, one woman was injured after debris from a Russian drone hit a 16-story residential building in the Holosiivskyi district, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. The strike damaged walls and shattered windows on the 14th floor.

articles.title: Ads appear in the Moscow metro promising ‘alternative service’ with no front-line deployment. Recruits still sign standard military contracts.
articles.body:
Ads appear in the Moscow metro promising ‘alternative service’ with no front-line deployment. Recruits still sign standard military contracts.
Advertisements for “alternative civilian service” have begun appearing near Moscow metro stations, the independent Russian news outlet Vot Tak reported, citing a reader who spotted the signs.
The human rights project Get Lost had already reported on August 17 that stands advertising alternative service appeared in the Moscow metro.
Vot Tak published a photo of the advertisement, which describes the service as including a one-time payment of 2.3 million rubles, a 5/2 work schedule, benefits, and exemption from mandatory conscription, and rules out deployment to a combat zone. The position is based in Naro-Fominsk, in the Moscow region.
The advertisements seek communications specialists, telecommunications engineers, IT specialists, and drivers. The organization Zashchitnik.rf placed the stands and ads in the metro; according to Vot Tak, it has actively promoted its services on social media since December 2024, acting as an intermediary for people signing contracts with the Defense Ministry.
A Vot Tak correspondent called the number listed in the brochure, posing as a prospective candidate. A Zashchitnik.rf representative said enrolling in alternative service requires signing a standard military contract. Asked whether that person could later be sent to the front, the representative said, “No, that can’t happen.”
Get Lost has said Russians have previously been lured into signing contracts disguised as alternative service. “If you’re told it’s “alternative service by contract,” “one-year service,” “training near Moscow,” “drones,” “air defense,” “computer work,” “not the front,” or a “3/3 schedule” — and you’re handed a contract to sign, that’s not AGS. […] AGS is never arranged through a contract with the Defense Ministry, a volunteer unit, BARS, or any other military structure,” the project wrote.
Alternative civilian service, known as AGS, is work performed “in the interests of society and the state” in place of mandatory military service. The Russian Constitution guarantees it to people whose beliefs or religion conflict with military service, as well as to some members of indigenous peoples with small populations.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Deep Inside Russia Despite Starlink Limits
articles.body:
Ukraine has carried out a series of strikes using FP-2 attack drones against Russian military targets deep inside Russia, including radar stations and facilities in Rostov Oblast, raising questions over how the drones maintain connectivity in areas where Starlink cannot be used, according to Russian and Western OSINT analysts on Tuesday, Aug. 25.
The Russian Telegram channel Military Informant reported strikes against several radar stations and the Kamensky industrial plant in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, Rostov Oblast.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It also reported that drones targeted Russia’s Millerovo airbase, hitting what appeared to be a decoy Ka-52 helicopter and another MiG-29 aircraft that the channel said was likely also being used as a decoy.
The channel noted that Rostov Oblast is not a coastal region and argued that the strikes could therefore not be explained by Ukrainian drones operating through Starlink connectivity.
“Either Starlink’s operation is gradually spreading deep into Russian territory and the US is giving Ukraine the green light for such strikes, or the Ukrainian Armed Forces are using a similar network of repeaters and controlling their drones through a mesh network,” the channel said.
French OSINT analyst Clément Molin similarly highlighted the significance of the strikes, saying that Ukraine was expanding its use of medium-range drones with video feeds deeper into Russian territory.
Kanye West’s Russia Concerts in Limbo After St. Petersburg Arena Pulls Out
Molin said dozens of Ukrainian strikes in 2026 had targeted Russian air-defense systems, radars and aircraft, with more than 250 such assets reportedly damaged or destroyed this year, including air-defense systems, jammers and radars.
How Ukraine could control drones beyond Starlink coverage
According to Molin, Starlink connectivity allows Ukrainian FP-2 drones to operate across occupied Ukrainian territory, the Black Sea and coastal areas of Russia.
However, he said the recent footage from strikes against Russian airbases and air-defense systems was significant because Starlink reportedly cannot be used at those locations.
Molin suggested that Ukraine could be using a mesh network with repeater drones to maintain communications with the attacking drones over longer distances.
A mesh network would allow drones or other relay devices to pass communications between each other, potentially extending the range at which operators can maintain contact with a drone.
The analysts did not provide evidence confirming that Ukraine is using such a system in these specific attacks.
Strikes could open gaps in Russia’s defenses
Molin said the destruction of Russian radars and air-defense systems could create new vulnerabilities along Russia’s southern border.
He argued that this could eventually allow Ukraine to conduct longer-range strikes against Russian energy infrastructure and industrial facilities in areas including Voronezh, Rostov and Krasnodar.
The strikes could also potentially affect Russian missile systems positioned close to Ukraine, including Iskander and S-400 launchers in Bryansk, Kursk and Belgorod oblasts that are used to attack Ukrainian targets.
The analysts’ assessments remain preliminary, and the precise communications technology used to control the drones in these strikes has not been independently established.

articles.title: 'He's sort of like Hitler' — Trump's ex-Ukraine envoy Kellogg warns Putin won't stop at Donbas
articles.body:
'He's sort of like Hitler' — Trump's ex-Ukraine envoy Kellogg warns Putin won't stop at Donbas
Russia would not end its war against Ukraine even if it captured all of Donbas, former U.S. Special Envoy for Ukraine Keith Kellogg told the Kyiv Independent in an interview conducted on Ukrainian Independence Day.
Kellogg made the comments during his sixth visit to Ukraine and his first since leaving office. He met with President Volodymyr Zelensky and received briefings on the latest war developments.
For Kellogg, the central issue is not how much territory Russia captures, but whether Russian President Vladimir Putin would actually be satisfied with it.
"He doesn't end there. That's who Putin is," Kellogg said, comparing Moscow's territorial demands to Nazi Germany's demands over Czechoslovakia before World War II.
"He's sort of like Adolf Hitler."
Kellogg recalled British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain's agreement with Hitler over the Sudetenland in 1938.
"Adolf Hitler told Chamberlain, 'Well, we only want the Sudetenland,'" he said. "One year after Hitler said that, and Chamberlain came back after Munich and said, 'Peace in our time.'"
"One year from that day when he came back from Munich, we were in World War II. And that's my concern, is that we're going to end up in World War III."
Kellogg's return to Kyiv
Kellogg, a highly decorated retired three-star U.S. Army general, stepped down from his post on Dec. 31, 2025. He has since joined the America First Policy Institute, a Washington think tank.
His return to Kyiv comes at a time when questions about the direction of U.S. policy toward Russia remain central to Ukraine's war effort.
A career military officer whose views on Russia were shaped during the Cold War, Kellogg has long advocated a "peace through strength" approach.
That position made him a trusted figure in Kyiv during his time in the Trump administration. His departure was met with concern in Ukraine over what it could mean for Washington's policy toward Russia and Ukraine.
During his tenure, Kellogg played a central role in several sensitive diplomatic efforts. He led negotiations over the U.S.-Ukraine minerals deal and repeatedly condemned Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities in unusually blunt terms for a Trump envoy.
Now outside the administration, Kellogg remains convinced that Putin could end the war almost immediately if he wanted to.
"Putin could stop the war in five minutes if he wanted," Kellogg said while arguing that the Russian leader's ambitions extend well beyond the territory Russia currently seeks in eastern Ukraine.
That, in Kellogg's view, is why any peace agreement needs to be judged not only by what happens on the battlefield today, but by what Moscow might try to do next.
'Ukraine is Ukrainian'
Kellogg also argued that Ukraine should think about victory as a long-term process rather than simply measuring it by the territory Kyiv controls when the fighting stops.
He pointed to the Soviet occupation of the Baltic states after World War II as an example of how territorial control does not necessarily determine international recognition.
The West never legally recognized the Soviet occupation, he noted, suggesting that Crimea could similarly remain internationally recognized as Ukrainian territory even if Russia continues to control it.
"Is Crimea still Ukraine? It is part of Ukraine," Kellogg said.
"So you have to start thinking five to 10 years down the line. If you look at it tomorrow, is it going to happen tomorrow? No. But is it going to happen, potentially, long-term?"
His argument also reflects his assessment of the Alaska summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Putin.
Kellogg said Putin expected Washington to accept Ukrainian territorial concessions in Donetsk Oblast. Instead, he said, the U.S. position remained that "Ukraine is Ukrainian."
"I really believe this, Putin thought he was coming to that summit with the U.S. guaranteeing that Ukraine would give up (Donbas). That didn't happen," he said.
"In fact, what happened was that there was a lunch left on the table. They got on the airplanes and went home. I think what happened is Putin came in with one set of expectations, and the United States said, clearly, Ukraine is Ukrainian."
One person familiar with the Alaska discussions previously told the Kyiv Independent that Moscow asked Washington to pressure Ukraine to withdraw from Donbas, which includes both Luhansk and Donetsk oblasts.
Later in November, Washington and Russia came up with a 28-point peace plan, which envisioned Ukraine would surrender the entire eastern Donbas region — both Russian-occupied areas and the parts still controlled by Ukrainian troops.
Under the plan, Ukrainian forces would withdraw from these remaining areas, which would then be designated a demilitarized zone.
The Alaska meeting, however, in Kellogg's telling, failed to deliver what Putin had expected from Washington. And that, he argues, is important because Moscow's territorial demands have to be tested against what Russia can actually capture on the battlefield.
'Fight for it'
Kellogg also praised Ukraine's military capabilities and continued Western support, comparing Ukraine's resistance to Britain's fight against Nazi Germany during World War II.
His message was that Ukraine's allies need to be prepared for a long struggle rather than allowing Moscow to dictate the terms of a peace settlement simply because the war has continued for years.
"I have high hopes that Putin is getting frustrated with it," Kellogg said. "As I told President Trump, if Putin wants the rest of Donetsk, then let him fight for it."
"I've got great confidence in Ukrainians that they will do quite well in that regard."
For Kellogg, Russia's battlefield losses are also evidence that Putin's war has not produced the results Moscow expected.
He even suggested that the scale of Russian casualties could create political risks for Putin inside Russia.
"I think he's got a problem. Yeah. The problem is, is he going to fall out of a 73-floor building window because he sacrificed so much?"
Kellogg put Russia's losses at between 1.2 million and 1.4 million dead, while comparing them with the Soviet Union's losses during its war in Afghanistan.
"The Soviet Union lost 18,000 in Afghanistan and left. Putin has not taken Kyiv, he's not taken Kharkiv, he's not taken Odesa, he has not crossed the Dnipro River."
That leads Kellogg to a conclusion that differs sharply from the idea that Putin is steadily winning the war.
"There are a lot of people who have said that Putin is succeeding. I don't think he is. I think he is not succeeding. He is in Ukraine's hands."

articles.title: 'Economic D-Day': How the US is trying to crush Iran's economy
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
'Economic D-Day': How the US is trying to strangle Iran's economy
After almost six months of military stalemate, the US is reverting to economic warfare in its bid to force Iran's surrender.
In what was bombastically marketed as "economic D-Day", Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday announced new sanctions to "asphyxiate" the country and sever its links to the global economy.
Here's what you need to know as one of the most sanctioned countries in the world prepares to face yet more sanctions.
What are the new sanctions?
In what he dubbed "Operation Economic Outcast", Bessent said the Treasury would be imposing a new round of sanctions aimed at foreign companies doing business with Iran.
They target several Iranian industries including shipping, aviation, gold, tech, and cryptocurrency.
The goal is to force countries to cut all business ties with Iran, hermetically sealing it off from the global economy.
The Treasury also announced it would sanction almost 60 Iran-linked companies, people and ships in the United Arab Emirates, China, Singapore and Europe.
"No-one is above this," Bessent told reporters, vowing to go further than ever before to trigger Iran's economic collapse.
"Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system," he said. "The clock just started ticking."
However, he declined to outline a timeframe that companies will need to comply and indicated the administration will pursue "quiet diplomacy" over an aggressive push for compliance.
Wasn't the US already applying "maximum pressure"?
During both Trump's terms in office, the Treasury has pursued a so-called maximum pressure campaign aimed at crippling Iran's economy.
After withdrawing from the nuclear deal in 2018, the US set about not just restoring Obama-era economic sanctions but intensifying them.
This involved expanding secondary sanctions on key Iranian industries, including oil, petrochemicals and financial institutions.
The measures have succeeded in devastating the Iranian economy. The Iranian rial has crumbled, inflation has surged, and poverty levels have spiked.
But the Treasury has also been reluctant to fully enforce existing sanctions – particularly against Chinese institutions - because of their potentially destabilising impact on the world economy.
Bessent himself acknowledged the dangers during the press conference, intimating that the measures had the potential to "blow up the global financial system".
This has enabled Iran to skirt some of the sanctions, using the UAE and Hong Kong as offshore hubs to move money and buy and sell goods.
Why is it introducing new sanctions?
That the Trump administration is returning to economic pressure is an indicator that it no longer sees a military solution to its predicament.
Concerns about munitions stockpiles, souring public opinion, and limited military options have left the White House hesitant to return to open conflict.
The deadlock comes at a particularly sensitive time for Trump. Polls show that public support for the war and his presidency is continuing to erode just a few months ahead of the crucial midterm elections.
Will the sanctions work?
Trump officials have deployed a raft of superlatives to sell the measures, describing them variously as the "toughest sanctions in history" and the "greatest financial offensive ever".
Whether this turns out to be the case will depend on the responses from Iran's major economic partners, in particular China and the UAE.
The two countries are key to keeping Iran's battered economy afloat. Not only are they Iran's largest trading partners but both are crucial in enabling it to bypass existing US sanctions.
The UAE said last week that it was severing all trade and financial ties, depriving Iran of its third-largest export market and a major offshore hub for its shadow economy.
China, the largest buyer of Iranian oil, has responded less favourably. The Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday it opposed the measures and that it would "take all necessary measures" to defend its interests.
"Cooperation between China and Iran has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be interfered with or disrupted," a ministry spokesperson said.
How has Iran responded?
Hopes in Washington that the prospect of further economic pressure would convince Iran to give up its control over the Strait of Hormuz had been dashed even before Bessent's press conference.
Key Iranian officials had brushed off the threats and vowed to retaliate against countries that cooperate with the US.
The country's powerful national security chief Mohsen Rezaei warned that not "even a single drop of oil" would leave the region if the US doubled down on its economic war.
Similar messaging was reiterated on Tuesday by Iran's economy minister Ali Madanizadeh, who claimed the country is "fully prepared" for the sanctions and issued a fresh threat.
"Our defence is no longer so defensive. The enemies should wait for an attack," he said on state TV.
What hopes are there for a diplomatic outcome?
Regional mediators have continued efforts to revive peace talks after the 60-day ceasefire collapsed earlier this month.
Pakistan struck an optimistic note on Monday after high-level discussions in Tehran, which Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said had made "significant progress".
"The Iranian president candidly shared his government's perspective and we had a very constructive exchange on the issues involved," he wrote on X.
Iran has not yet commented on the talks.
Neither Iran nor the US have signalled willingness to return to the negotiating table since the Islamabad memorandum of understanding expired on 17 August.
Both countries have instead doubled down on their demands and threatened to escalate the war if the other does not concede.
The Strait of Hormuz remains the biggest sticking point. Iran is continuing to prevent ships from accessing the Gulf and insists it will retain control over the strategic waterway after the war. The US is demanding Tehran drop its claims over the strait and re-open it to maritime traffic.

articles.title: Philippines to expand military drone fleet as South China Sea tensions rise
articles.body:
Philippines to expand military drone fleet as South China Sea tensions rise
Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro has pitched a 6.3 per cent budget increase to fund the advanced drones and warships
US defence ally the Philippines also planned to acquire additional guided-missile corvettes and other major defence assets to strengthen its external defence capabilities, Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro told a budget hearing in the lower house of Congress.
The armed forces currently operate a fleet of unmanned aerial vehicles that provide intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, Teodoro said.
“As we mature on the cycle, then we can acquire more,” Teodoro said in pitching to lawmakers a 6.3 per cent increase in the defence ministry’s budget for 2027, from the 305.5 billion pesos (US$4.95 billion) spending plan approved for this year.
Drone expansion is part of a proposed 50 billion pesos allocation for the Philippines’ modernisation programme next year, 25 per cent higher than that of the current budget.

articles.title: Lawmakers question U.S. Navy’s handling of Iran deployment strain
articles.body:
- Senate Democrats are calling for an Armed Services Committee hearing on extended U.S. Navy deployments tied to operations against Iran.
- The USS Abraham Lincoln has been at sea more than 250 days, and the USS Gerald R. Ford suffered a fire and plumbing failures during its own extended deployment.
A group of Senate Armed Services Committee Democrats is asking Chairman Roger Wicker to hold a public hearing on extended deployments tied to U.S. military operations against Iran, according to a letter released August 24 by Senators Gary Peters (D-Mich.), Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.).
The letter cites conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, which left San Diego on November 21 and has remained at sea for more than 250 days without a scheduled return date. The carrier’s roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines went more than 200 consecutive days without a port call, according to Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a modern-day record for a U.S. Navy carrier.
Military Times reported August 11 that multiple sailors aboard the Lincoln had attempted to go overboard during the deployment, based on accounts from family members. CNN separately confirmed with U.S. officials that a sailor went overboard on August 3 and was recovered within an hour by a search-and-rescue helicopter, treated aboard ship and transferred for further care. A second overboard incident involving the same strike group occurred last spring, according to a sailor aboard the Lincoln and two U.S. officials who spoke to CNN.
Family members confronted Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao at a town hall in San Diego, with one spouse describing a message from her husband saying he hoped he would not wake up the next morning, according to Military Times and Stars and Stripes reporting cited in the letter.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has disputed the Military Times account, calling it “completely misrepresented.” The Navy has said no service members aboard the Lincoln have died and that the August 3 sailor was quickly and safely recovered.
The senators’ letter also points to the USS Gerald R. Ford, which suffered a laundry-room fire on March 12 that took more than 30 hours to extinguish, injured two sailors and damaged roughly 100 sleeping berths. The Navy initially described the fire as contained and said the ship remained fully operational. Later footage obtained by CNN showed more extensive damage, including burned bunks and exposed wiring in crew living spaces.
The Ford left frontline operations and sailed to Souda Bay, Crete, for repairs, then stopped in Split, Croatia, before returning to sea on April 2. The ship had also experienced recurring failures in its roughly 650-toilet vacuum waste system throughout the deployment. The carrier ultimately spent about 11 months at sea, exceeding the Navy’s typical seven-month deployment target, before returning to Norfolk in May for scheduled maintenance.
Both carriers were redirected from other missions to support Iran operations. The Lincoln had been headed for a routine Indo-Pacific patrol before its diversion to the Middle East in January. The Ford was pulled from a planned deployment to Europe, sent briefly to the Caribbean in connection with operations against Venezuela, and then routed to the Middle East.
“The toll this unauthorized, disastrous war is taking on our troops is unconscionable,” the senators wrote, characterizing the military campaign against Iran as illegal and citing what they described as a pattern of inadequate planning for extended deployments.
The senators asked the Armed Services Committee to examine morale conditions, financial strain on military families, and the Department of War’s plan for ending the extended deployments. They also requested that the department detail how it plans to sustain troops in the region if the campaign continues.
The USS George Washington has since been ordered to relieve the Lincoln, according to a U.S. official cited by CNN. As of the senators’ letter, no public timeline had been given for the Lincoln’s return to San Diego, and Chairman Wicker had not publicly responded to the hearing request.

articles.title: UK’s Burnham plans US trip to lobby Trump on Ukraine Patriot missiles
articles.body:
UK’s Burnham plans US trip to lobby Trump on Ukraine Patriot missiles
Following his first international visit to Kyiv, the new UK leader seeks a multi-nation deal to secure vital interceptors for Ukraine
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he and other European leaders plan to travel to the US next month to lobby President Donald Trump to let Ukraine access some of its Patriot air defence missile stocks ahead of the winter.
“I’m looking forward to going to New York in September,” Burnham said in an interview with Bloomberg in Kyiv on Monday evening, referring to the coming UN General Assembly meeting in New York. It would be his first trip to the US since becoming prime minister.
“I’ve not fully confirmed the details yet but it’s likely I will go, particularly after today’s discussion,” he said. “Leaving today, I’m quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks.”
Burnham’s comments came on his first international visit since becoming premier, after chairing a meeting of Ukraine’s allies for the first time and holding a bilateral meeting with Ukraine’s President, Volodymyr Zelensky.
Zelensky has made repeated pleas to European nations and the US to help Ukraine obtain Patriot missile interceptors and to replenish its stocks in time for winter, when Russia is expected to ramp up attacks on energy infrastructure again. The interceptors are the most potent weapons to shoot down Russian cruise and ballistic missiles.
Burnham said he left feeling “really optimistic” that Ukraine’s current struggles defending against Russian ballistic missile strikes due to its low stockpile of interceptors are “fixable”.

articles.title: Ukraine mapped Russia’s Su-35 down to individual control units—and found 22 firms nobody has sanctioned
articles.body:
Ukraine's military intelligence has named the Russian companies that build the Su-35S fighter jet and singled out those no country has sanctioned, according to the Main Intelligence Directorate of Ukraine's Defense Ministry (HUR). The unsanctioned suppliers make parts as ordinary as wheels and fuel-system units, and one of them helped develop the aircraft. Kyiv wants sanctions efforts synchronized across every link of Russia's military-industrial complex.
The 22 firms no one has sanctioned
HUR identified 79 companies in the Su-35S production chain. Of those, 22 face no sanctions from any country restricting Russia over the war. The agency highlighted three. Rubin Aviation Corporation supplies the aircraft's braking and non-braking wheels. Gidroavtomatika builds the AU46-05 control units inside the fuel system. The Oktava research institute carried out design and development work on the Su-35S itself.
What the rest of the network builds
The 79 firms develop and produce the engines and fuel system, the control, communications, and guidance systems, the electronic warfare suite, and the main aviation missiles the jet carries into the war against Ukraine. HUR set the data out in the "Components in weapons" section of its War&Sanctions portal. The page carries a rotatable 3D model of the aircraft whose parts open onto the firms behind them, alongside directory listings and a profile for each company.
Ukraine mapped Russia’s Su-35 down to individual control units—and found 22 firms nobody has sanctioned
Three sanctions regimes, loosely aligned
The gaps HUR points to exist because the restrictions are not one list. The EU legislates in packages, the US and other G7 states maintain their own designations, and Ukraine issues sanctions by presidential decree, each covering a different set of firms. Kyiv has spent years asking partners to synchronize those lists, and its own designations often run ahead of them. A company can therefore supply a frontline fighter and still trade freely under most of them.
Previously, HUR ran the same exercise on the Su-34, where a third of the production network was still unsanctioned. The same pattern shows up above the component level, with Russia's largest arms conglomerate covered by EU measures while hundreds of its subsidiaries are not, and Western machine tools still sitting inside Russian missile plants.
