articles.title: Trump ignored top-level warnings before launching Iran war: Report
articles.body:
Muhammed Yasin Güngör
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
US President Donald Trump launched the February offensive against Iran despite explicit warnings from his intelligence chief, vice president and senior military advisers that the conflict could trigger a global energy crisis and lead to a more hard-line Iranian leadership, The Wall Street Journal reported.
According to people familiar with pre-war meetings, then-Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard told Trump that killing Iran’s supreme leader would likely “usher in a more hard-line” successor and force the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway through which one-fifth of global oil and gas trade passes.
US Vice President JD Vance also advocated a more “cautious,” negotiation-first approach, arguing that a diplomatic deal would be less costly than a war with “unwieldy consequences.”
While top military officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine, briefed Trump on “decisive” strike options, other officials raised concerns about munitions shortages and risks to an “overstretched force.” Trump reportedly dismissed those concerns, suggesting the military could “handle any problems” as they arose.
The report said Trump was initially pleased with the start of the war and “puffed out his chest” at a Mar-a-Lago fundraiser when informed of the killing of then-Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.
However, as fuel prices soared and the war stalled, regional leaders from Saudi Arabia and Qatar pressed the White House for a diplomatic solution. Internal polling showed nearly 80% of Americans favored an agreement to end the war, prompting Trump to pursue the June interim truce.
Some Republicans also warned Trump about the potential impact of a prolonged war on their chances in the November midterm elections.
The 60-day window for nuclear negotiations ended on Aug. 17 without a final settlement.
The administration has since shifted back to Operation Economic Outcast, a campaign of economic warfare aimed at weakening the Iranian government through a sustained naval blockade and sanctions.

articles.title: Ukraine holds 1st-ever drone parade on 35th Independence Day
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
The Ukrainian capital Kyiv hosted the country’s first-ever parade of aerial, ground and maritime drones Monday as the nation marked its 35th Independence Day, the presidential press service said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine is now able to share technologies developed during the war with Russia to help protect its partners.
“Today we will see Ukrainian might. What we use to protect the lives of our people. What is making this war special right now, and what will allow Ukraine, after this war, to become a true security donor for its partners, its friends, and our Europe and everyone who has helped us,” he said. “Ukraine knows how to be grateful.”
According to the statement, 30 ground robotic systems traveled along Khreshchatyk Street, including TerMIT, Rys, Simba, Ardal, Zmiy and Ratel, which are designed to reduce risks to Ukrainian troops.
Nine Ukrainian unmanned boats, developed and tested in combat during the war, traveled along the Dnipro River.
The Sea Baby, Magura and Sargan platforms conduct reconnaissance and patrol missions, strike maritime targets and launch drones.
Eighteen P1-Sun, Litavr and Sting aerial interceptors, developed to combat Iranian-designed Shahed drones and other types of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), flew over Kyiv, followed by 27 bomber drones, including the Vampire, Lazar and Heavy Shot.
Eight reconnaissance drones, including SHARK and LF-400, also took part.
The parade concluded with seven Morok and Sichen drones designed for long-range strikes.

articles.title: US can still strike Hormuz targets, Hegseth warns as 'Economic D-Day' takes aim at Iran's economy
articles.body:
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Monday that US President Donald Trump's administration was not ruling out using military force against Iran, even as Washington unveiled an "economic D-Day" against Tehran.
"By no means are we foreclosing using kinetic strikes anywhere in the Strait of Hormuz or around Iran," Hegseth told reporters, adding that Iran could not handle the economic pressure being put on it.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the start of "Operation Economic Outcast" on Iran in remarks at a press conference on Monday following earlier threats of an "economic D-Day" against the regime.
"Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," said Bessent.
Bessent described the operation as "a sustained campaign to collapse every last option for Iran," saying that those involved in "any" economic cooperation with Tehran would expose themselves to "the full reach of American power."
'Economic Outcast' to last until Iran 'stands alone,' Bessent said
"Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US Dollar system," he emphasized. "the clock just started ticking."
He further warned against any nation "testing" the resolve of the US government.
"It is now a time for world leaders to make a decision between prosperity and isolation, peace and terror, America and Iran," he declared.
Bessent concluded his remarks by noting that Operation Economic Outcast would continue until Iran "stands alone."
Iran won't have nuclear weapon, State Dept. spox. maintains
Trump is still set on preventing Iran from attaining a nuclear bomb, US State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a Newsmax interview on Monday afternoon.
"The president has been clear that he is going to see the Iranian nuclear weapons threat come to an end," he said, adding that "He will see that objective be completed one way or another."
"Past presidents have simply identified the threat."
"President Trump is taking action to prevent that threat from becoming a reality, the untenable threat of the Iranian regime having a nuclear weapon."

articles.title: US vows 'economic asphyxiation' of Iran with new sanctions
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US vows 'economic asphyxiation' of Iran with new sanctions
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday laid out plans for the "economic asphyxiation" of Iran, expanding Washington's secondary sanctions threats and warning of dire consequences for countries that do not join the campaign.
The announcement comes almost six months into a war on Iran that has ground to a stalemate, with stalled peace talks and Tehran blocking most traffic through the crucial Strait of Hormuz.
Bessent earlier said the US was declaring an "economic D-Day" on Iran, but his announcement named no specific countries beyond Iran and gave no timelines.
"Around the globe, our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone," Bessent told journalists.
"We are going to hold everyone accountable, and this is economic asphyxiation of this regime."
He added that countries not joining US sanctions would "share in the isolation" of Iran, and noted that President Donald Trump was making phone calls to world leaders with requests to stop interactions with Tehran.
The Treasury Department said expanded secondary sanctions would target Iran's digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping sectors.
It also issued new sanctions against 60 individuals, companies and vessels that allegedly aid Iran in oil revenue generation, weapons procurement and cyber operations.
The sanctions hit entities around the world, including in the United Arab Emirates, Hong Kong, China, Singapore and in Europe.
Bessent vowed that any entity "that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system."
Iran had been dismissive of the threat of additional sanctions, and on Monday its economy minister predicted "another defeat" for Washington.
"We've been waiting for these plans for a long time, and the government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," said Ali Madanizadeh.
Decades of sanctions
Iran has weathered decades of crushing international sanctions, and before the war it continued to export millions of barrels of oil, mostly to China, and to evade sanctions through complex international financial networks.
Asked on Monday if Chinese banks would be targeted by the new sanctions, Bessent said "no one is above the reach of US sanctions."
Ali Vaez of the International Crisis Group said Washington was seeking to impose maximum economic pressure through various levers, but that Iran "has faced all of these before."
"While there is little doubt in Washington's ability to impose substantial pain, Tehran believes that it has a high threshold for absorbing it, as well as the potential to respond to financial pressure with military counterpressure," he said.
The US naval blockade of Iran has seen its oil exports via the Strait of Hormuz fall from two million barrels a day pre-war to just 0.4 million by mid-August, according to maritime tracker Kpler.
Speaking to reporters on Monday, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that the pivot to applying economic pressure did not mean that military strikes were off the table.
"Economic pressure, we know, hurts them the most right now," he said. "But by no means are we foreclosing using kinetic strikes anywhere in the Strait of Hormuz or around Iran."
For ordinary Iranians, the standoff is likely to bring only more economic pain after years of rampant inflation, which in December and January fueled massive anti-government protests.
Sarah Hassanbeigi, a 32-year-old pharmacist in Tehran, said: "I don't think people can really take this much longer."
Pakistani delegation
Last week, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, considered a relative moderate, said Tehran should "bring the war to an end now as we are in a position of power."
That followed Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei's appointment of hardliners to key security positions.
On Monday, Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir -- a key mediator in the conflict -- visited Iran and met separately with Iran's president, chief negotiator and the head of its highest national security body.
The meetings took place after Trump spoke last week with Munir, a US source familiar with the matter told AFP earlier on Monday.
Islamabad was a leading mediator in talks that helped secure an April ceasefire that later fell apart. It is also a major trading partner of Iran, possibly opening it up to the threat of the new sanctions.
Oman's foreign minister was due in Iran on Tuesday, as Muscat and Tehran seek a deal on regulating passage through Hormuz.

articles.title: Tehran warns countries supporting US military actions of consequences
articles.body:
Tehran warns countries supporting US military actions of consequences
TEHRAN — Iran warned on Monday that countries allowing the United States or Israel to use their military bases, facilities or equipment for operations against Iran could face consequences, as Tehran hardened its position over the ongoing regional crisis and rejected any attempt to end the conflict on terms dictated by its adversaries.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said Iran’s diplomatic strategy was being adjusted to reflect changing regional and international conditions, while emphasizing that Tehran would continue using bilateral and multilateral channels to defend what it considers its national interests, sovereignty and territorial integrity.
Speaking at his weekly press conference in Tehran, Baqaei said Iran could not rely on diplomatic methods developed under different circumstances and needed to continuously strengthen its diplomatic capabilities. He described the US campaign of economic pressure as “economic warfare” and said Tehran had repeatedly characterized such measures as economic terrorism.
The spokesperson said Washington was using multiple forms of pressure against Iranians because of their insistence on national sovereignty, independence and dignity. He warned that Iran had already issued, and would continue to issue, warnings concerning countries that cooperate with US actions against the Islamic Republic.
Tehran rejects war settlement dictated by aggressor
The Iranian spokesman also sought to clarify President Masoud Pezeshkian’s recent comments that it would be preferable to end the war while Iran was in a position of strength.
Baqaei rejected interpretations that the remarks indicated Tehran was prepared to make concessions to its adversaries. He said Iran had not initiated the conflict and would not permit the war to end on conditions imposed by the party responsible for the aggression.
“We will show no leniency toward the aggressors,” Baqaei said, arguing that Iran had been defending its territorial integrity and national sovereignty. He added that the aggressor should be held accountable.
According to Baqaei, the Iranian leadership had repeatedly made clear that the country would not surrender to coercion or domination. He said the government and all branches of the Iranian state had acted with unity during the 40-day conflict as well as during an earlier 12-day war.
The remarks underscore Tehran’s insistence that any future diplomatic process must take place without what it regards as coercive demands from Washington or its allies.
The spokesman also criticized the United States for what he described as repeated breaches of commitments in previous negotiations, including the 2015 nuclear agreement and other diplomatic understandings. He said Iran had repeatedly responded to what it considered goodwill gestures from Tehran with broken promises.
Warning to countries providing bases
Baqaei issued one of his strongest warnings to countries whose military infrastructure could be used by the United States or Israel in operations against Iran.
Responding to reports concerning American military facilities and aircraft in European countries, he said Tehran had previously made clear its position on Bulgaria and confirmed reports that several US KC-135 refueling aircraft had departed the country.
Baqaei argued that allowing foreign military forces to use national bases and facilities for attacks on Iran could amount to participation in aggression under international law. He said Iran had no dispute with the people of Bulgaria but viewed the use of facilities there in support of US and Israeli military operations as problematic.
He further warned that Iran considered itself entitled to respond against the source of an attack.
“It is Iran’s right to target the source and origin of any act of aggression,” Baqaei said, adding that Tehran would show no leniency in defending the country.
The warning comes amid heightened sensitivity over the role of foreign military bases and logistical facilities in any potential resumption of hostilities.
Strait of Hormuz becomes a key flashpoint
The Strait of Hormuz was another major focus of the briefing, with Baqaei rejecting claims in US media and official circles that the strategic waterway had become fully open to shipping.
He disputed reports citing oil flows ranging from 5 million to 17 million barrels per day and claims of a sharp increase in maritime traffic. Baqaei described the figures as part of what he called a media and psychological campaign, arguing that insecurity created by US and Israeli actions had affected conditions in the region and around the strait since February 28, 2026.
The comments highlight the strategic importance of Hormuz, through which a significant share of global energy supplies normally passes, and signal that Tehran continues to regard security and traffic through the waterway as closely linked to the wider regional conflict.
Baqaei said Oman’s Foreign Minister Badr bin Hamad Al Busaidi, who was scheduled to visit Tehran, would discuss bilateral relations as well as security and shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz. At the same time, he rejected suggestions that the Omani visit was connected to the simultaneous visit by Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir.
Diplomacy continues amid economic pressure
Despite the confrontational rhetoric, Tehran said diplomatic engagement with neighboring countries remained active.
Baqaei described relations with Pakistan as being at their strongest stages and said Munir’s visit was aimed at further expanding bilateral ties. He also pointed to efforts to improve economic relations with Afghanistan, including reducing border and customs barriers.
He said a meeting between Afghan Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Affairs Mullah Baradar and President Pezeshkian had addressed ways of facilitating economic cooperation, adding that measures to remove obstacles to trade had subsequently been placed on the agenda.
Iran is also dealing with the consequences of US economic pressure and damage to its energy infrastructure. Baqaei said the government was taking the necessary measures to meet winter energy requirements, with the Oil Ministry handling technical preparations and the Foreign Ministry engaging with countries capable of supplying energy if needed.
He accused Washington of seeking to undermine Iran’s sovereignty while also damaging the international free-trade system by pressuring other countries to restrict commerce with Tehran. He called such pressure a violation of international relations and the principles of the U.N. Charter.
Tehran maintains regional policy
Baqaei also reaffirmed Iran’s opposition to Israel’s occupation and military presence in the region, describing resistance to what Tehran calls Zionist occupation as a principled element of Iranian foreign policy.
He said Iran’s position was not dependent on which political group or faction governed other Islamic countries and reiterated Tehran’s opposition to what it described as continued Israeli occupation and aggression in Syria.
At the same time, Baqaei denied reports that Iran had received an official invitation to join a proposed trilateral defense arrangement involving Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye. He said regional proposals presented to Tehran so far had centered on dialogue, consultations and collective security rather than formal membership in a new defense bloc.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Putin Talked Greatness for 27 Years—Now Russia is Queuing for Gas
articles.body:

Zelenskyy: Putin Talked Greatness for 27 Years—Now Russia is Queuing for Gas
Ukraine will not surrender its territory to Russia or ease the enormous military cost Moscow is paying for its invasion, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a defiant Independence Day address on August 24.
Zelenskyy rejected the idea that handing over Donbas could quickly end Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, arguing that the Kremlin continues to misjudge both Ukraine’s willingness and its ability to resist.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Putin is stuck in the past. He still looks at an old-style Ukraine—one that will stay silent, swallow it, endure it,” Zelenskyy said.
“That Ukraine exists nowhere anymore, except in his ‘little folders of reports.’ Our state has long been different. Not an observer, but a player. Not a victim, but a fighter.”
The Ukrainian leader said Kyiv would not allow Russia to regain the initiative or convince Ukraine’s partners that territorial concessions could provide a shortcut to peace.
“We will not let them seize the initiative, deceive Europe and the entire world into thinking that they simply need to give up Donbas, and everything will be over soon,” the President said.
Zelenskyy said there were no grounds for trusting such Russian promises and made clear that Ukraine would continue resisting rather than effectively rescuing Moscow from further battlefield losses.
“We have no illusions. We don’t trust them. We are not going to save the Kremlin half a million soldiers,” according to Zelenskyy.
He pointed to Russia’s repeatedly delayed ambitions to capture the entirety of Ukraine’s Donetsk region as evidence that Moscow’s military plans continue to fall short of its own timelines.
“Russia keeps pushing back the dates when they will ‘definitely, any day now, take the entire Donetsk region.’ It will keep pushing those dates back. Ukraine is different, and it does not give away what is its own,” he stated.
Zelenskyy also said Russia was preparing for another wave of mobilization rather than genuinely seeking an end to the war. For Ukraine, he said, the response must be to strengthen its military and ensure frontline troops have the weapons and equipment necessary to maintain the defense.
“We have to strengthen our military, have everything needed to hold our defense. Our warriors must be supplied and equipped with everything so that the replenishment of the enemy army can be turned into fertilizer for our soil.”
Zelenskyy ended his Independence Day address by directly challenging the expectations of Russian leader Vladimir Putin and contrasting Moscow’s original ambitions with the losses Russia has suffered during more than four years of full-scale war.
“Putin hopes that we are tired. But we know that he is mortal. He never understood us. Now he will not have time to. You wanted to take all our Ukraine, all our land; instead, you lost your oil refineries, your fleet, your profits, your entire generation that you sent into the meat grinder. You wanted us erased from the map; now you are absent from the international agenda of the future civilization,” he said.
Zelenskyy also pointed out the image of power the Kremlin has spent decades trying to project.
“For 27 years, the head of Russia has talked about greatness, while Russia is standing in lines for gasoline,” he concluded.
Earlier, reports emerged that fuel availability at Russian gas stations has plunged sharply, with gasoline reportedly available at only 28.1% of stations nationwide as authorities open dozens of antitrust cases against oil companies and independent fuel operators.

articles.title: State-backed hackers targeted EU officials on WhatsApp, document shows
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — Foreign governments have been trying to hack the messaging accounts of high-ranking European Union officials, the bloc’s cyber defense unit said in an internal presentation obtained by POLITICO.
The presentation, given to officials from EU national governments in July, lists “account takeover targeting high-ranking officials” as one of the top threats facing the bloc this year.
The presentation is the first official acknowledgment that EU officials were targeted by cyberattacks through messaging apps, after several national cyber agencies flagged an ongoing campaign linked to Russian threat groups earlier this year. The presentation is also the first reported instance in which an EU authority formally links such attacks to a foreign government.
Advertisement
The officials were the targets of so-called “state-sponsored spearphishing,” the presentation said, a term for state-backed, targeted and bespoke campaigns to get specific people to click on dodgy links or open malicious attachments. Hackers used "social engineering techniques" to trick EU officials, crafting personalized messages that were more likely to get targets to take the bait.
Earlier this year, POLITICO first reported that the European Commission told some of its most senior officials to shut down a Signal group over hacking fears. It came at the same time as a series of warnings by national cyber authorities telling governments to move away from commercial messaging apps like WhatsApp and Signal for official business.
In March, at least five national cyber and intelligence agencies publicly warned about ongoing hacking campaigns on Signal and WhatsApp. Dutch intelligence services specifically pinned this on Russia, and Germany warned that hackers were targeting “high-ranking individuals in politics, the military, and diplomacy, as well as investigative journalists.”
The agencies warned then that hackers were posing as a fake Signal support chatbot to persuade users to share their codes, allowing them to take over an account to read incoming communications and group chats.
EU cybersecurity officials said in the presentation that the bloc's institutions had faced eight "significant incidents" so far this year. One key challenge, they flagged, is that the different EU institutions still use different technical cybersecurity solutions and lack a common solution to exchange sensitive and classified documents.
The European Commission declined to give details on internal security practices in response to POLITICO's questions on the presentation.
WhatsApp and Signal did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

articles.title: Gaza's Sheikh Radwan residents say Israel bombed water station
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israel claims it struck a weapons depot, Gaza's Sheikh Radwan residents say it was a water station
For weeks, Palestinian residents of Sheikh Radwan in northern Gaza City had been waiting for a newly built desalination station to begin supplying water to their homes and displacement shelters.
The facility, which was under construction for about a month and nearing completion, sought to provide water for hundreds of families struggling with severe shortages because of the Israeli genocidal war and destruction.
But several Israeli missiles struck the station on Monday, destroying it before it could become operational, according to residents and eyewitnesses.
The strikes also damaged dozens of tents surrounding the facility and caused further damage to homes already weakened by previous bombardment.
The Israeli public broadcaster Kan claimed that the strike targeted a "Hamas weapons depot" in the area. Palestinian residents, however, have lost another desperately needed water source during Gaza's sweltering summer.
'We were waiting for the water to reach us'
"We were eagerly waiting for the station to start operating. They told us the work was nearly finished and that water would soon reach the area. Then the airstrikes came and destroyed everything," Abu Mohammed, a resident of Sheikh Radwan, told The New Arab.
"We are not asking for the impossible. We just want water to drink and to wash our children," he added.
Abu Mohammed said his family has been forced to store water whenever it becomes available, regardless of how small the quantity.
"In summer, you cannot live without water. Children need to bathe, women need water for cooking and cleaning, and even drinking water now has to be carefully rationed," he described.
Near the destroyed station, Nuha Abu Issa, a mother of three, described how shrapnel damaged her family's tent.
"The tent was hit by shrapnel and parts of it were blown away," she said. "We thought the place where we live would be safer, but even the water station was not spared. Where will we go now? How will we get water?"
"In this heat, the tent becomes an oven. There isn't enough water for drinking, bathing or washing clothes. When we find a water tanker, we wait for hours, and sometimes we return empty-handed," she added.
Because of the Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, obtaining water has become a daily ordeal, beginning with searching for a functioning source, followed by hours of waiting in queues and, finally, returning with quantities that often do not meet their families' needs.
Qusay Ghaleb, another resident, described to TNA how families have had to teach even young children how to ration water.
"We divide the water between drinking, cooking and washing. We cannot use it as we used to," Ghaleb said. "Even the children now know there is water for drinking and water for cleaning, and that every extra cup means the water will run out faster."
He said the destruction of the station had deepened a crisis that residents were already struggling to survive.
"We are living among the rubble of our homes and tents, and now even the water source we were waiting for has been destroyed. Summer waits for no one, and the children cannot bear the thirst," he continued. "When a house is destroyed, you can look for a tent, and when a tent is destroyed, you can try to repair it. But what do you do when you cannot find water? Water is not something you can do without."
On the brink
The destruction of the Sheikh Radwan water station comes as Gaza's wider water infrastructure faces unprecedented collapse due to Israeli attacks.
In a press statement released earlier in August, Al-Mezan Centre for Human Rights said Israeli forces have continued to target vital infrastructure, including water and sanitation facilities and desalination plants, while restrictions on fuel and maintenance supplies have further damaged the territory's ability to produce and distribute water.
According to the centre, Gaza relies on three main water sources: groundwater, seawater desalination plants and water supplied through pipelines operated by Israel's Mekorot water company.
Around 80 per cent of water and sanitation infrastructure and facilities are now located within areas subject to evacuation orders, the centre said.
Its figures include 97 of 121 groundwater desalination plants, 52 of 58 water reservoirs, 302 of 392 water wells and 58 of 70 wastewater pumping stations.
The centre said 91 per cent of households in Gaza suffer from water insecurity, while around 65 per cent of the population receives only between three and five litres of water per person per day for drinking and cooking.
In Gaza City, the gap between available water and actual demand is particularly severe.
Husni Muhanna, spokesperson for the Gaza Municipality, told TNA that the city currently has access to only about 30,000 cubic metres of water per day, while summer demand reaches approximately 100,000 cubic metres.
About 12,000 cubic metres come from the Israeli Mekorot pipeline, another 12,000 from remaining municipal wells, and around 6,000 from private and commercial wells, he said.
Muhanna attributed the shortage to extensive damage to water infrastructure by Israel. "About 85 per cent of Gaza City's central water wells have been destroyed, while more than 150,000 linear metres of main and secondary water distribution networks have been destroyed or bulldozed," he said.
The destruction of the seawater desalination plant in the Sudaniya area has further reduced supplies, he added, warning that remaining facilities are also at risk of shutting down due to shortages of fuel, spare parts, filters, and pipes.
Between 55 and 70 per cent of Gaza City residents may not receive regular water supplies on some days, forcing the municipality to rely on alternative methods to distribute water to affected neighbourhoods.
Struggle for survival
"Water in Gaza is no longer just a basic service; it has become part of the struggle for survival," Political analyst Ahed Ferwana told TNA. "When water facilities are destroyed at a time when the population is already living on scarce quantities, the impact extends beyond the targeted building to the lives of hundreds of thousands of civilians."
He noted that the destruction of the station should be viewed within a wider pattern of damage to wells, water networks, pumping stations and desalination plants, alongside difficulties in bringing in fuel and spare parts.
"Residents are not facing an isolated incident, but rather a cumulative collapse of the water system," he added.
He warned that continued water shortages during the summer could increase health risks, particularly among children, older people and those with illnesses.
The crisis also affects basic hygiene, food preparation, sanitation and efforts to prevent the spread of disease.
The bombing of the Sheikh Radwan station came as Hamas accused Israel of violating the ceasefire agreement and continuing to target civilians and vital infrastructure.
Hamas spokesperson Hazem Qassem described the destruction of the desalination station as "a continuation of the genocide" and "a continuation of drying up all possibilities for life".
He also said that the bombing of displacement camps and the destruction of tents were evidence of what he described as an ongoing displacement policy.
According to Gaza's Government Media Office, Israel has committed thousands of violations of the ceasefire agreement, resulting in the deaths and injuries of thousands of Palestinians.

articles.title: Board of Peace demands Israel comply with Gaza ceasefire, calls for end to kite attacks
articles.body:
The Board of Peace (BoP) has conveyed a message to Hamas in recent days through Egyptian, Qatari, and Turkish mediators, demanding that the terrorist organization halt the launching of kites and all other activity directed at Israel, The Jerusalem Post has learned.
The message was delivered through a recently established monitoring mechanism led by the United States and BoP Director-General Nickolay Mladenov.
“There will be serious consequences for continued violations,” the message warned.
“All militant activity in the Gaza Strip must stop, including the flying of kites. We have conveyed this message directly through the established mechanism,” a BoP official told the Post.
The official stressed that Israel must also comply with the ceasefire agreement, adding that “military action cannot extend beyond responding to genuine and imminent threats.”
The BoP is seeking to calm the situation in Gaza and create the conditions necessary to implement the agreements and begin the process of disarming Hamas.
“We want to get onto a path of ending mutual violations so that we can begin collecting Hamas’s weapons,” the official said. “The sooner we reach that stage, the sooner we can move into the phase in which Hamas is disarmed.”
IDF accelerates efforts to kill October 7 terrorists
Israel has accelerated its efforts in recent weeks to kill terrorists who participated in the October 7 massacre and held hostages.
On Monday, Israel carried out several strikes across the Gaza Strip, targeting five weapons storage facilities and a Hamas launch site.
“The warehouses that were targeted contained rockets, weapons, explosive devices, grenades and additional military equipment,” the IDF and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) said in a joint statement. “The targeted warehouses were established inside mosques and adjacent to humanitarian infrastructure in the Gaza Strip.”
The strikes came after several kites were launched from Gaza into Israel in recent days at the direction of Hamas, reviving memories of the incendiary and explosive kites and balloons the terrorist organization launched toward Israel during the previous decade.
BoP warned of increased IDF attacks if kites persist
Israeli officials warned the BoP on Sunday that Israel would escalate its activity in the Gaza Strip if the launches were not halted within 72 hours, an Israeli official told the Post.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz also warned in a joint statement that if the launches toward Israel were not stopped immediately, “the IDF will act to intensify targeted operations against those responsible for the launches and will evacuate civilians from areas from which kites, drones and balloons are launched.”

articles.title: Israel steps up attacks on Syria hours after top Syrian diplomat meets Mossad chief
articles.body:
Israel steps up attacks on Syria hours after top Syrian diplomat meets Mossad chief
TEHRAN — Before dawn on Monday, six Israeli armored vehicles and an infantry company crossed into western Daraa, sweeping homes in the Syrian village of Ma’ariya under hovering surveillance drones before withdrawing back across the occupied Golan frontier.
Hours later, another Israeli unit moved into southern Quneitra, raiding the village of Sayd al-Hanout after detaining a local shepherd near al-Rafid the day before. The ground advances coincided with a blast near Palmyra’s regional directorate.
The raids unfolded hours after the top diplomat of the Ahmad “al-Jolani” al-Sharaa government, Asaad al-Shaibani, sat across from Mossad Director Roman Gofman in Jordan, according to reports from Axios and AFP.
The U.S.-mediated meeting was advertised as an effort to lower regional temperatures following an August 18 Israeli strike on the Abu al-Duhur airbase in Idlib.
Instead, the rapid sequence of military operations demonstrated the stark reality on the ground: the so-called diplomatic negotiations in Amman have done nothing to halt Israeli troop movements inside Syria.
The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights documented seven Israeli ground incursions across Daraa and Quneitra within a single 24-hour window on Monday.
Local monitors counted over 60 military violations between August 15 and August 21 alone, ranging from land-leveling and surveillance camera installations to makeshift military checkpoints.
Rather than isolated raids, these operations form a continuous campaign to carve out operational freedom deep inside Syrian territory.
Air operations follow the same aggressive logic. The August 18 attack on Abu al-Duhur involved eight separate waves of strikes targeting runways and storage facilities.
Israeli officials claimed the strike pre-empted a Turkish military buildup at the base. Both Ankara and Damascus denied the existence of any such deployment, while U.S. Special Envoy Tom Barrack called the bombing “an unnecessary escalation.”
Yet, days after briefly announcing a pause in contacts over the incident, al-Shaibani traveled to Jordan to discuss a proposed U.S.-supervised special operations room supposedly meant to deconflict Israeli, Turkish, and Syrian military movements.
Since the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s government in December 2024, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has framed the new political reality in Damascus as a strategic opportunity.
Tel Aviv unilaterally voided the 1974 disengagement agreement, seized Mount Hermon, and established forward outposts in the buffer zone.
Roughly 80 percent of subsequent Israeli air strikes have hit Quneitra, Daraa, and Damascus, aiming to keep Syria’s military infrastructure dismantled.
Accommodation has brought the “al-Jolani” al-Sharaa government no security.
In Jordan, the Syrian side reportedly insisted on a full Israeli withdrawal to pre-December 2024 lines and reaffirmed its right to rebuild a national army.
Tel Aviv treats negotiations as a stall tactic to solidify its presence on the ground, while Washington brokers talks without placing boundaries on Israel’s aggressive maneuvers.

articles.title: UK forces to deploy to Jan Mayen for Arctic operation
articles.body:
Royal Marines and RAF personnel will deploy to the remote Norwegian island of Jan Mayen alongside US and Norwegian forces for an Arctic operation combining sensors, command networks and long-range fires.
British forces are preparing to deploy to the Norwegian Arctic island of Jan Mayen alongside personnel from Norway and the United States for an operation designed to integrate surveillance, command-and-control and precision-strike capabilities in the High North.
Operation Atlantic City will run from 26 August to 4 September as part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry enhanced vigilance activity. According to a US Marine Corps news update, Royal Marine Commandos and personnel from RAF LXX Squadron will join Norwegian and American forces on the isolated island, which sits around 1,000 kilometres from mainland Norway and north of the Greenland-Iceland-United Kingdom Gap.
The US Marine Corps says the operation will connect multinational sensors, command-and-control nodes and precision fires into what it describes as a joint “kill web”. In practical terms, the exercise is intended to test how forces from different nations can detect activity, share targeting information and coordinate military effects across a dispersed Arctic operating area. The claims surrounding its ability to deliver rapid targeting and sea denial are those of the US Marine Corps and will be tested during the exercise.
Lieutenant Colonel David Palacio, fires officer for US Marine Corps Forces Europe and Africa, said, as quoted in the news update: “We want to prove the Marine Corps’ role as the contact-layer enabler of lethality for the joint and combined force.”
He added: “By deploying to Jan Mayen, we are ensuring the Alliance can instantly target and deny adversary freedom of maneuver in highly contested maritime terrain.”
The American contribution will include Marines from Marine Corps Forces Europe and Africa and II Marine Expeditionary Force, alongside elements of the 10th Marine Regiment and Marine Air Support Squadron 1. A High Mobility Artillery Rocket System platoon from the New Hampshire Army National Guard’s 3-197th Field Artillery Regiment will provide a precision fires element, while US Air Force Special Operations Command MC-130 and US Air Forces Europe C-130 aircraft will support air mobility and rapid insertion. Elements of the US Navy’s Sixth Fleet and Task Force 68 are also participating.
Norway will contribute personnel from the Royal Norwegian Navy and Norwegian Home Guard. The British contingent consists of RAF personnel and Royal Marines, although the US announcement does not detail the number of UK personnel involved or specify the exact aircraft and Commando Force capabilities being deployed.
Vice Admiral Rune Andersen, Commander of the Norwegian Joint Headquarters, said: “By operating alongside our Allies, we demonstrate that we have both the capability and the will to defend Norwegian territory. This includes the Arctic islands, the High North and our territorial waters.”
Jan Mayen’s position gives the exercise a particular maritime focus. The volcanic Norwegian island lies in the Norwegian Sea to the north of the GIUK Gap, the broad maritime approaches between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom that connect the North Atlantic with northern European waters. Those routes are strategically important for movement between North America and Europe and have long featured in NATO planning for surveillance, reinforcement and anti-submarine operations.
Operation Atlantic City will take place at the same time as naval manoeuvres associated with Northern Viking 26, allowing participating forces to make use of overlapping maritime surveillance and sensing activity. Northern Viking is centred on Iceland and the strategically important sea routes through the GIUK Gap, while Atlantic City pushes elements of the wider Arctic Sentry activity farther north onto Norwegian territory.
Major General Frode Kristoffersen, Deputy Chief of Staff for Operations at Joint Force Command Norfolk, described the wider purpose of the NATO activity, saying: “Arctic Sentry is our way of synchronizing all Arctic activity conducted by Allies to increase Arctic security, gain the most deterrent effect possible from those activities, and make sure that we have increased our common situational awareness in the Arctic.”
The deployment will also test the more mundane but critical challenges of operating from an isolated Arctic location. Forces on Jan Mayen must contend with long supply lines, limited infrastructure, difficult weather and rapidly changing environmental conditions. Moving personnel, sensors and weapons onto the island and sustaining them there is therefore part of the operational problem being exercised alongside targeting and command integration.
For the British contingent, the exercise will provide another opportunity to integrate Royal Marines and RAF personnel with US and Norwegian forces in the High North while NATO develops procedures for operating dispersed forces across the Arctic and the northern approaches to the GIUK Gap.

articles.title: Indian national security adviser holds border talks in China
articles.body:
Indian national security adviser holds border talks in China
Indian National Security Adviser Ajit Doval held talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi on Tuesday on the border issue between the two countries and improving relations.
”We are meeting in keeping with the guidance of our leaders, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping, who have given clear and positive direction to our relationship, both at the highest and working levels,” Doval said in his remarks, reports said. “I am happy that, over the past year, our relationship has been steadily returning to normalcy.”
Doval noted that the talks are “particularly important against the backdrop of the BRICS Summit.” The summit will be held in New Delhi next month and Chinese President Xi Jinping will reportedly attend.
The two officials are the designated special representatives for the border talks mechanism, which was established in 2003. It is the main channel for negotiations between the two countries on the border issue and communication on issues of mutual interest.
Doval, who is on a two-day visit to China, met with Chinese Vice President Han Zheng on Monday and discussed ways to strengthen peace in the border areas and improve economic, political, and multilateral relations, the Indian Embassy said in an X post.
National Security Advisor Ajit Doval held the 25th round of Special Representatives’ talks on the India-China boundary question with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing.
During his visit, NSA Doval also met Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, with discussions focusing on… pic.twitter.com/QyEcnOaYN3
Ahead of the talks, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar reiterated that “peace and tranquility” along the border areas are a prerequisite for good relations with China.
Relations between the two nuclear-armed neighbors froze after a skirmish between their troops in the Ladakh region of their common Himalayan border in 2020, which left 20 Indian soldiers and at least four Chinese soldiers dead.
The two countries have been rapidly normalizing relations recently, with the resumption of direct flights and updates to the visa regime. India has started allowing Chinese investments into critical sectors of its economy. Border trade, which once connected remote Himalayan communities to the Silk Route, was also resumed earlier this month.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to attend the BRICS summit in New Delhi next month with a 400-strong delegation, Reuters reported, citing three unnamed sources.
Xi’s participation in the summit, which Russian President Vladimir Putin will also attend, has not been officially confirmed yet. India, which holds the rotating chair of the BRICS group, has engaged in intense diplomacy ahead of the summit.

articles.title: From Colombia to Venezuela, Palestine is a global litmus test
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
From Colombia to Venezuela, Palestine is a global litmus test
This month, Venezuela revived consular services with Israel after severing diplomatic relations 17 years ago, while Colombia went beyond, recognising Israel’s sovereignty over the Syrian Golan Heights it occupied in 1967 and annexed in 1981. Both moves should be read as declarations of ideological alignment.
Venezuela has not yet restored full diplomatic relations, which the late Hugo Chávez severed in 2009 during Israel’s war on Gaza. The recent channel grew out of Israeli assistance following Venezuela’s earthquake. Yet Israel’s foreign minister immediately celebrated it as a diplomatic success.
Colombia’s decision is more obscene. Until Bogotá’s announcement, only Donald Trump’s United States had recognised Israeli sovereignty over the territory. Gustavo Petro had broken relations with Israel in 2024 over the Gaza genocide. However, only days after the right-wing Abelardo de la Espriella took office, his government restored ties and security cooperation with Israel and recognised Israel’s Golan annexation claim.
His incoming foreign minister had already met Gideon Saar in Washington, where they agreed to appoint ambassadors, eliminate visa requirements and move Colombia’s embassy to Jerusalem. De la Espriella had called for Colombia to acquire advanced weapons, drones and technology from Israel and the United States.
David and Goliath
We have just watched the same play in Slovenia. A centre-left government recognised Palestine, sanctioned Benjamin Netanyahu and two far-right Israeli ministers, banned imports of settlements and imposed an arms embargo. When Janez Janša’s conservative government arrived, it scrapped those measures, removed the Palestinian flag from a government building and reopened the door to Israel.
This shift in domestic power in three states—two in Latin America and one in Europe—produced an immediate policy shift towards Palestine. This is hardly a coincidence. Palestine is a global political litmus test.
Whenever the left is rising, the Palestinian flag is rarely far away. It appears at a small anti-racist protest in an American town, at campaigns challenging the power of money and lobbies in congressional races, and among the progressive ultras of Celtic, who have repeatedly defied their club and UEFA to turn the stands green, white, red and black.
It flew in Tahrir Square, where solidarity with the Palestinian Intifada had helped educate generations of Egyptian activists long before the 2011 revolution.
The flag appears because Palestine condenses the central questions confronting every emancipatory movement. Who is the underdog resisting the powers that be? Who is the little David fighting the giant Goliath? Who is entitled to control the land and decide who lives and who dies?
Any person or political movement struggling to change society with a progressive vision starts drawing parallels with other struggles over similar causes elsewhere and begins to understand how they are connected.
Is it a coincidence that Egyptian striking workers on the eve of the revolution accused the riot police of behaving like Israelis when they suspended by force their sit-in around the parliament? Is it a coincidence that Greta Thunberg began fighting against climate change only to swiftly connect the dots and sail to Gaza?
The reverse pattern is equally visible. When reaction, conservatism and fascism advance, Israel’s flag often follows.
Far-right and Israel
Israeli flags have appeared at Tommy Robinson’s anti-migration mobilisations in Britain, including a 2024 rally where the crowd booed a Palestinian flag. For Germany’s AfD and Europe’s far right—certainly some of the worst antisemites on the planet—support for Israel runs high because the admiration is for walls, militarised borders, demographic engineering, and a state organised around ethnic supremacy.
American white nationalist Richard Spencer made the logic explicit when he called himself a “white Zionist”, presenting Israel as a model for the white ethnostate he desired. The far right sees no contradiction between its hatred toward Jews at home and support for Israel. The latter offers a worldview which embodies the far right’s wildest dreams: minorities separated, migrants expelled, and each population confined to its supposed place.
Latin America has seen first-hand this worldview in action. During the Cold War, Israel armed and assisted right-wing regimes fighting revolutionary dissent, from Somoza’s Nicaragua to the Guatemalan military during its counterinsurgency war. It developed lasting security relationships with governments and armed forces in Colombia, Argentina, and elsewhere.
When the US faced legal constraints, Israel stepped in to supply weapons, training and intelligence to its allies. Such a partnership was natural. Israel and the juntas shared a view of popular movements as enemies to be surveilled, displaced or eliminated.
The same logic is at play today. Washington reasserts its domination over Caracas, and a government born from US intervention opens a channel with Israel. A Colombian administration eager to restore intimacy with Trump restores relations with Israel and endorses Trump’s Golan decree.
Janša, another Trump admirer, takes Slovenia to the right and begins dismantling its Palestine policy. In each case, alignment with the United States carries an Israeli entrance fee.
This is why Palestine is more than just a local conflict in the Middle East. A country at the far end of the world that wishes to identify with US imperial power is expected to make peace with Zionism. It buys Israeli weapons, repeats Israeli security narratives, and treats Palestinian rights as disposable. In so many ways, Israel is the quickest and most important gateway into the reactionary club.
Victories for progressive forces are therefore essential to keeping Israel isolated and making its leaders pay a political price for occupation, apartheid and genocide. Every election that defeats the far right, every successful anti-racist mobilisation and every workplace or university that adopts boycott and divestment helps keep Palestine visible.
Latin America shows what happens when power shifts to the right. But power shifts because people actively push it. Palestine remains the flag that tells us who is pushing, in which direction, and towards what kind of world.
Hossam el-Hamalawy is an Egyptian scholar-activist in Germany, focusing on the military, policing, and labour.
Follow Hossam on X: @3arabawy

articles.title: Strategic vacuum: Why is Trump's economic warfare against Iran doomed to fail?
articles.body:
Strategic vacuum: Why is Trump's economic warfare against Iran doomed to fail?
TEHRAN- Six months into his military campaign against Iran, Donald Trump finds himself trapped in the very quagmire he promised to eliminate. What began as a boastful declaration of "decisive action" to crush Iran and effect regime change has devolved into a strategic fiasco that not only fails to achieve its objectives but is inflicting profound damage on the U.S. economy and global stability. The administration's latest gambit—announcing the "largest financial attack in history" against Iran on August 24, a self-styled "D-Day" of economic warfare—appears less a stroke of genius and more an act of desperation from a presidency with no viable strategy left.
The irony is palpable. As U.S. Treasury officials threaten economic Armageddon against Tehran, America's own energy reserves are collapsing. Official data from July 2026 reveals that U.S. crude oil stockpiles, including the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), have plummeted to their lowest level in half a century—just 41 days of coverage, compared to the historical average of 65 days. Washington has depleted its most powerful tool for market intervention, leaving itself exposed to any future supply shock. This is not strength; this is strategic bankruptcy disguised as aggression.
The root cause of this self-inflicted wound lies in the Strait of Hormuz, the world's most vital energy chokepoint. After nearly six months of severe disruption triggered by the U.S.-Israeli military aggression against Iran, the waterway that once carried one-fifth of global oil and LNG supply has been reduced to a fraction of its normal flow. Daily transits have plummeted from 130 vessels to just a few, and war-risk insurance premiums have soared to 40 times normal levels. Hundreds of ships remain trapped in the Persian Gulf, and global oil flows have collapsed from 21 million barrels per day to a trickle. Iran, facing a U.S. naval blockade, has responded with controlled restrictions on the strait, creating a standoff that punishes everyone.
The economic devastation is global in scope. Asia, which historically received 80 to 90 percent of Hormuz-shipped oil and LNG, is enduring its largest energy shock in history. Japan, South Korea, India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh face crippling fuel shortages, soaring inflation, and industrial paralysis. European nations grapple with surging gas and electricity prices, while African countries dependent on food and energy imports confront acute shortages. The World Bank and institutions like Wood Mackenzie and Capital Economics warn that prolonged disruption could shave 0.5 to 1 percent off global GDP growth—a staggering blow to an already fragile world economy.
But perhaps the most telling consequence is the blowback on the United States itself. Trump's "maximum pressure" campaign has not broken Iran; it has made the regime more resilient. Airstrikes have weakened Iran militarily but strengthened its internal cohesion. The war has destroyed Iranian infrastructure and claimed lives, yet for most Americans, the conflict remains a distant abstraction—except at the gas pump, where prices have surged, and in the inflationary pressures now spreading through the U.S. economy. The SPR depletion is not a sign of American might; it is a warning that Washington has overextended itself and lost its ability to respond to future crises.
Trump's strategy rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of Iran. The Islamic Republic is simultaneously ideological and pragmatic. It resisted U.S. pressure for decades; it will not capitulate to coercion. Instead, by controlling the Strait of Hormuz, Tehran has demonstrated that it can impose reciprocal costs on its adversaries—and those costs are now painfully evident.
The administration's D-Day economic offensive is not a game-changer; it is a last gasp. Trump has repeated the same flawed playbook that has failed U.S. presidents since 1979: pressure as a substitute for strategy, military bluster as a cover for diplomatic bankruptcy. But this time, the consequences are not confined to Iran. The global economy is reeling, U.S. strategic reserves are depleted, and America's credibility is eroding with every empty threat. Far from breaking Iran, Trump's war has exposed the limits of American power and inflicted greater harm on the United States and its allies than on the intended target. The red light is flashing—not for Tehran, but for Washington.

articles.title: The ICC is under attack. Ukraine’s special tribunal must not be allowed to fail
articles.body:
Oleksii Shevchuk, advocate, Finalist for Ukraine’s nomination to the International Criminal Court (ICC) as a Judge
The international criminal justice system is facing one of its most consequential tests since the adoption of the Rome Statute. Its outcome will determine not only whether Russia’s leaders can be held accountable for the aggression against Ukraine, but whether powerful states can again conclude that war, occupation and mass violence carry no meaningful personal consequences.
For years, Russia has pursued a systematic campaign to discredit the International Criminal Court. That campaign has intensified as the possibility of individual accountability for the invasion of Ukraine has become more real. It is expressed through political pressure, information operations, legal arguments designed to deny the court’s reach, attacks on the legitimacy of international institutions and attempts to turn concern for sovereignty into a shield for impunity.
The pressure on the ICC should not be understood as an isolated institutional dispute. It is part of a broader struggle over whether international law applies when the alleged perpetrators are senior officials of a nuclear-armed state with global influence. Russia’s objective is clear: to ensure that Vladimir Putin and the political and military leadership responsible for the war against Ukraine are never brought before a court.
The removal of the ICC prosecutor, Karim Khan, from his duties amid the controversy surrounding the court’s work, together with withdrawals or threatened withdrawals from the Rome Statute system by states including Mali, Niger and Venezuela, sends a worrying signal. Every institutional crisis, every public attack on the court and every retreat from the principle of international criminal accountability is exploited by those who have the greatest interest in weakening the system.
The danger is not merely reputational. The ICC depends on political support, state co-operation, arrest warrants, access to evidence and the willingness of governments to uphold its decisions even when doing so is inconvenient. A court without enforcement capacity cannot function effectively. And a court whose legitimacy is repeatedly questioned by states, politicians and well-organised disinformation networks becomes easier to ignore.
For Ukraine, this makes the establishment of a special tribunal for the crime of aggression an urgent necessity.
The ICC’s role remains indispensable. Its investigations into war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are essential for victims and for the preservation of evidence. But the crime of aggression presents a distinct legal and political problem. It concerns the decision by a state’s leadership to launch an illegal war. It is therefore directed at those who planned, prepared, initiated or executed the invasion: the highest political and military authorities of the aggressor state.
This is precisely why a special tribunal is needed. It should focus specifically on Russia’s aggression against Ukraine and establish individual criminal responsibility among those who made the decision to unleash the war. The tribunal would not replace the ICC. It would complement it by addressing the jurisdictional gap that has prevented existing international mechanisms from fully prosecuting the leadership crime at the heart of the conflict.
The stakes could hardly be higher. If Russia succeeds in evading responsibility for aggression, it will reinforce a message already heard far too often in international affairs: that international law is binding on weaker states but negotiable for stronger ones. Such an outcome would encourage future aggressors, undermine the prohibition on the use of force and weaken the basic security architecture established after the second world war.
The special tribunal is therefore not a symbolic project. It is a practical legal mechanism intended to protect the principle that borders cannot be changed by force and that political leaders cannot hide behind state power when they authorise an unlawful war.
There are already efforts to discredit this idea. Critics argue that the tribunal would be selective, politically motivated or incompatible with international law. These arguments must be addressed seriously, but they should not become excuses for paralysis. Every international court operates in a political environment. That does not mean its work is illegitimate. The appropriate response is to ensure that the tribunal has a clear legal basis, robust procedural guarantees, independent judges, fair-trial protections and a credible institutional structure.
The alternative is not neutrality. The alternative is impunity.
The debate also exposes a wider problem within international criminal justice. The ICC has faced persistent criticism over its historical concentration on African situations. These concerns deserve respect: international justice cannot be credible if it is perceived as unevenly applied, or as a system in which some regions are subjected to scrutiny while the conduct of powerful states receives insufficient attention.
But the answer is not to weaken the ICC or to reduce its work further. It is to strengthen the universality of its mandate.
The ICC is not an “African court”. It is a court designed to deal with the gravest crimes wherever they occur, when national jurisdictions are unwilling or unable genuinely to prosecute. Its legitimacy depends on demonstrating that its principles apply across regions and against all perpetrators, regardless of geopolitical status.
Russia understands the political importance of this debate. Its growing influence in parts of Africa is not only economic or military; it is also diplomatic and informational. By presenting international criminal justice as a western political instrument, Moscow seeks to build support for a broader narrative: that accountability mechanisms are selective, colonial and therefore disposable.
This narrative is powerful precisely because it exploits real frustrations and historical grievances. European states cannot counter it merely with statements of principle. They must demonstrate, through consistent conduct, that international law is not a tool to be used only against political opponents. Supporting accountability for Ukraine while ignoring atrocities elsewhere would weaken the very cause they claim to defend.
The future of the ICC and the future special tribunal for Ukraine are therefore connected. Both depend on the same principle: no leader should be above the law.
Sanctions against ICC officials, political attempts to limit the court’s jurisdiction and campaigns questioning its authority are not technical disagreements. They are attacks on the idea that international crimes require an international response. If those attacks succeed, the consequences will extend far beyond Ukraine.
Ukraine’s struggle for accountability is not only about the past. It is about the rules that will govern future wars. A credible special tribunal for the crime of aggression would show that the decision to launch a war of conquest is not an act beyond legal reach. It would preserve the possibility that even the most powerful decision-makers may one day be called to account.
Europe, Ukraine and states committed to the international legal order must not allow this track to be abandoned. The ICC must be defended, reformed where necessary and given the political support required to fulfil its mandate. At the same time, the special tribunal must move from political discussion to institutional reality.
Justice may be delayed by war, power and diplomacy. But it must not be defeated by them.

articles.title: Britain and Ukraine signed a partnership agreement in the fields of defense and artificial intelligence
articles.body:
Britain and Ukraine signed a partnership agreement in the fields of defense and artificial intelligence

articles.title: Uganda's Gaza 'stabilisation force' plan sparks debate in Africa
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Uganda's participation in Gaza 'stabilisation force' sparks debate in Africa
Uganda's parliament approved the deployment of army troops to the" International Stabilisation Force" in the Gaza Strip at the beginning of August as part of US President Donald Trump's plan. The move marks the first official declaration by an African country of its readiness to participate in Gaza.
The approval came on 6 August after Ugandan Defence Minister Kiria Kiwanuka told lawmakers that Trump had asked President Yoweri Museveni in July for Uganda to contribute to the proposed international force in Gaza.
After the Ugandan parliament's approval, a Ugandan soldier in military uniform posted a video on social media in which he appeared alongside the words, "Gaza, we are coming", indicating that the idea of a military deployment had begun circulating within Uganda's military and media circles.
The Ugandan government has not yet specified the number of troops it may deploy to the territory or when they would be sent.
Israel's public broadcaster reported last Monday, 17 August, that senior officers from Uganda and Burundi had arrived at the US command headquarters in Kiryat Gat in the occupied Palestinian territories as part of advanced talks with the two countries to send hundreds of soldiers to the territory as part of the multinational stabilisation force.
The broadcaster also said last Thursday, 20 August, that Morocco had been chosen to train members of the force.
Ugandan forces in the Gaza stabilisation force has sparked debate inside the Ugandan parliament, with opposition lawmakers calling for more information about the nature of the mission, the number of troops, its funding, and the guarantees provided to soldiers and their families.
The opposition also warned of the security and political risks associated with sending troops to a devastated territory and under highly complex field conditions.
Uganda has extensive experience in peacekeeping operations, particularly in Africa, where its forces participate in missions in Somalia, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The defence minister cited this experience to justify the Ugandan army's ability to participate in a new international mission.
Without African backing
The decision has also raised questions about Kampala's approval of it and whether it has broad African backing or bypasses African consensus by being taken without Uganda consulting its partners in the African Union.
The African Union has consistently supported the Palestinian cause in principle and calls for the implementation of a two-state solution.
However, Israel has built relations with several African countries over decades, viewing the continent as an arena of Arab-Israeli competition.
In 2021, the union accepted Israel as an "observer member", a move that prompted Palestinian and Arab protests and was later revoked.
Uganda's relations with Israel, meanwhile, have continued to grow.
The Ugandan judge Julia Sebutinde, vice-president of the International Court of Justice, has attracted attention after she was described as believing that "God relies on her to stand with Israel". Sebutinde opposed the six rulings imposed by the court in 2024 to protect Palestinians and stop the genocide in Gaza.
Ugandan military leadership also recently said that any attempts to "destroy" Israel, amid the US-Israeli war on Iran, could prompt Uganda to intervene in support of the occupying state.
Uganda is also one of the largest importers of military technology and spyware from the occupying state.
In this context, Sudanese writer and researcher Abbas Saleh, who is based in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa, told The New Arab that Uganda's potential participation in the proposed international force for the Gaza Strip reflects a renewed predicament facing the African Union.
Decisions and positions adopted by the continental organisation often appear non-binding on member states, which may adopt unilateral policies that conflict with the union's collective positions.
"Despite the clear positions adopted by the African Union on the Palestinian cause, its rejection of Israeli violations and its repeated calls for an end to the war and the protection of civilians, the involvement of some member states in international security arrangements linked to Gaza could weaken the unity of the African position and expose the organisation's limited ability to turn its political positions into practical commitments by its members," he pointed out.
According to Saleh, Uganda is among the countries whose name has for years been associated with a broad security and military role in Africa, as well as close relations with Western powers, particularly in the Great Lakes region and the Horn of Africa.
He explained that this role "has given it a prominent position in several regional security issues but has at times made its foreign policy a subject of debate over the extent to which its decisions are independent of the calculations of international powers".
"The Ugandan move is significant beyond the participation of a single country, as it could set a precedent encouraging other countries that had been hesitant or reluctant to join the proposed international force, particularly if they are provided with appropriate political and security guarantees or international incentives," Saleh opined.
He stressed that participation in a military mission inside Gaza carries significant risks, given the complexities of the security and political situation, continuing disagreements over the future of the territory and governance and security arrangements, and the sensitivity surrounding the presence of foreign forces in the Palestinian territories.
"Uganda's move places the African Union before a difficult test: how can the organisation maintain a unified African position on the Palestinian cause while each member state has broad scope to make its foreign and security decisions independently?" he added. "The union's ability to deal with these contradictions could be an important indicator of the effectiveness of its political positions, not only towards Palestine, but also towards international crises affecting the continent and the interests of its countries."
Contradictions, differences
Meanwhile, researcher on Sahel and Sahara affairs Mohamed Torshin told The New Arab that the participation of Ugandan forces in the peace process in Gaza clearly reflects the scale of contradictions within the African Union and its limited ability to impose or implement decisions taken collectively, whether at the level of the AU Commission, the Peace and Security Council or the General Assembly.
Although African Union decisions and collective positions are supposed to form a common political framework for member states, the Ugandan position, along with other previous cases, reveals clear differences in the positions of African countries towards several sensitive regional and international issues.
In many cases, these differences push some countries or regional blocs to adopt policies and approaches that conflict with the union's collective position.
According to Torshin, the repercussions are not limited to a particular issue but extend to the effectiveness of African decision-making in general.
When a member state, in his view, adopts a position that clearly contradicts the union's collective position, this weakens the organisation's ability to present itself as a unified political actor and limits its ability to exercise diplomatic influence on issues requiring a coherent continental position.
In this context, Torshin noted that the repetition of such cases could widen the gap between decisions issued by African Union institutions and the policies pursued by some member states at the national level.
"This would gradually weaken the ability of the AU Commission and its political bodies to turn collective positions and decisions into effective and binding policies, making African decision-making more vulnerable to fragmentation and differences between countries and regional blocs," he added.
Torshin pointed out that the lack of protocol and political coordination between different African countries, ministries and institutions, and the absence of unified positions and decisions on common issues, could create space for international parties with interests and programmes in Africa to deal with countries individually and implement their policies and projects according to their own interests, away from the collective frameworks and decisions of the African Union.
He argued that "as this divergence and the multiplicity of positions within the continental organisation continue, international powers may find themselves with greater room to manoeuvre and negotiate with African countries bilaterally, gradually weakening the union's ability to formulate and defend a unified African agenda".
"In the long term, the continuation of this fragmentation could affect the future of African integration, making the implementation of continental policies and projects more closely tied to the interests of countries and external partners, and less subject to the collective vision that the union is supposed to represent," Torshin warned.
