articles.title: Third drone and suspected military explosives found near Leipzig airport
articles.body:
German investigators uncovered a third drone and suspected military explosives thought to be connected to an attempted attack on Leipzig airport, local media have reported.
The drone was discovered in Kabelsketal, just to the west of the airport, along with about 50g (1.8oz) of a suspected military explosive on 14 August, 10 days after the unsuccessful sabotage. Leipzig airport is a cargo and military logistics hub used by Nato and Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines for transporting military supplies.
The office of the prosecutor general, which is leading the investigation, declined to comment on Tuesday. But the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said the government would soon provide information about who it believed was behind the drone attacks.
“They will pay for this,” Merz said, stopping short of naming a suspect, before a cabinet meeting in Brandenburg. He added that the government was “working intensively on this together with the security authorities and we will present our findings and comment on them shortly”.
Intelligence sources cited by the broadcasters NDR and WDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung said they suspected the involvement of Russian intelligence in the attempted attack. Moscow has denied involvement.
The German government has so far avoided expressing a clear position as to whether it thinks Russia, or an actor close to it, is responsible.
Merz said the attempted attack showed that Germany was increasingly becoming a target. “Attackers are increasingly ruthlessly accepting even serious property damage, and even injuries and deaths,” he said on Tuesday.
A drone carrying explosives was found on 4 August near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane used for military supplies. According to investigators, the drone was apparently intended to land on the wings of the aircraft, which was filled with kerosene, but the explosive device did not detonate.
Investigators say that about 20 minutes after the discovery of the first drone, a second drone possibly collided with a DHL cargo plane, which was forced to abort its landing manoeuvre and was diverted to Marseille.
According to the latest media reports, an inspection of the DHL aircraft revealed damage to the tail section, suggesting a collision with an object. However, the drone has not yet been found. Investigators believe it could have been sucked into the engines after the collision and shredded into small pieces.
The third drone was found in a field in a municipality that directly borders the western edge of Leipzig airport. Forensic technicians from the federal criminal police office found residues of a substance that initial assessments indicated could have been the highly explosive substance hexogen. This explosive also failed to detonate, but the investigators’ report, according to the media reports, stated: “The perpetrators may have had a far larger attack in mind than previously known to the public.”
Other suspicious traces and components were also discovered close to the airport, the report said. In Kursdorf, investigators found an antenna attached to a tree, and other electronic parts, which may have been used to control the drones. Close by and near where witnesses reported hearing a loud bang on the day of the incident, investigators discovered a burnt patch and charred metal parts.
If the drones had exploded, they could have caused a catastrophe, German officials said.

articles.title: US Air Force C-17 makes unusual flight to Moscow
articles.body:
CIA chief was aboard mystery US C-17 flight to Moscow.
We now know why a US Air Force C-17 made an unusual flight from Riga to Moscow: CIA Director John Ratcliffe was reportedly aboard the aircraft for meetings in the Russian capital.
The reason behind an unusual US Air Force C-17 Globemaster III flight into Moscow has now emerged, with CBS News reporting that CIA Director John Ratcliffe travelled aboard the aircraft for meetings in the Russian capital, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The development answers the central question raised when the aircraft appeared on civilian flight-tracking services earlier on 25 August. What initially looked like a highly unusual American military transport movement into Russia was, according to CBS News senior White House reporter Jennifer Jacobs, carrying the CIA Director on a visit to Moscow. Jacobs reported, citing sources, that Ratcliffe travelled to Russia aboard a C-17 for meetings in the city and said it appeared to be his first known trip to the country since becoming CIA Director, although he has maintained contact with Russian intelligence counterparts.
It appears to be Ratcliffe’s first known trip to Russia as CIA director, though he has maintained contact with Russian intelligence counterparts. https://t.co/J9ugJvGnSj
— Jennifer Jacobs (@JenniferJJacobs) August 25, 2026
The aircraft was identified through open-source flight data as US Air Force C-17A Globemaster III serial 07-7191, using the callsign REACH 4555. It had first been tracked leaving the Washington area for Riga on 23 August, before departing the Latvian capital two days later and heading east towards Moscow, a routing that immediately drew attention because direct movements by identifiable US military aircraft into Russia have become extremely uncommon amid the deterioration in relations between Washington and Moscow.
UK Defence Journal Senior Editor Jon, known as DefenceGeek on X, followed the movement as it developed, first noting the aircraft’s arrival in Riga and then its subsequent flight into Russia. Tracking data showed REACH 4555 approaching Moscow before video and photographs from the city showed a C-17 descending towards the Russian capital, confirming that the aircraft had completed the unusual journey.
At that stage, however, the aircraft itself offered little indication of what the mission involved. The C-17 is the US Air Force’s principal heavy strategic transport aircraft and is routinely used to move personnel, vehicles and outsized cargo over intercontinental distances, while REACH callsigns are commonly associated with US Air Mobility Command missions, meaning the route could be followed in public without revealing who was aboard or why the aircraft had been sent to Moscow.
The CBS reporting changes that picture considerably, placing the flight in the context of a senior US intelligence visit rather than an unexplained logistics movement. Ratcliffe’s reported presence also helps explain why a conspicuous military aircraft was being used on a route that would otherwise have appeared highly unusual, although the precise purpose of his meetings, the Russian officials he met and the subjects discussed have not been made public.
Separate activity around the flight had already suggested that the movement involved more than a routine cargo mission. Imagery circulating after the C-17 arrived appeared to show US government vehicles travelling in convoy through Moscow, with open-source observers pointing to registration plates that appeared consistent with Latvia-issued diplomatic plates. The timing now makes a connection with Ratcliffe’s visit more plausible, although the available imagery does not establish whether those vehicles carried the CIA Director, formed part of his security detail or had any direct connection with the delegation.
There was also additional US government aviation activity at Riga before REACH 4555 continued to Moscow. A Boeing C-40, serial 02-0042 and using the callsign REACH 790, was tracked arriving at Riga International Airport from Joint Base Andrews on 23 August, with open-source imagery suggesting that it was parked close to the C-17. That movement can now be viewed alongside Ratcliffe’s reported journey, but there is still no confirmation that the C-40 continued to Russia or that it played a direct role in the CIA Director’s visit.
Jacobs’ reporting that Ratcliffe has maintained contact with Russian intelligence counterparts is also significant because it indicates that direct intelligence channels between Washington and Moscow have continued despite the wider breakdown in political and military relations. What those contacts have covered remains unknown, and there is no public information establishing whether the Moscow meetings concerned Ukraine, detainees, strategic stability, intelligence liaison or another issue.
The known sequence is now considerably clearer than it was when REACH 4555 first appeared over Russia: the aircraft travelled from the United States to Riga, later flew onward to Moscow, and was subsequently identified by CBS News sources as carrying the CIA Director for meetings in the Russian capital. The reason for the flight is therefore no longer the mystery it was when the movement was first detected, even if the substance of Ratcliffe’s discussions remains undisclosed.
The US Air Force declined to comment when approached about the flight, while no detailed public account of Ratcliffe’s meetings has yet been issued by the CIA or Russian authorities. What remains unanswered is not why an American C-17 was in Moscow, but what brought the CIA Director there and what was discussed once he arrived.

articles.title: Israeli airstrike, artillery shelling hit southern Lebanon despite US-mediated deal
articles.body:
Sahin Demir
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
Israeli army forces carried out an airstrike and artillery shelling in southern Lebanon early Tuesday, and erected new earth barriers in the area, in the latest violation of a US-mediated framework agreement, Lebanese media reported.
Israeli warplanes struck the course of the Litani River below the Deir Mar Mima monastery in the town of Deir Mimas at around 4 am local time (0100GMT), according to Lebanon’s official National News Agency (NNA).
Separately, the town of Markaba in the Marjayoun district came under Israeli artillery shelling as Israeli military vehicles were seen moving in the town, the agency said.
NNA also reported that Israeli forces stationed in Kfar Kila and Tall al-Nahhas erected an earth barrier at the Deir Mimas-Burj al-Muluk-Kfar Kila junction toward Tall al-Nahhas, around 150 meters (492 feet) from inhabited homes in Burj al-Muluk.
Israeli forces erected another earth barrier at the Deir Mimas-Burj al-Muluk-Houra junction toward the Houra area, it added.
The violations come amid continuing tensions between Israel and Lebanon following the outbreak of a new round of hostilities on March 2.
Israel has launched extensive attacks on Lebanon since March 2, claiming they targeted Hezbollah, while the group responded with attacks against Israel, effectively ending the ceasefire that had been in place since November 2024.
US-led diplomatic efforts led to the signing of a framework agreement between Israel and Lebanon in June, which provides for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from all occupied Lebanese territory in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army there and the disarmament of armed groups.

articles.title: Bail set for ex-Zelensky aide accused of money laundering
articles.body:
Bail set for ex-Zelensky aide accused of money laundering
Ukraine’s top anti-corruption court has set bail for the former deputy head of Vladimir Zelensky’s office, Irina Mudraya, at under $450,000 – less than one-seventh of the amount requested by prosecutors. She is suspected of channeling illicit funds into a bail payment for a defendant in a separate corruption case.
The High Anti-Corruption Court ruled on Tuesday that Mudraya must remain in Kiev and comply with any summons even if she posts bail, which she said she intends to do with the assistance of unnamed sponsors.
Zelensky fired Mudraya last week after she was formally accused of laundering about $3.3 million in cash to pay bail for former Energy Minister Herman Galushchenko. The latter had previously been implicated in an alleged $100 million kickback scheme blamed on Timur Mindich, a longtime associate of the Ukrainian leader.
The National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), two agencies established under Western pressure to tackle government graft, accused Mudraya of pressuring financial-monitoring officials to overlook suspicious transfers through Sense Bank. The lender was formerly the Ukrainian branch of Russia’s Alfa Bank before being nationalized by Kiev in 2023.
Surveillance recordings previously leaked to Ukrainian media suggested that Mindich’s group was interested in placing loyal figures on Sense Bank’s cabinet-appointed supervisory board. Ukrainian media dubbed Mindich “Zelensky’s bagman” amid suspicions that he was merely a frontman for corruption at the highest levels of government.
Mudraya trained as a lawyer specializing in banking and worked for several major clients in the sector before becoming a deputy justice minister in 2022. She moved to Zelensky’s office in 2024, ostensibly to contribute to Kiev’s efforts to obtain war reparations from Russia.
The former Zelensky aide has also been accused of participating in criminal schemes intended to expropriate real estate in Kiev worth some $16.75 million by illegally altering government records and pressuring judges to deny the legitimate owners legal recourse.
NABU and SAPO presented extensive records of conversations reportedly involving Mudraya and other suspects. The exchanges were allegedly recorded by former lawmaker and banker Maksim Mikitas.
Ukrainian media have speculated that Mikitas agreed to participate in the sting operation in return for leniency in other criminal cases being investigated by the two agencies.
During the bail hearings, Mudraya blamed a provocateur, apparently referring to Mikitas, for abusing her trust in order to produce incriminating recordings. She suggested that references to her alleged involvement in corruption were false but did not explain why she had failed to challenge the statements at the time.
Her defense team called several character witnesses, including Jonathan Markovitch, the chief rabbi of Kiev. He told the court that he knew Mudraya as a trustworthy member of the Jewish community and did not consider her a flight risk.
Mindich fled to Israel in November 2025, reportedly hours before he was due to be arrested. One of his key associates, Aleksandr Zukerman, also left for Israel. Both suspects hold Israeli citizenship.

articles.title: US sanctions Chinese entities, issues global warning on ‘Economic D-Day’ against Iran
articles.body:
China vows to safeguard interests after ‘Economic D-Day’ sanctions over Iran ties
Washington warns Iran-linked entities face removal from US dollar system as Trump presses world leaders to cut financial ties
China has condemned fresh US “Economic D-Day” sanctions imposed on Chinese entities over their ties to Iran, pledging “all necessary measures” to protect its interests.
Launching the measures on Monday against Iran and its trading partners, the United States unveiled new sanctions against 60 entities, individuals and vessels around the world, including some in mainland China and Hong Kong, and demanded “immediate action” from nations maintaining economic and commercial ties with Iran.
The measures are part of the Trump administration’s latest efforts to choke off Tehran economically after military strikes and diplomatic negotiations failed to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the six-month conflict.
In Beijing on Tuesday, the Chinese foreign ministry said Beijing’s cooperation with Tehran was conducted “within the framework of international law and should not be disrupted”.
Economic wars and maximum pressure were “not the solutions”, ministry spokesman Lin Jian said.
The new actions aim to expand Washington’s secondary sanctions, putting entities in multiple jurisdictions on notice.
“Let me be clear: any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system. The clock just started ticking,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.

articles.title: The oil market now ignores Trump’s messages
articles.body:
The oil market now ignores Trump’s messages
Kayhan, in an article, examined Trump’s desperation in the current situation. Trump’s frustration and anger come at a time when Axios acknowledged that changes in oil prices in response to Trump’s social‑media posts about the Iran war have steadily declined over time.
Fluctuations in oil prices ripple across the US and global economies, and the conflict has caused unprecedented disruption in supply. In the early weeks, markets overreacted to many of Trump’s posts. But for months now, the market has been ignoring them, because they do not reflect reality and have no connection to the number of barrels actually leaving the Strait of Hormuz. The erosion of Trump’s influence over oil markets carries political consequences, as Democrats use energy prices as a cudgel against Republicans in the midterm elections. In the first few months, the White House was highly successful in controlling the narrative and pushing prices down — but it has now lost that leverage.
Ettelaat: Maintaining good relations with neighbors is essential for Iran
Ettelaat evaluated the Mecca Pact. Although Iran currently has no tension with Turkey or Pakistan, it is possible that under certain circumstances — and with Saudi financial assistance to these two countries combined with US provocation — tensions could emerge. For this reason, Tehran need not be overly sensitive about the Mecca Pact. If the pact adopts a strongly oppositional stance toward Israel, it would be an opportunity for Tehran. If it remains indifferent toward Israel but shows sensitivity toward Iran, it becomes a threat. The Mecca Pact could, at a critical moment, be inflamed by Riyadh and Washington, clouding Iran’s relations with Ankara and Islamabad. In any case, it is better for Iran to keep its good relations with its neighbors strong and to further reinforce them, while remaining highly alert and prepared for all possible scenarios, risks, and breaches of commitment, even in the worst case.
Arman-e-Emrooz: A challenging situation
Arman-e-Emrooz assessed the intensification of US sanctions and the naval blockade of Iran through three possible scenarios. Amid these developments, it appears that one of the three scenarios will soon unfold. One possibility is that the Trump administration steps back and announces progress in negotiations, meaning the harsh sanctions will not be implemented. The second scenario is that the plan is announced and executed, but after a short period it is quietly set aside as both sides show flexibility and a negotiation process begins. The third possibility is that the severe economic sanctions continue until the US midterm elections and are then accompanied by military strikes to reshape the situation on the ground. Each of these three scenarios has its supporters, but two factors strongly influence them: first, the degree of firmness on current positions; and second, the election results soon to be held in the US and Israel.
Shargh: A crisis in the global economy
Shargh, in an analysis, examined the global economic crisis triggered by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The flight of oil tankers from the strait amid escalating military tensions has pushed shipping rates to more than four times their pre‑war levels. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has now become a crisis for the global economy. This unprecedented surge in transport costs brings a chain of negative consequences. First, the final cost of oil for consumer countries has risen sharply, meaning greater pressure on household budgets and intensified inflation worldwide. Second, countries lacking sufficient strategic reserves face serious challenges in securing their required oil and may encounter fuel shortages. Third, higher transport costs raise the final price of essential goods and industrial raw materials, since oil plays a key role in the production and transport of many products. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has imposed a full‑scale economic crisis on the world — one that affects all countries, from major importers to ordinary consumers.
Resalat: Disrupting the Arab–American coalition‑building game
American strategists openly speak of efforts to unite the Persian Gulf Arab states against Iran. Our diplomacy must anticipate the adversary’s moves and deprive them of the pretexts for coalition‑building. The agreement to restore relations with Saudi Arabia, along with expanding ties with the UAE and Qatar, must be upgraded from a mere political truce to deep economic and security linkages. If the Persian Gulf states develop tightly interwoven commercial and economic interests with Iran, they will not easily play Washington’s anti‑Iran puzzle. We must show our neighbors that regional security is unified and indivisible. Any provision of bases to the United States or the Israeli regime for actions against Iran’s interests endangers the security and investment climate of the entire region.
At the same time, proposing non‑aggression pacts and cooperation for securing maritime navigation neutralizes the pretext for foreign fleets to remain present.

articles.title: IRGC Spokesman: Threats to Iran's infrastructure will draw heavy strikes on US vital interests
articles.body:
IRGC: Threats to Iran's infrastructure will draw heavy strikes on US vital interests
TEHRAN- Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, spokesman for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), issued a stark warning on Monday, asserting that any US attempts to target Iran's critical infrastructure would provoke severe strategic retaliation against America's vital interests.
Speaking in a televised address, General Mohebbi dismissed 'the enemy's miscalculation' regarding Iran's military capabilities. "Contrary to the enemy's assumption that Iran's weapons stockpiles are limited, our production of smart and precision-guided missiles continues unabated," he stated.
The IRGC spokesman further emphasized that the United States has now come to fully comprehend the consequences of military action against Iranian infrastructure. "Today, America has understood well that if it operationalizes its threats against Iran's infrastructure, it will face heavy strategic blows at energy chokepoints and against its own vital interests," he warned.
General Mohebbi also highlighted the failure of "the enemy's theatrical attempt to reopen the Strait of Hormuz," noting that such objectives have remained unachieved due to Iran's deterrence posture and regional influence.
The remarks come amid heightened tensions between Iran and the United States, with both sides exchanging warnings over military posturing and strategic assets in the Persian Gulf region.
The spokesman for the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps dismissed US President Donald Trump s remarks claiming the Strait of Hormuz belongs to America as baseless, unrealistic and pure fantasy, stressing that not a single American warship is currently present in the Persian Gulf.
Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, in an interview with Fars News Agency, referred to Trump s recent comments on the Strait of Hormuz and said: Even members of Trump s own administration have not taken his words seriously. These claims are unacceptable on the global stage as well.
Mohebbi stated that if it is claimed the Strait of Hormuz belongs to the United States, or that America has kept it open so that ships can pass through it, journalists and media outlets can use their extensive resources and satellite data to examine the actual status of vessel traffic and reveal the reality to the people of the world.
He emphasized that if the strait is truly under American control, they should demonstrate their presence in the region and prove on the ground what they claim.
Mohebbi noted: Before the war, at least 30 to 40 US warships were present in the Persian Gulf, but today not even a single American warship is in the Persian Gulf. US military assets are currently positioned at least about 400 kilometers away from the Strait of Hormuz.
Regarding Iran s level of readiness, he stressed: Our readiness is 100 percent, and no disruption has ever occurred in the readiness of the Islamic Republic of Iran. The field conditions and what is observed in the region today differ from the claims of the other side.

articles.title: Israel intensifies airstrikes, artillery shelling across southern Lebanon
articles.body:
Israel intensifies airstrikes, artillery shelling across southern Lebanon
TEHRAN — Israeli forces escalated their unprovoked assault on southern Lebanon through the weekend and into Monday, combining high-explosive airstrikes with systematic home demolitions and brutal scorched-earth tactics.
The expanding offensive shreds the remnants of a United States-sponsored June framework agreement that Washington falsely presented as a mechanism for a gradual Israeli withdrawal.
Instead, American diplomacy has functioned as a reliable shield for continued aggression. The regime currently occupies ground more than ten kilometers inside Lebanese territory and shows absolute intent to remain.
The weekend violence centered heavily on the strategic Ali Al Taher heights east of Nabatieh.
Israeli fighter jets hammered the ridge and the adjacent Dabsha hills with heavy missiles, while artillery batteries fired illegal white phosphorus shells.
Some have indicated that these strikes may be preparing the battlefield for broader incursions to isolate the heights and create a so-called buffer zone.
Similar tactical maneuvers define the central sector. Ground units launched military operations targeting Beit Yahoun, Haddatha, and Ayta al-Jabal, villages that had escaped direct Israeli occupation prior to the supposed June truce.
On Monday, the sheer destruction accelerated across dozens of civilian areas.
In the border town of Houla, Israeli engineering units deployed heavy bulldozers to raze civilian infrastructure while artillery bombarded the adjacent Wadi al-Saloqi valley.
Further west, an Israeli quadcopter dropped sound bombs to terrorize residents in Al-Mansouri.
Israeli forces stationed in Khiam systematically detonated residential blocks in the town's western neighborhood near the Al-Mabarrat schools.
Deliberately ignited fires consumed nearby agricultural properties. Thick smoke blanketed the sky above the leveled homes.
Israeli warplanes simultaneously hit the Dawha neighborhood in Kfar Romman.
A drone strike there targeted a motorcycle, assassinating two individuals.
A massive explosion ripped through Haddatha following yet another deliberate military demolition.
Over 45 separate strikes punished the south within a 24-hour span, relentlessly tearing through Qanatra, Barachit, Mayfadoun, Mays al-Jabal, and Srobbine.
The human cost of this U.S.-backed war continues to compound. Lebanese health authorities count over 4,348 people killed and 12,307 wounded since the March offensive began, with more than a million displaced.
Israel routinely ignores United Nations resolutions demanding it leave occupied Palestinian and Syrian lands, instead applying the exact same expansionist violence to Lebanon.

articles.title: UN chief tells countries to rein in autonomous weapons
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — Countries should ban or restrict the use of autonomous weaponry, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said on Tuesday, in a joint appeal with the Red Cross.
The world is inching closer to "crossing a moral red line", the "autonomous targeting of humans by machines," Guterres said. The UN press release referred to "unconfirmed reports" that drones guided by artificial intelligence are being deployed on the battlefield.
On Monday, the New York Times ran a story which claimed that a Russian AI-guided drone killed three Ukrainians, highlighting how AI could evolve drone warfare.
Advertisement
Guterres and ICRC chief Mirjana Spoljaric underlined that targeting civilians in war is a violation of international humanitarian law, and said they fear that machines won't be able to tell the difference between combatants and non-combatants.
Both called for a ban on autonomous weapons which produce unpredictable results and anti-personnel weapons that deliberately target human beings.
The UN is set to hold a conference in Geneva in November to review its treaty on conventional weapons. Lethal autonomous weapon systems are expected to be a subject of that gathering. The UN has long been pushing countries to progress on legally binding rules.
"When we speak about AI, we want human oversight," European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told reporters on Tuesday when asked about the Commission's assessment on whether humans should be kept in the loop of military applications.
Human oversight is a key concept of the bloc's Artificial Intelligence Act, which doesn't apply, though, to defence or security applications.

articles.title: Yemen's increased violence leaves thousands hungry, displaced
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen's increased violence leaves tens of thousands displaced and hungry
The increase of military conflict in Yemen is not limited to traditional front lines, with the fighting impacting different aspects of life.
The UN-sponsored de-escalation agreement reached between the conflicting parties in Yemen in April 2022 failed to protect what remained of the necessities of life amid a new threat of all-out war, bringing the spectre of the ongoing humanitarian disaster to the fore since the Ansar Allah group, also know as the Houthis, took control of the capital Sanaa in September 2014.
During the current military round, infrastructure and service facilities are direct targets in attacks, almost completely paralysing local trade, disrupting supply chains and leaving millions of Yemenis, particularly displaced people, facing a daily struggle for survival in a country where even the most basic rights are an unattainable luxury.
The present fighting also affected Mocha Port, one of the most important arteries for the flow of food supplies along Yemen's western coast, which has come under repeated shelling.
According to port director Abdulmalik Al-Sharaabi, the attacks caused extensive damage to vital facilities, with direct losses estimated at $16 million, as well as deaths and injuries among workers and civilians.
This disruption immediately impacted living conditions for thousands of people, particularly due to the halt of basic goods flows, foremost among them food and fuel products.
Wide areas under the control of the internationally recognised government along the western coast and parts of the neighbouring highlands have been hit by severe shortages.
In addition to the alarming figures related to living conditions, this paralysis has another particularly harsh dimension.
Hundreds of workers at Mokha port suddenly found themselves deprived of their only sources of income, accompanied by severe food shortages and sharp price increases that have placed a heavy burden on all citizens exhausted by years of prolonged war.
Meanwhile, residents of Marib province are facing immense suffering being the largest refuge for internally displaced people.
The province, which carries significant demographic and humanitarian weight, is facing repeated and intense waves of ballistic missile and drone attacks, threatening the lives of hundreds of thousands of civilians, particularly those living in dilapidated tents in informal displacement camps.
Displaced from Al Mahwit province, Umm Ziad told The New Arab, "We are living in a catastrophic situation, as we have no food to live on away from our homes since we were displaced while fleeing the Houthis' brutality. We depend on aid, and we have begun to fear that we will be forced to flee to another province because of the continued shelling of Marib."
The danger of further war extends to harming the main lifeline of livelihoods by targeting energy facilities and domestic gas supplies that serve most Yemeni provinces.
This direct threat risks causing a complete paralysis of supply chains, early signs of which have already emerged in the shortage of domestic gas cylinders in several cities.
From Taiz, Abdu Saif Al-Bakari told TNA, "I have been trying for four days to obtain a gas cylinder. I searched all the petrol stations in Taiz and all the cylinder shops, but I could not find one. They told me that gas was unavailable because of the shelling of Marib, and I was forced to buy it on the black market for 20,000 rials, although its official price is 9,500 rials (One dollar is equivalent to 1,550 rials in areas controlled by the internationally recognised government.)."
The repercussions has also suffocated the capital, Sanaa, under the Houthis' control.
As commercial activity at Mokha port has halted and major supply lines have been cut, Sanaa's markets have suffered severe food shortages, immediately reflected in unprecedented waves of price rises that have consumed what little money remains in residents' pockets.
In a city already suffering a chronic humanitarian crisis because salaries have remained unpaid since 2016, with no prospect of an end to the crisis, the latest escalation has closed the last avenues of survival for millions of families unable to afford food or medicine.
"We have reached a situation in which we can no longer bear living," From Sanaa, Ibrahim told TNA. "For more than 10 years, we have lived without salaries and suffered fear, repression and security crackdowns to the extent that if a person says he is hungry, he is threatened or kidnapped. Despite this, the Houthis impose financial levies on citizens under the pretext of celebrating the Prophet's birthday."
As the health, education and other basic services sectors collapse under the strain of shortages of supplies and fuel, Sanaa is now living through an extremely harsh reality.
Citizens find themselves trapped between the burden of excessive price rises and the complete helplessness imposed by a parallel economy that is draining the resources needed for their daily lives.
Residents are also facing heavy financial levies imposed under the name of commemorating religious occasions, alongside a growing wave of online protests launched by citizens on social media platforms under hashtags denouncing escalating policies of starvation.
Experts warn the current conditions is pushing the country towards extremely dangerous territory.
Wafik Saleh, executive director of the Taiz Centre for Studies, told TNA that Mokha Port going out of service would inevitably trigger a rapid wave of inflation, leading to unprecedented increases in the prices of food and basic goods at a time when markets are unable to absorb the shock or provide sustainable alternatives.
"The spectre of collapse does not stop at food. It extends to the most basic necessities of survival," Saleh explained. "Targeting the vicinity of energy facilities in Marib is emptying markets of their supplies of domestic cooking gas and other petroleum products, automatically fuelling black and parallel markets whose prices double the burden on Yemeni families."
"As people's purchasing power collapses, thousands find themselves forced to exhaust what remains of their income to cope with harsh living conditions, driving a catastrophic deterioration in humanitarian crises on the ground," he added. "These accumulating crises are outlining the features of a comprehensive disaster that is undermining the efficiency of the health and food sectors as a result of interruptions to cold chains and rising hospital operating costs, threatening to increase the number of people in need of urgent assistance to unprecedented levels," Saleh concluded.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

articles.title: Occupation officials involved in deportation of 53 Ukrainian children to Russia served with notices of suspicion in absentia
articles.body:
Occupation officials involved in deportation of 53 Ukrainian children to Russia served with notices of suspicion in absentia
Four occupation "officials" involved in the deportation of 53 children from three children's homes in temporarily occupied Donetsk and Makiivka to Russia have been served with notices of suspicion in absentia.
Source: Ukraine's Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko
Details: The children were illegally taken to Russia in October 2022.
"This was not an evacuation. This was a planned deportation of Ukrainian children, organised at the highest level of Russia's military-political leadership," Kravchenko said.
According to the investigation, four officials carried out the crime in the occupied territory:
- "Donetsk People's Republic" health minister Dmytro Hartsev provided administrative processing
- Svitlana Maiboroda, head of the occupation "State Service for Family and Children's Affairs", coordinated transport, the transfer of personal files and subsequent placement of the children
- heads of children's homes Viacheslav Vysiahin and Viktor Honcharov organised the gathering of the children and personally accompanied them during their removal
Law enforcement established that the Ukrainian children were transported by bus to Rostov-on-Don, Russia. From there, they were flown by a special Rossiya flight detachment aircraft to Moscow Oblast and distributed among social centres.
Immediately after arrival, Russian agencies began processing documents under Russian law: granting the Ukrainian children Russian citizenship, entering them into the state database and placing them with Russian families.
The children's profiles subsequently appeared on an adoption portal. The investigation established that 28 Ukrainian children were placed under the guardianship of Russian families.
"To this day, not a single child from this group has been returned to Ukraine. They have effectively spent their entire conscious lives in the aggressor state. They are growing up in a Russian educational, informational and cultural environment. A foreign identity is being imposed on them and attempts are being made to permanently sever their connection with Ukraine.
This is not a side effect of deportation. This is its continuation: a deliberate state policy of Russification of Ukrainian children," the prosecutor general said.
Dmytro Hartsev, Svitlana Maiboroda, Viacheslav Vysiahin and Viktor Honcharov have been served with in absentia suspicion notices for violations of the laws and customs of war committed by prior conspiracy of a group of individuals.
"Their decisions, orders, meetings held, transfer of documents and the entire deportation route have been documented in detail. Notices of suspicion served in absentia are only the first step towards the personal accountability of each of them. War crimes have no statute of limitations," Kravchenko stressed.
Background: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine previously named 10 more individuals involved in the militarisation of Ukrainian children under occupation.

articles.title: Ukraine fires state bank chair after alleged $3.3 million bail-laundering scheme
articles.body:
Ukraine has dismissed Mykola Hladyshenko as chair of the supervisory board of state-owned Sense Bank after NABU released recordings that it says show the bank was used to launder 150 million hryvnias ($3.3 million) to post bail for a former minister.
The Cabinet’s 21 August decision ended Hladyshenko’s powers and appointed a state representative to the board to help restore a quorum. The Finance Ministry and National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) must now ensure the bank is properly governed and prepare it for sale.
New recordings changed the NBU’s assessment
The NBU’s 20 August decision followed a review opened in May, when recordings linked to the wider Mindich case raised questions about Hladyshenko’s independence. The regulator twice asked Ukraine’s anti-corruption agencies for evidence, but they could not release pretrial investigation materials. Hladyshenko stepped aside while the review continued.
NBU Governor Andrii Pyshnyi told Parliament that new public evidence changed the regulator’s assessment. The material suggested that Hladyshenko’s withdrawal had been merely formal and that he continued to influence the bank.
It also raised questions about the remaining board members’ oversight. That evidence emerged on 19 August as part of Operation “Forest Gump”.
The Mindich tapes are recordings from NABU’s investigation into an alleged $100 million kickback network at state nuclear operator Energoatom. They are named after businessman Tymur Mindich, a former business partner of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The Mindich tapes: anti-graft recordings expose Zelenskyy associate’s $100M nuclear operator protection racket
The NBU also demanded that Sense Bank suspend Liudmyla Snihur, head of the bank’s financial and currency monitoring department, while it investigates possible interference with the bank’s operating systems. The government initiated suspension proceedings against the chair of the management board, Oleksii Stupak.
According to Ekonomichna Pravda’s account of the NABU materials, investigators allege that the group moved illicit cash through Sense Bank, companies under its control, and private individuals before using the money to post bail for former Energy and Justice Minister Herman Halushchenko, a suspect in the Mindich case.
Snihur allegedly helped create a temporary “window” during which transactions passed without the bank’s usual checks.
Sense Bank was already for sale
Trending Now
Ukraine nationalized Sense Bank, formerly Alfa-Bank Ukraine, in 2023 after sanctions barred its Russian-linked owners from controlling it.
Kyiv was preparing to privatize Sense Bank before the current investigation. The government accelerated sale preparations on 20 August and said the proceeds would fund Ukraine’s defense forces.

articles.title: US removes Syria from 'state sponsor of terrorism' list
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US removes Syria from 'state sponsor of terrorism' list in 'historic' step
The United States on Monday removed Syria from its blacklist of "State Sponsors of Terrorism" after over 40 years, in a move described as a "historic step" for the country.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement that the removal "will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability".
Bessent added the moves were "in line with President (Donald) Trump's promise to deliver sanctions relief to Syria".
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa welcomed the move, saying: "Today, Syria shakes off a dark stain and tears away a painful chapter of its past to embark on a path of development, reconstruction and rebuilding".
Al-Sharaa thanked US President Donald Trump, as well as countries that have supported Syria.
Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani described Washington's delisting as a "historic milestone", while Finance Minister Mohammed Barnieh described the move as a "success for Syrian diplomacy".
The designation made Syria a high-risk, heavily restricted jurisdiction in the US-led financial and trade system, impacting it on all fronts, including legal, economic, diplomatic and humanitarian.
"It's really the last piece of the puzzle when it comes to trying to not only provide the boost to the post-war Syrian economy and Syrian reconstruction efforts, but additionally, the boost that many of Syria's security and political agencies will need to build capacity after the fall of the Assad regime," Caroline Rose, Senior Director at The Soufan Center, told The New Arab.
"The designation carried a lot of weight when it came to providing dual-use items, military assistance, also collaborating directly with Syrian defence and security agencies and forces, and so as a result, this is going to, I think, open up a whole new portal, so to speak, when it comes to US security and defence collaboration with the new Syrian administration."
Syria was subject to restrictions on US foreign assistance, a ban on defence exports and sales, strict controls on exports of dual-use goods and technology, and financial and other miscellaneous restrictions.
Yazan Al-Saadi, The New Arab's International desk editor, says the move "will untangle a lot of the day-to-day challenges that Syrians and Syrian institutions face when they try to work within the international financial sphere".
"There is hope that this will alleviate a lot of the economic pressures facing the country at the moment after 15 years of a brutal civil war uprising as well as the fallout from what's going on worldwide with price increases, gas increases," Al-Saadi added.
"This is another obstacle removed for them."
The US initially announced in July its intention to delist Syria as a state sponsor of terrorism, in a move seen as a vote of confidence in Sharaa.
The US Department of State has also removed the designation of al-Nusra Front, which later became known as Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), as a global terrorist organisation. HTS rebels, led by al-Sharaa, overthrew Syria's long-running ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
The Treasury Department announced corresponding sanctions relief, while asserting that its removal of restrictions on Syria "does not change Treasury's posture with regards to countering global terrorism and our commitment to hold bad actors in Syria accountable".
Fadel Abdulghany, founder of the Syrian Network for Human Rights (SNHR), cautioned that the moves by the US "must not be portrayed as full normalisation".
"Delisting does not remove targeted sanctions against individuals and entities implicated in serious human rights abuses, illicit finance, terrorism or other destabilising conduct," Abdulghany said.
"Nor does it resolve the structural challenges that continue to deter responsible investment, including weak public institutions, uncertainty over property rights, lack of judicial independence, corruption, damaged infrastructure and ongoing insecurity."
Syria was first blacklisted by the US in 1979, making the designation one of the longest-standing, lasting throughout the Assad family's rule.
Al-Saadi notes that the blacklisting had a negative impact on how Syrians were perceived, and hopes that the new move will change this.
"With Syria being on such a list and so forth, Syrians have been vilified for a long, long time and they continue to be, I would say, as terrorists, as Barbarians, as savages," he said.
"For Syrians in particular, they've been dehumanised for so long that maybe it's time to start humanising them more and more in a very natural and much needed way, just like other people, Palestinians and so forth."
The blacklisting concerned successive Syrian governments' support and logistical assistance for armed groups that Washington classified as terrorist organisations. The listing was also not internationally agreed.
Other countries on the list include Iran, North Korea and Cuba. States included in the list are accused of providing support for "acts of international terrorism".

articles.title: Iran Vows Retaliation After U.S. Widens ‘Economic D-Day’ Sanctions
articles.body:
Iran has pledged to “attack” the U.S. financially after Washington unveiled a sweeping set of sanctions as part of ‘Economic D-Day', an attempt to further isolate Tehran and curb its access to the global financial system as the war between the two countries drags on.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled the measures as part of President Donald Trump’s announcement of the "most crushing economic operation" against Tehran, labeled “Operation Economic Outcast.”
"D-Day marked a historic campaign with our allies,” Bessent said Monday. “Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe."
After the measures were announced, Tehran’s Economy Minister Seyed Ali Madanizadeh said the government was prepared to counter the newly-unveiled U.S. sanctions.
“They want to launch an economic terrorist attack against us. We also have our own tools, and we know the rules of this game,” he said in response to Bessent’s announcement during a televised interview with Iranian state media Monday.
“This time, they shouldn't think that our approach is purely defensive; they should also expect an attack from us.”
Although the Iranian minister did not elaborate on what such an attack would entail, he said the country had developed plans in preparation for the economic threats.
“Plans have been developed for various scenarios, including what actions should be taken if they attempt to cause damage in the financial sector or in the country's financial relations,” he said, adding that “the global financial system is not structured in a way that allows anyone to claim they can cut off” Iran’s economy.
During the announcement, Bessent stopped short of immediately imposing secondary sanctions on countries that trade heavily with Iran, instead favoring an approach that would give them time to decouple from that trade.
When asked why he was waiting to impose those sanctions, Bessent responded: "Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?"
“We believe that it is important to level set and give people a cure period, but they should know that that will move very quickly, and that we are serious,” he added.
Bessent did not name any countries that could face sanctions, but said "they know who they are."
China, one of Iran's biggest trading partners and the primary buyer of Iranian oil exports, has already pushed back against the threat.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said China-Iran cooperation "should not be disrupted or undermined," noting that it had been conducted in accordance with international law.
“China has made clear on many occasions its firm opposition to illicit unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law or the authorization of the U.N. Security Council. Economic warfare and maximum pressure provide no solution,” Jian said during a press conference Tuesday.
The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has sanctioned nearly 60 entities, individuals, and vessels connected to Iran’s regime, while also gaining powers to impose additional sanctions on any person operating within the digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping sectors of the Iranian economy.
Iranian leaders had previously dismissed the impact of extensive economic sanctions on the country and instead sought to highlight struggles within the U.S. economy.
Trump, meanwhile, claimed Monday that Iran is "completely collapsing,” without elaborating on what he based the claim.
Strait of Hormuz attack raises stakes after sanctions announcement
Following Bessent's economic announcement, an oil tanker was hit by a projectile off the coast of Oman in the Strait of Hormuz, according to a report by U.K. Maritime Trade Operations.
The incident highlights the continued danger for shipping companies attempting to transit the key waterway, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil supply passed before the war. The closure of the Strait has rattled energy markets and thrown the global economy into disarray.
Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi had previously threatened heavy blows against vital U.S. interests and energy chokepoints if Iran’s economy was targeted with sanctions.
"The U.S. President says that he ordered an economic war and launched the most severe economic campaign against Iran,” he said, as reported by Iranian state media Sunday. “We have repeatedly announced that we have scenarios in place for any hostile action by the enemy. One of the enemy’s hostile actions is economic measures and warfare.”
The attack came as a high-level delegation from Pakistan, which has been a key mediator between the United States and Iran, was wrapping up meetings in Tehran aimed, once again, at bringing a return to negotiations and an end to the nearly six-month-old war.
The cease-fire established under the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) signed between Washington and Tehran expired on Aug. 17, but the agreement had already deteriorated after each side presented differing interpretations of its terms.
Both parties had vied for control of the Strait of Hormuz, eventually leading to tit-for-tat strikes, the reimposition of the American blockade on Iranian ports, and minimal dialogue between Washington and Tehran.
Iran has since released a comprehensive list of demands for the U.S. to meet, which Trump immediately rejected. Both sides have since shown little sign of progress in negotiations, despite relatively limited fighting in recent weeks.

articles.title: Is Mojtaba Khamenei Dead?
articles.body:
Is Mojtaba Khamenei Dead?
The office of Iran’s supreme leader has fallen quiet, fueling uncertainty in a country with decisions to make.
Last Tuesday, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei hosted a wake for his father and predecessor, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Among the thousands who thronged Tehran’s biggest mosque were the country’s most prominent political figures and several of the elder Khamenei’s sons. One person was notably absent: Mojtaba, the event’s official host.
Almost six months since his anointment, Iran’s supreme leader has been entirely obscured from the public eye. Not a single contemporaneous picture, video, or audio recording of him has been released. Many of the country’s top political leaders admit that they haven’t seen him—among them Abbas Araghchi, Iran’s foreign minister and a member of the National Security Council. IranWire, a London-based opposition outlet, reports that not a single cabinet member has met with Mojtaba since he became supreme leader.
Not even Mojtaba’s close friends and relatives have seen him. Fewer than five people have met with Mojtaba since his ascent to power, Mohammad Hossein Khoshvaght, a former official and a relative of Mojataba’s told me, “due to security precautions.”
The rationale is not implausible. Mojtaba would be a likely target for an Israeli or U.S. air strike, such as the one that killed his father. Direct communication from him could supply Iran’s enemies with clues to his whereabouts. He is also said to have sustained injuries in the February strike on his family that have made public speeches and appearances difficult.
But the totality of Mojtaba’s invisibility and a recent decline in statements from his office have set Tehran abuzz with new rumors of his death. Some sources inside and close to the government speculated to me that Mojtaba recently died from the injuries that he had sustained in February. And irrespective of his actual status, the uncertainty might have major implications for Iran.
“I believe Mojtaba has either passed away or is brain-dead,” a staffer at a government institution in Tehran told me, citing the tailing off of even indirect communication from the leader to the outside world. At least two other government officials told me the same. One said that he believed Mojtaba died or became brain-dead earlier this month.
Two sources in the Iranian government recently told IranWire that word had spread among those at the “highest level of the regime” that Mojtaba was doing very poorly and could die at any moment. About two weeks ago, a public appeal went out on a domestic messaging service, asking Iranians to pray for Mojtaba’s health and sacrifice sheep to bless him, as is customary in Islam. Mojtaba’s life was “under threat,” and some “clerics” had warned that he might be killed, the appeal said.
Since he was appointed, Mojtaba has ruled by decrees disseminated by his office. Iran’s supreme leader is a religious authority in addition to being the head of state, and on July 27, Mojtaba’s office published a list of his answers to practical questions posed by the devout. One correspondent had requested guidance on eating with bleeding gums, because blood is haram—forbidden—in Islam. Any food contaminated with blood, including from one’s own gums, must be thrown out, Mojtaba ruled. If his office is to be believed, then the leader was well enough to ponder Islamic law and issue relevant rulings as recently as a month ago.
The office’s most recent statement came on August 9 and reported that Mojtaba had met with President Masoud Pezeshkian. It didn’t say when the meeting had taken place but noted that it was on the occasion of the president’s third year in office, which puts it on or after July 28. Pezeshkian confirmed to the Iranian media that he spent seven hours with Mojtaba discussing the war and the country’s beleaguered economy. (According to Khoshvaght, Pezeshkian was taken to that meeting “without knowing where it was,” which suggests that he was transported blindfolded, mafia-style.) Also on August 9, Mojtaba issued a slew of decrees, appointing several generals to top military positions and swapping out one of his representatives on the National Security Council. Since then, the office has been silent.
Khoshvaght assured me that Mojtaba is definitely alive. The rumors about the leader’s death are “part of a psychological war hoping to demoralize Iran’s officials and its people, for them to give up to the pressures and threats of America,” he said. He added that the rumors also aim to embolden Iranians opposed to the regime, giving them “courage to come to the streets so that the plans of the U.S. and Israel can be realized.” Abdolreza Davari, a former adviser to the interior ministry and a vocal supporter of Mojtaba’s, told me that the leader is “in full health” and will soon be revealed to the public. But the two weeks with no communication, the public appeal for sheep sacrifice, and the rumors emanating from government circles have led many Iranians to doubt such assurances.
Whether Mojtaba is dead or alive, his public absence creates problems for the Iranian regime. The supreme leader holds most of the constitutional power in the Islamic Republic and has in the past served as the final arbiter among the system’s warring factions and institutions. Mojtaba appears to be sitting these conflicts out, at a moment when their outcome could be particularly consequential.
The country’s 13-person National Security Council is effectively running the country as a collective. It is chaired by Pezeshkian, a reformist who favors an end to the war with America, and includes Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the powerful parliamentary speaker who led the talks with the United States. But it also includes General Ahmad Vahidi, the head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and other military leaders.
Back in June, 12 of the council’s 13 members voted in favor of the memorandum of understanding that Iran reached with the United States in Islamabad. Mojtaba sent a message endorsing the deal but also noting that he had initially opposed such an agreement “in principle.” Hard-line critics of diplomacy seized on this to claim that Ghalibaf had usurped power and forced the memorandum on the leader. A news outlet linked to a faction in the IRGC even issued a documentary called Ghalibaf’s Coup.
Mojtaba neither endorsed this view nor put it to rest. Rather, he has remained mum as various factions have purported to speak for him. Pezeshkian has told reporters that in his meeting with Mojtaba, the leader stressed that regime officials should “keep unity and cohesion” and avoid infighting.
But the infighting goes on. In June, a statement signed by 63 of the 88 members of the Assembly of Experts, a clerical body tasked with supervising the supreme leader, admonished regime officials that none of them was authorized to act against Mojtaba’s “definite opinion.” At the same time, the statement called on any Muslim “who could gain access” to kill Donald Trump—not quite the message of Iran’s negotiators, but rather more consonant with Mojtaba’s statements promising “blood revenge.”
The Iranian regime has existential choices to make as it decides between diplomacy and conflict. Iran’s constitution is clear about who has the authority to set the country’s course. But no one seems able to say for sure whether that person is alive or dead. And without a firm hand at the top, indecision can become a purgatory without a foreseeable end.

articles.title: Ukraine's Defense Forces struck the Afipsky Oil Refinery in Russia's Krasnodar Krai - Fire Point
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defense Forces struck the Afipsky Oil Refinery in Russia's Krasnodar Krai - Fire Point
Kyiv • UNN
The Ukrainian military struck the Afipsky Oil Refinery with FP-1 drones. Russian authorities reported a fire, damage to the railway station, and casualties.
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck the Afipsky Oil Refinery in Russia’s Krasnodar Krai overnight. According to local authorities, the railway station and the oil refinery were damaged, and there were casualties, UNN reports.
"Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck the Afipsky Oil Refinery in Russia’s Krasnodar Krai. The Afipsky Oil Refinery has a designed capacity of 6.25 million tonnes of oil per year and specializes in processing crude oil and gas condensate, producing gasoline, diesel fuel, and other petroleum products," reported Fire Point, whose FP-1 long-range drones are usually used for such attacks.
The governor of the Russian region said that debris had damaged the railway station and caused casualties, and that "a fire also broke out on the premises of the oil refinery."
We remind you
Using FP-1 long-range drones, Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck the Novokuibyshevsk Oil Refinery and the first logistics hub of the Russian marketplace Ozon in Russia’s Samara Region overnight on August 22. Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense noted that after the strikes on Wildberries, it was Ozon’s turn.
Earlier, Ukraine’s Defense Forces put out of operation most of the major logistics centers of the Russian marketplace Wildberries. One of the latest targets was the company’s logistics hub in the Koledino industrial park. It was Wildberries’ largest warehouse by area—250,000 sq. m.
According to analysts, the direct losses of Wildberries alone, which lost about 20% of its warehouse capacity within several weeks, could exceed 100 billion rubles ($1.24 billion), and in the worst-case scenario—200 billion ($2.45 billion). In addition, due to the outflow of sellers, many of whom instantly lost their businesses and goods worth hundreds of billions of rubles, Wildberries’ turnover has already fallen by a quarter.
The Bell reports that Wildberries’ total need for funds could reach 1.3 trillion rubles ($16.36 billion). The company will have to increase its debt by at least that amount. The marketplace has requested assistance from the state, but it is not yet clear how much funding will be provided, as the federal budget deficit has already reached 5.7 trillion rubles—1.5 times the plan for the entire year.
Fire Point CEO and CTO Iryna Terekh stated that Ukraine is capable of exerting a real impact on the enemy, and that Russians understand only the language of force.

articles.title: Kremlin adviser warns UK drone factories could face attacks
articles.body:
Kremlin adviser warns UK drone factories could face attacks
Russia says the UK’s decision to share missile blueprints with Ukraine is evidence of its direct military involvement in the war.
Factories manufacturing drones in the United Kingdom for export to Ukraine could come under attack from “unknown sources”, a Kremlin adviser has said, after Britain agreed to share long-range missile blueprints with Kyiv.
Andrei Fedorov, an adviser to the Kremlin and a former deputy foreign minister, told British broadcaster BBC on Tuesday that he could not “exclude 100 percent” that there might be some “semi-military” action against Britain, as UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham visited Ukraine.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Ukraine’s offensive against Russia causes petrol panic across Central Asia
- list 2 of 3UK to help Ukraine build Storm Shadow long-range missiles: Why it matters
- list 3 of 3Russia to seize poorly protected infrastructure amid Ukraine drone attacks
The UK shared missile blueprints with Ukraine for it to manufacture French-British designed long-missile drones during Burnham’s first overseas trip to Kyiv on Monday. Sharing these blueprints, according to the Russian adviser, is seen by Moscow as proof of the UK’s “direct military involvement” in the Russia-Ukraine war.
Fedorov said that “sooner or later, there might be not only verbal but maybe some visible reaction from Russia towards the UK”.
Asked to elaborate, he said: “There are different discussions how it should look like – it might be so-called technical reaction, maybe some hackers attack from unknown source, not from official level, of course.”
“There might be different political steps, and I cannot exclude 100 percent that there might be some semi-military.”
“For example, something might happen with enterprises, with the factories which are producing drones for Ukraine, etc.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov shared similar sentiments with reporters on Monday, stating that the UK is “participating in this war” by its missile support and that this is adding “fuel to the fire”.
Burnham responded in Kyiv by asking reporters who started the fire in the first place. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The UK has agreed to declassify blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French-produced version of the Storm Shadow that has already been used to hit targets in Russia.
The Scalp missile can hit targets that are heavily fortified, such as bunkers, unlike existing Ukrainian missiles. It has a range of about 240km (149 miles).
Ukraine has increased its production of cheaper drones significantly in the past year, attacking more economic and military targets within Russia.

articles.title: Qalibaf tells Asim Munir: US bad faith hinders regional stability
articles.body:
Qalibaf tells Asim Munir: US bad faith hinders regional stability
TEHRAN — Pakistan’s Chief of Defense Forces (CDF), Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, held talks with senior Iranian officials, including Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, in Tehran on Monday.
During the meeting, Qalibaf pointed to the US failure to honor its commitments under the memorandum of understanding President Donald Trump signed with Iran on June 17.
“The commitments made by both sides under the memorandum of understanding are clear. It was the United States’ failure to honor its commitments that undermined regional stability and gave us yet another reason not to trust Washington,” Qalibaf said.
Munir, for his part, said he would continue efforts to help restore regional peace. He arrived in Iran earlier on Monday.
The Pakistani-mediated MoU established framework terms to cease hostilities. While subsequent US aerial strikes and naval blockades disrupted the agreement, Pakistan had already demonstrated its diplomatic role by helping facilitate the April 8 ceasefire that paused the 39-day war that the US and Israel launched on Iran on February 28.
Tehran has repeatedly expressed its gratitude to Pakistan for its diplomatic support and conflict-resolution efforts during critical moments of crisis.  Beyond defense cooperation, economic partnership remains central to their bilateral relationship. Under comprehensive joint agreements, Tehran and Islamabad are actively expanding cross-border infrastructure, trade market access, and energy links. These initiatives aim to scale bilateral trade volume from over $3 billion to a targeted $10 billion, reflecting a mutual commitment to leveraging shared geography for long-term economic integration and regional peace.

articles.title: US launches ‘economic D-Day’ against Iran, threatens sanctions on its global partners
articles.body:
ALBAWABA- The United States on Monday launched what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent described as an “economic D-Day” against Iran, unveiling a sweeping campaign designed to cut Tehran off from international financial networks and choke the revenues sustaining its government and Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Bessent warned that no country, company or financial institution would be beyond the reach of US sanctions. He said Washington would target those helping Iran convert oil into cash, finance the government or IRGC, or facilitate transactions through the international financial system. Any institution found helping Iran launder money could be excluded from the US dollar system.
The campaign includes expanded secondary sanctions against foreign entities dealing with Iran. The Treasury announced measures against nearly 60 individuals and entities, including brokers, companies and vessels linked to Iran’s oil trade and shadow fleet across the United Arab Emirates, Hong Kong, Singapore, Switzerland, Europe and China. The new measures also focus on Iran-linked activities in digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping.
Bessent also delivered a direct warning to Iran’s trading partners, including China. He said every country would have a defined period to wind down activities identified by Washington, while stressing that the United States would not immediately impose a universal deadline because it wanted countries to have an opportunity to change course. “Our patience is not infinite,” he said.
The campaign comes after nearly six months of US-Iran conflict and amid a broader deadlock over efforts to end the war. Washington has sought to use military and economic pressure to force Tehran to make concessions, while Iran has continued to resist demands for capitulation. The US also faces the difficult task of enforcing secondary sanctions without triggering a major confrontation with China, Iran’s most important trading partner.
Iran’s economy is already under severe pressure. The Iranian rial fell to a record low on Monday, reaching about 2 million rials to the US dollar on the open market, as inflation, disrupted oil exports and the effects of the war intensified economic strain.
Iranian officials have rejected the US strategy, arguing that Washington has imposed sanctions for years without succeeding in collapsing the Iranian economy. Iran’s economic leadership says the country has developed mechanisms to circumvent sanctions and rebuild damaged industries, insisting that the latest US campaign will not sever the “arteries” of the Iranian economy.
Diplomatic activity has meanwhile intensified. Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, arrived in Tehran for talks aimed at helping break the deadlock between Iran and the United States. Oman is also pursuing a diplomatic channel. Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr Albusaidi is scheduled to visit Tehran on Tuesday for talks on the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: technical teams to agree schedule of next steps after decision on Storm Shadow technology
articles.body:
Following a positive decision to provide Ukraine with technology to produce Storm Shadow cruise missiles, technical teams will meet to agree a schedule of next steps, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said.
"We have positive news. I consider this strong positive news and a strong decision. We need to move forward on when this can happen. Right now, following the positive political decision, technical teams will meet and show us the schedule," Zelenskyy said at a press conference with Estonian President Alar Karis in Kyiv on Tuesday.
The head of state expressed hope that, following the positive response from the United Kingdom on Storm Shadow, "everything won’t get bogged down in the bureaucracies of our countries, and we will act."
In addition, according to the president, a schedule of meetings on the Freyja anti-ballistic project should be ready in 7-10 days, during which the sides are to identify problematic issues in cooperation with individual companies and countries and ways to resolve them.
"In 7-10 days we’ll have a schedule for Freyja, for when we’ll be meeting, where we’re facing blockages, with which company, with which country something isn’t working out. Because everyone is taking this very seriously. We will unblock everything," Zelenskyy said.
On Aug 24, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham confirmed he had approved a request to provide Ukraine with technology to produce Storm Shadow cruise missiles.
"The UK was the first to give Ukraine long-range weapons back in 2023. Now Volodymyr [Zelenskyy – Interfax-Ukraine] has asked us to share our Storm Shadow technology so that Ukraine can build up these capabilities on its own. I am pleased to confirm today that I have approved this request," Burnham said, speaking at the Coalition of the Willing summit meeting in Kyiv on Monday.

US President Donald Trump said the US Navy told him all mines have been cleared from the Strait of Hormuz in a Tuesday Truth Social post.

articles.title: China urges US not to disrupt its cooperation with Iran amid fresh sanctions
articles.body:
Riyaz ul Khaliq
25 August 2026•Update: 25 August 2026
China on Tuesday urged the US not to disrupt its cooperation with Iran after Washington announced “Operation Economic Outcast,” a sweeping campaign intended to completely isolate Tehran from the global financial system.
“China’s cooperation with Iran is conducted within the framework of international law and should not be disrupted,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian told reporters in Beijing.
He warned that the new US sanctions risk disrupting the global financial order, stressing the need for the warring sides to hold talks to end the conflict.
“Economic wars and maximum pressure are not the solution,” Lin said, when asked about the new sanctions regime launched by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday.
Lin said such moves “will only lead to escalation and risks of spillover, which will disrupt the global economic and financial order and harm the legitimate interests of other countries.”
“The pressing task is to facilitate de-escalation and return to dialogue and negotiations as soon as possible,” said the spokesman, stressing that China “will take necessary measures to safeguard its rights and interests.”
China is one of the largest importers of Iranian oil as the two countries maintain a “comprehensive strategic partnership,” driven primarily by economic ties and discounted energy imports.
Bilateral trade volume climbed to over $41 billion last year.
Stating that China "is closely monitoring the developments," Lin reiterated China’s “firm opposition to illicit, unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law or the authorization of the UN Security Council.”
US Treasury Secretary Bessent said the US “objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone.”
The US is “no longer managing the Iranian threat” but rather “ending it,” Bessent said, adding that the “strength of America's economy” enabled Washington to conduct such a financial offensive alongside military operations.
Also on China, Bessent said: “The best way to engage with countries is through quiet diplomacy,” adding that the US was currently “level setting” expectations with Beijing.

articles.title: Swedish military seeks to take over Russian-owned estate near naval base
articles.body:
Swedish military seeks to take over Russian-owned estate near naval base
- Published
Sweden's armed forces have asked the government to expropriate a Russia-owned property near a naval base on security grounds.
The military requested the seizure of the beach plot near Muskö base in Stockholm archipelago, citing "the threat from Russian drones and the ownership situation of the property".
Swedish reports say a businessman with links to the Russian state, has been building a luxury house on Muskö island – although his wife, who holds both Russian and Swedish citizenship, is the registered owner.
Two years ago, Sweden ended two centuries of military non-alignment and joined Nato because of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In its statement, the military said the location had "unique conditions for strengthening the defence of Muskö Naval Base, particularly against drones".
The development of Russian drone warfare has "changed the threat landscape for Sweden", the military added.
Public broadcaster SVT said the property has been "a thorn in the armed forces' side".
Defence Minister Pål Jonson said the country needed to "make sure there's no risk of anyone gaining visibility into the site or any kind of tactical edge", Sweden's TV4 reported.
The armed forces' statement quoted Chief of the Defence Staff Carl-Johan Edström as saying that Sweden was "facing the most serious security situation since the end of World War Two".
It is unclear whether the Russian businessman is currently living in Sweden.
His wife is reported to have owned the property since 2017.
